text:
Law or Economics: Why the Latest Bar Examination Results Deserve Greater Scrutiny

By Joel Abdulai Kallon @KallonJoel 

I have no difficulty with the proposition that admission to the legal profession should be demanding. Lawyers are entrusted with people’s liberty, property and livelihoods, and the public has every right to expect that those who qualify have demonstrated the competence their work requires. But I would want considerably more information before accepting that a large number of failures demonstrates the quality of a professional school.

When I questioned the presentation of the 2022 #WASSCE results, my concern was with the explanations attached to the numbers. That principle applies equally to disappointing examination results. High pass rates do not, by themselves, establish educational success just as low pass rates do not establish professional rigour. Both require a careful examination of the conditions under which students were selected, taught and assessed. 

The latest reported #SierraLeone Law School Bar Final results deserve precisely that examination. Truth Media reported on 12 November that 641 candidates sat, with 120 passing outright, 306 failing and 170 required to resit one or two modules. A close source who is familiar with happenings at the school told me that the pass rate was initially much lower with only 84 students hiting the pass mark, prompting an adjustment of grades that took the number to 122. But let’s stick with the @TruthmediaSL figures.

The three examination outcomes add up to 596; including the absentees brings the total to 641. If these categories are complete and separate, 596 actually sat. The implied proportions would then be 20.1% passing outright, 51.3% failing outright and 28.5% referred. These are provisional calculations from the reported figures, and the Council of Legal Education needs to clarify them.

Even with those qualifications, the reported outcome warrants an explanation. Were these all first-time candidates, or were some returning after an earlier unsuccessful attempt?

The admission question deserves particular attention. The School describes its programme as a one-year course designed to prepare candidates for the final examination and the practical work of a solicitor or barrister. An entrance examination covering core legal subjects was also announced for the 2025/2026 intake. Selection and preparation are therefore part of the institution’s responsibilities, and both belong in any examination of these results. 

Surely, admitting a candidate to such a programme should reflect a considered judgment that the person has a reasonable prospect of reaching the required standard through the training available. It cannot be a guarantee of qualification. Students must still study, attend classes and take responsibility for their work. But a fair admission process should also mean that the institution has considered what it can reasonably achieve with the people it accepts.

If the explanation for widespread failure is that students lacked essential foundations, the Council should explain how its admission process identifies those weaknesses and what follows. Did admission assessments for the 2026 intake reveal difficulties that could have been addressed? If the weaknesses were foreseeable, discovering their consequences only at the final examination would be a costly way of managing them.

An entrance examination also needs to measure the abilities required to benefit from the course. Making it harder would not necessarily make it more useful. And even an appropriate selection process can produce an unsustainable intake if the institution accepts more students than it can adequately teach. A lecture room may accommodate additional chairs without creating additional opportunities for practical work, individual feedback or help with difficult material.

This brings me to the economics of the arrangement. How are admission numbers determined? By the number of candidates the School can realistically prepare for qualification, or by the number whose fees are required to sustain its operations? Those considerations may sometimes coincide but what happens when they do not?

There is a documented history that makes this a reasonable question. Parliament’s record of 14 December 2023 includes a committee account that problems with government allocations had left the School depending on tuition fees for some staff and administrative costs. It recorded revenue of Le7,750,650 in 2023 against a Le7.5 million target, with the Director attributing the excess to higher fees. The revenue target for 2024 was Le9 million. 

The same sitting also contains an unmissable qualification from the the  Finance Minister Sheku Fantamadi Bangura that allocations covering half the year had been provided and the remainder was being processed. He also said the Ministry was monitoring fee income and balancing it against the public resources provided to the School. 

While that exchange does not establish the School’s current funding position, or prove that revenue determined the admission decisions affecting these candidates, it nevertheless establishes the importance of fees in the financing discussion.

The potential incentive is straightforward. If an institution relies heavily on fees to meet its expenses, admitting fewer students may create a financial problem. The temptation may then be to increase numbers without a corresponding expansion in teaching and support. The final examination can remain demanding while the decisions made at admission leave too many candidates inadequately prepared to meet it.

Within such an arrangement, an institution could collect fees, enforce its exit standard and still have serious questions to answer about the educational opportunity it provided. As an accountability issue therefore, It should be able to explain why it believed it could successfully train the people it accepted, and what it actually provided after accepting their fees. A demanding final examination would not, on its own, answer those questions.

Nor should that question be answered simply by insisting that professional education costs money. Of course it does. Qualified instructors, learning materials and practical training require resources. If public funding is inadequate or unreliable, government should account for its contribution to the problem. But financial difficulty cannot make it reasonable to admit students whose needs the programme has no credible capacity to meet.

There have also been specific allegations involving admissions and money. In March, the Council reportedly alleged unauthorised admissions and collection of funds outside approved procedures. The then director denied the allegations. A September report described the subsequent inquiry as unfinished.

Tuition fees for new entrants in the 2026 year was NLe 45,000 up from NLe 39,000 the previous year.

The reported charge for the current reference exams also increased from NLe 1500 in 2025 to NLe 2,000 per subject for the 170 or so students who are required to resit. Fees for a recently introduced entrance examination also spiked from about NLe 500 last year to a reported NLe 2000 in 2026.
 
First and foremost, such dramatic cost changes almost yearly  makes the economics of this conversation difficult to ignore. Even more importantly,  very little is often done by the  School to explain how it arrived at those figure and what the charges actually cover. Resit examinations, for instance, cost money to organise, and the fee alone proves nothing about anyone’s motives. But students (and perhaps the parents, friends and families that often have to come together to pay those fees) are entitled to know what they are paying for, particularly when they are being asked to pay more each year. 

For a student who needs to repeat or resit examinations, the cost can extend beyond another payment. It may include additional accommodation and transport, delayed employment and further demands on family resources. Where those costs arise from weaknesses in admission or teaching that could reasonably have been addressed, treating the outcome solely as the student’s failure would be difficult to defend.

The handling of the results raises another more immediate concern. Reporting on the School’s November notice says candidates who did not receive an email could have failed, supplied incorrect or missing email details, or owed fees. The Sierra Leone Bar Association subsequently — and rightly so — called for individual written results and a formal complaints procedure. A candidate should not have to work out an examination outcome from an email that never arrived. 

The School was reported to have emailed results on 7 November, with resit exams due to begin on 16 November. That is a nine-day interval. For candidates still seeking confirmation of their results, there are practical questions about preparation and the opportunity to have an error corrected before the next examination. Private notification is perfectly compatible with public accountability, provided every candidate receives a clear result and can obtain a timely review and that there are no ulterior motives for not publishing the anonymized results as has been customary. 

The Council can lead a review process by examining what it already knows about these candidates. Their admission qualifications and entrance scores should be considered alongside their performance during training and in the final examinations. If candidates who entered with strong foundations also failed widely, that would require scrutiny of teaching and assessment. If difficulty was concentrated among entrants whose weaknesses were already apparent, selection and support would require closer attention. That exercise would help the public to ask more precise questions than the overall failure rate permits.

It would also be in the interest of transparency and accountability for the School to consider releasing result summaries by subject and comparable outcomes across several years, distinguishing initial results from those after resits. Those figures should be considered alongside intake numbers, teaching resources and financial accounts. If the School admits more students and collects more fees, what additional instruction and support does that income purchase? That is a question the institution should be able to answer with records.

The appropriate response may include better admission assessments, preparatory teaching, stronger support during the course or an intake that reflects available capacity. Where the examination itself has weaknesses, those should be corrected. None of this requires awarding qualifications to candidates who have not demonstrated the necessary competence. It requires finding out why so many reportedly did not, and acting on the explanation.

I would be reluctant to accept an account of these results that placed the entire burden on students while leaving the institution’s decisions unexamined. The School has a responsibility to uphold the standard for legal practice. It must also account for its high admission numbers, the preparation it offers the people it admits and the use it makes of the fees they pay.

Citizens who will eventually entrust their freedom or property to these graduates have an interest in both their competence and the integrity of the system that produces them. The Council should now account for its own decisions with the same seriousness that it expects candidates to bring to their examinations.

Joel Abdulai Kallon is CEO of @AnalyticsMeraki, a research and analytics consulting firm based in Sierra Leone.

text:
Some of the most powerful prayers Heaven ever hears don't come out sounding like prayers at all.
Sometimes they sound like a cracked Hallelujah.
Sometimes they're whispered through tears, spoken in the middle of the night, or buried so deep in your heart that you can't find the words to say them.
And sometimes all you can manage is, "Jesus, please."
But hear me…
God doesn't need you to have the right words to hear your heart.
He hears the prayers you can't speak.
He sees the heartache behind the smile.
He knows the weight you're carrying, even when everyone else thinks you're doing just fine.
And just because you can't see Him moving doesn't mean He's standing still.
He's moving in the waiting.
He's working through the pain.
He's making a way where you can't see one yet.
The same hands that formed the mountains, hung the stars, and breathed life into creation are still reaching down to hold you today.
So cast those burdens on the Savior.
You don't have to carry what He has already offered to carry for you.
You don't have to have perfect faith. You just have to bring Him what little faith you have.
Even if it's trembling.
Even if it's broken.
Even if all you have left is a cracked Hallelujah.
He hears you. He sees you. He hasn't left you. And He's not finished writing your story.
Your prayer doesn't have to be pretty to reach Heaven.
Sometimes the most beautiful Hallelujah is the one you sing with tears in your eyes and a broken heart that still believes God is good.

🐂Chelsey Nelms

text:
Who wanted Nvidia’s Huang out? ‘Honeypot’ scandal raises questions over AI power struggle
Jensen Huang’s exit removes a powerful opponent of US chip restrictions, exposing divisions in Washington over how to preserve America’s technological dominance
Published 13 Nov, 2026 (fFULL)
https://t.co/7HAvq0pxTJ
The downfall of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang in a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy has raised a politically explosive question: who benefits from the removal of one of Washington’s most influential critics of chip restrictions on China?
Huang resigned on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, former head of Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Anonymous US intelligence officials reportedly suspect that she was recruited by Beijing to potentially influence the Nvidia CEO to push Washington to ease AI chip export restrictions.
The scandal came at a pivotal moment in the US-China technology war, just days before a planned summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. With congressional hawks already pushing for tougher restrictions, the timing of Huang’s downfall has fueled questions about the political interests served by his resignation.
RT examines the intrigue surrounding Huang’s exit and the struggle for control of the global AI industry.
So who benefits from Huang’s departure?
Huang’s resignation removes one of Washington’s most prominent advocates of keeping China connected to American AI technology, potentially handing China hawks a major political advantage. The Nvidia founder repeatedly warned that cutting Beijing off from American technology would accelerate China’s push for independence. In a May interview with Fox Business, he pointed to Huawei’s growing influence: “They’re flourishing in our absence.”
His exit has immediately intensified congressional demands for tighter export controls and investigations into Nvidia’s China dealings.
Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, has seized on the scandal to question whether whether Chinese intelligence had obtained sensitive information through Huang or influenced US technology policy.
“[Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls,” Moolenaar said. “This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast has also pushed for stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent chip smuggling and restrict access to advanced semiconductor equipment.
Trump defended Huang as a “very honorable guy” and said he believed the executive’s denial that he knew Alice Huang was allegedly involved in espionage. However, the controversy appears to have given advocates of tougher restrictions on China fresh ammunition against one of their most influential opponents.
Who benefits more – China hawks or AI rivals?
Huang’s abrupt exit has also raised questions over whether rival American technology firms could benefit from his downfall.
Independent journalist Lee Fang suggested rival US AI companies could gain, pointing to Huang’s support for cheaper Chinese open-source models that threaten established American competitors. He drew parallels with earlier campaigns targeting Huawei and TikTok.
Venice AI founder Erik Voorhees went further, calling Huang’s removal a “coup.”
Journalist Glenn Greenwald questioned whether extramarital affairs alone explained the removal of one of America’s most powerful technology executives.
“I don’t know who wanted Jensen Huang out but I know that whoever it was wields extreme levels of power,” he wrote on X.
The resignation also provoked a backlash across Silicon Valley. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao called it “a mistake,” Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney described it as “a sad day,” and Elon Musk said hiring Huang would be “an honor.”
“Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the US and the western world,” wrote Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado.
The media has some questions to answer
Questions have emerged over how the story reached the press. New York Times reporter Tripp Mickle, who helped break the story of Huang’s affair, revealed on The Daily podcast that he and colleague Ana Swanson began investigating Megaspeed after receiving a tip from an unnamed technology industry contact.
The disclosure reinforces suspicions that journalists may have been deliberately steered toward Megaspeed, raising questions about who supplied the tip – and why.
What did Washington know – and when?
The intrigue deepened following reports that senior US officials knew about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang months before the scandal erupted.
According to Axios, a highly classified intelligence memorandum overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated before Trump’s May visit to China. Based on surveillance of Alice Huang and an investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, the warning reportedly reached Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Rubio also reportedly briefed Trump.
Megaspeed operates AI computing infrastructure, allowing customers to rent access to powerful Nvidia processors outside China – a potential route around restrictions on shipping advanced chips directly to the country.
Washington was also approving direct sales to Chinese buyers. In May Reuters reported that around ten Chinese companies had been cleared to purchase Nvidia’s H200 processors, although deliveries had not begun. The approvals were separate from the Megaspeed investigation, and their precise timing relative to the intelligence warning remains unclear.
The dispute reportedly reached the highest levels of the Trump administration. Axios reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over his failure to blacklist Megaspeed despite repeated warnings. The Commerce Department denied the confrontation ever happened and Lutnick now faces congressional scrutiny over his department’s handling of chip exports and suspected diversion to China.
If Washington had been warned months earlier, why did the allegations become a public crisis only now?
How did Singapore become entangled in the scandal
Singaporean authorities had been investigating Alice Huang’s former company, Megaspeed International, long before her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence became central to the scandal surrounding Nvidia’s founder.
In a statement Thursday, Singapore’s Home Affairs Ministry said police began investigating Megaspeed in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving servers shipped through Singapore to Malaysia.
Alice Huang was questioned and had her passport seized in June 2025. By February 2026, however, investigators found insufficient evidence that she had committed the suspected offenses. She received a warning for knowingly providing inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed and was barred from re-entering Singapore.
Notably, Singapore stressed that she had never been investigated for espionage.
Meanwhile, the alleged Chinese spy narrative has come under growing scrutiny in Washington itself.
According to CNN, US intelligence officials remain divided over whether the evidence establishes that Alice Huang worked for Beijing. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that the Justice Department had reached “no conclusions” about her alleged intelligence ties.
The assessments leave a fundamental question unanswered: how did an unproven espionage allegation gain such traction despite the lack of conclusive evidence?
Why is Nvidia central to US technological dominance?
Founded by Huang in 1993, Nvidia has become the leading supplier of advanced processors powering the global AI boom.
Its chips and software underpin data centers and AI systems worldwide, making the company a strategic asset in Washington’s competition with Beijing.
By controlling exports of advanced processors and semiconductor technology, the US can influence which countries gain access to the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge AI.
Washington argues the restrictions are necessary to prevent China from strengthening its military and intelligence capabilities. Critics see a broader strategy of technological containment aimed at preserving American economic and geopolitical dominance.
That is what made Huang’s position so consequential: he challenged a central instrument of Washington’s effort to maintain its lead over China.
Could US chip restrictions hand China the advantage?
Washington’s campaign to contain China’s technological rise risks achieving the opposite: accelerating Beijing’s drive to build an AI industry beyond American control.
Chinese firms, including Huawei, are developing domestic alternatives to US processors, while Beijing is pushing for technological self-reliance.
In an August regulatory filing, Nvidia warned that US export controls, combined with Chinese restrictions, had effectively excluded it from China’s data-center computing market.
The company argued that its exclusion was allowing competitors to expand their developer and customer networks, potentially challenging American technology worldwide.
That was the central contradiction Huang repeatedly highlighted: cutting China off from Nvidia could weaken American influence while strengthening Chinese competitors.
Washington’s national security hawks argue the opposite – that selling powerful processors to Beijing risks advancing its military and technological capabilities.
Huang’s departure removes a prominent voice from that debate, but not the dilemma: could Washington’s efforts to preserve its technological supremacy ultimately help China escape American dominance?
Who will take control of Nvidia now?
Huang’s resignation has triggered a leadership crisis at Nvidia. According to Wired, an internal post urging the board to consider employee sentiment attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supporting Huang’s return.
Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor.
According to Reuters, Kress and Nvidia veteran Ian Buck, a key figure behind its CUDA computing platform, are among the possibilities. Other names floated include Arm CEO Rene Haas and AMD chief Lisa Su. On Polymarket, Buck has also emerged among the leading contenders, alongside Jensen Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, who serves at Nvidia as senior marketing director, and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, although betting odds offer no indication of the board’s intentions.
Trump has also weighed in, endorsing former Apple CEO Tim Cook, now executive chairman, declaring on Truth Social that “a Legend replaces a Legend.”
The succession debate has extended to Israel, where media have floated Nvidia technology chief Michael Kagan, Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, and Apple‘s Srouji. All three have strong ties to the Israeli technology sector.
Whoever succeeds Huang will inherit a company caught in the escalating US-China technology confrontation, with the stakes extending far beyond the boardroom. Huang’s replacement will have to choose whether to continue advocating for keeping China within the American technology ecosystem or bring Nvidia closer to Washington’s advocates of tougher restrictions.
The broader question, meanwhile, is not simply who replaces Huang, but whether his departure will also mark a fundamental shift in America’s AI strategy.

Something we sometimes hear from anglers who favor industrial offshore wind: “…but the pilings create artificial reefs.” They cite the amazing fishing around oil platforms in the Gulf of America.

Let’s talk about that for a second. 

First, artificial reefs can provide excellent habitat for marine life, but they don't become mature, thriving ecosystems overnight. Depending on the materials, location, depth, and environmental conditions, it can take several years or even decades for a diverse marine community to develop.

Second, offshore wind turbines create significant obstacles to navigation. Their foundations, connecting cables, maintenance requirements, and safety restrictions complicate navigation and fishing operations. Many offshore wind facilities impose 500-foot safety or restricted-access zones around individual structures, although the specific restrictions vary by project and jurisdiction.

Their foundations, connecting cables, maintenance requirements, and safety restrictions complicate navigation and fishing operations. Many offshore wind facilities impose 500-foot safety or restricted-access zones around individual structures, although the specific restrictions vary by project and jurisdiction.

Third, offshore wind turbine foundations use protective coatings, including zinc-rich primers, and may employ sacrificial anodes made from aluminum-, zinc-, or other metal-based alloys to prevent corrosion. These materials release metals into the surrounding marine environment as they corrode, which are ingested by marine life. 

Fourth, the United States already has a substantial inventory of inactive vessels that could be considered for artificial reef projects. The Maritime Administration's National Defense Reserve Fleet contains approximately 100 government-owned vessels, including 43 ships in the Ready Reserve Force. Not all are available for disposal, of course, but the inventory illustrates the potential supply of vessels that could be evaluated for reef deployment. 
Consider the recently scuttled SS United States, which was intentionally sunk off Florida on November 11, 2026, to create what is now the world's largest artificial reef. Its enormous steel structure will provide an intricate habitat with countless nooks, crannies, and sheltered spaces for marine organisms and fish. 

Why not make greater use of properly cleaned, environmentally prepared decommissioned ships to create artificial reefs? They offer substantial structural habitat without introducing hundreds of permanent industrial structures into busy fishing and navigation areas.

'They Put My Testicles In Bolt Cutters': White Farmer Details Terrifying Attack In South Africa That Left Wife's Breasts Scarred | Tyler Durden, Zerohedge

A white South African game farmer says three gunmen tortured him and his wife for about three hours at their cottage near Hartbeespoort Dam, cutting around her nipples with a knife and tin snips and clamping his testicles in a bolt cutter, before shoving his own AK-47 into his mouth and pulling the trigger. It misfired.

"That AK-47 has been faulty for the last two years. It never fires the last round. It didn't go off, otherwise I would have been dead now," Les Brett, an anti-poaching ranger and founder of the Dung Beetle Bush School, told The Citizen in an interview published Thursday.

Brett said three men came through a sliding door of the couple's home on the game farm in Broederstroom, North West province, at about 7:30 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1, and moved "with almost military precision. Within two seconds, I had a gun to my head and a gun to my stomach."

The men tied the couple's hands behind their backs and their feet together, blindfolded them, stuffed rags into their mouths and began beating them while demanding the keys to the safe and money. About half an hour in, one of them took off Brett's blindfold so he could see his wife, Natasha, lying next to him. Their clothes had been cut off.

"They wanted me to see what they were doing to my wife. They were cutting around her nipples with a knife and tin snips. They also had a bolt cutter and put my testicles in it," Brett said. "All this to intimidate and scare us. Eventually I told them where the key to the safe was."

Once the attackers had the guns from the safe, they wanted cash. They kept demanding "the million," threw the couple into the safe and poured boiling water on them, Brett said. He offered them his cars and offered to withdraw money from an ATM; they refused both and insisted on "the millions in the house that we didn't have." Between the beatings, he has said, they also shocked the couple with a taser.

"They then said I had to die, and pulled the trigger on the AK-47, but it misfired," he told The Citizen.

The men fled when a guard on patrol came by to check on the farm's water pump. "They just closed the safe door and disappeared," Brett said. Natasha freed herself and then him, and he went to the farm's main house to call for help.

Brett, who has spent more than four decades in the bush in conservation and anti-poaching training, said his head and knee were smashed with the bolt cutters and his hip is fractured. "We are okay. Natasha is a strong woman. I am still in pain."

Natasha was not raped, Brett told South African YouTuber Riaan Roux, correcting reports that said she was; she is 58, not 68 as first reported. He has said the men threatened her with sexual violence but did not carry it out.

Police registered the case as a house robbery. North West police spokesperson Sgt. Kelebogile Morake said the men took seven licensed firearms and ammunition from the safe, and provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Arthur Peter Adams condemned the attack. No arrests had been reported as of Nov. 12.

The Broederstroom raid came four days after Donovan Marx, a 50-year-old cattle farmer between Potchefstroom and Ventersdorp, was shot in the upper body, dragged into his house, tied with cable ties, stabbed and beaten, police spokesperson Capt. Majang Skalkie told TimesLIVE. His attackers cut off both of his earlobes, according to EWN. Police have since arrested five suspects, aged 26 to 56, on charges of house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.

On Oct. 5, 55-year-old Hannetjie van Zyl died after she was attacked with an iron bar at the gate of her farmhouse near Ottosdal. "The use of firearms and the brutal assault of an individual in the course of a robbery are serious criminal acts that will not be tolerated," Adams said of the Marx attack.

Pretoria's line is that farm attacks are ordinary violent crime, not a campaign against white South Africans. The Trump administration disagrees: Trump cut off US aid to South Africa in February 2025 and offered white farmers a fast track to the US, as we reported, and the first Afrikaner refugees left for America that May. Last week Washington said it will suspend South Africa from the duty-free African Growth and Opportunity Act from Jan. 1, 2027.

"They stole seven firearms, two cellphones and a laptop, but left cameras worth over R200,000, jewelry, wallets, cars," Brett said, rejecting the police's label. "This is a targeted farm attack. Nobody gets tortured for three hours, scalded with boiling water, in a house robbery."

The longer record is worse. On May 1 he wrote to Congress that hostilities had terminated. On July 10 he notified Congress that hostilities had resumed. In between and since, the blockade has held, a new task force stood up on November 7 to squeeze Iran's shipping, American strikes around Hormuz continued, and Tehran blames Washington for the strike on the Sirik communications tower that drew Iran's drone answer at Bahrain yesterday. His own intelligence agencies, per Reuters, assess that renewed strikes would not move Tehran's demands anyway. So the pause on offer is a pause he already announced once this year before unannouncing it, conditional on no provocations, with provocation defined in Washington, while the machinery of the war runs at full speed underneath it. Believe the record. The record says the bombing stops when it stops, and not one briefing sooner.

Reports that the United States offered Ukraine NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from the Donbas portray an exploratory question as a credible proposal. The circumstances suggest a different purpose: testing whether Ukraine is prepared to give up territory without first securing a commitment to the NATO membership supposedly offered in return.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said American negotiators asked, for the first time, whether Ukraine would withdraw from the Donbas if it joined NATO. He also said there is no finalized proposal and that the details of a broader security package remain under discussion.

The distinction matters because the United States cannot deliver NATO membership on its own. Admission requires the agreement of every alliance member. There is no indication that Washington has secured that agreement or that the Trump administration has committed itself to supporting Ukraine’s accession.

More fundamentally, Putin has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine abandon its NATO ambitions. Following his November 12 meeting with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Russian officials reiterated their demands for an end to NATO expansion and a return toward the alliance’s 1997 configuration. The American envoys were therefore aware of Moscow’s position when the question was raised.

Against that background, the question looks like a way to determine whether Ukraine might withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donbas under certain conditions, rather than giving a firm “ні,” “нет,” or “no.”

If Ukraine signaled flexibility, Washington would gain a potential Ukrainian concession that could be leveraged during subsequent negotiations, with no guarantee that it would hold up its end of the bargain.

Zelenskyy very shrewdly did not agree to withdraw. Instead, he said that if the United States and its NATO partners confirmed a concrete security package, he would put it before the Ukrainian people. He also said Ukraine would not recognize occupied territory as Russian.

The most credible interpretation is that the United States is probing Ukraine’s willingness to make a territorial concession while offering something it cannot unilaterally deliver.

text:
Impeach Hegseth Before More Damage Is Done

Listen · 17:02 min
12NOV2026
By David French
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/32AT96ok1k

Pete Hegseth has violated federal law, he’s violated the laws of war, he’s violated the Constitution, and he should be impeached, convicted, removed from power and barred from serving in federal office ever again.

Sadly, however, the first effort to impeach Hegseth has failed, at least for now. The lame duck Republican-controlled Congress voted 211 to 204 to essentially kill impeachment by referring the charges to a committee, where it will undoubtedly die — unless Democrats revive the effort in 2027.

They should. Impeaching Hegseth isn’t a matter of retribution or vengeance. It’s about imposing accountability for an unconstitutional war. But even more is at stake — impeaching and convicting Hegseth would help restore the primacy of Congress in the American government.

Last month, I wrote that Hegseth should be impeached, and in response I received a number of messages asking a fair question, even from people who very much oppose the Trump administration and Hegseth’s actions as secretary of defense: Why Hegseth in particular? What are the high crimes and misdemeanors he’s guilty of that require his removal?

Let me answer that question in detail.

As a starting point, we’ll turn to the failed resolution filed by Thomas Massie, the eccentric outgoing Republican representative from Kentucky. It contains eight separate charges against Hegseth.

The first three are directly related to the decision to wage the Iran war, accusing Hegseth of attacking Iran without congressional authorization, continuing the war after Congress voted to terminate hostilities and still fighting the war after the 60-day expiration period defined by the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 act of Congress that was supposed to sharply limit the president’s ability to wage war unilaterally.

Two charges are directly related to Hegseth’s conduct of hostilities, accusing him of ignoring laws that are designed to minimize civilian casualties and engaging in extrajudicial killings in his lethal campaign against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Massie’s resolution also accuses Hegseth of violating the free speech rights of Senator Mark Kelly (a retired Navy pilot and former astronaut) by attempting to punish Kelly for making a video with several other Democratic lawmakers that said service members had a duty to defy unlawful orders.

The final two charges accuse Hegseth of kidnapping Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores of Venezuela and of waging war against the Houthis in Yemen without congressional authorization.

I want to focus on what are, in my view, the three most important charges: the claims that Hegseth defied the War Powers Resolution in the decision to attack Iran and wage protracted war against Iran.

But first, it’s important to state (or restate) that impeachment is a political remedy for misconduct in office. It is not a criminal trial. It does not require proof beyond a reasonable doubt that an executive branch official committed a felony to merit impeachment or conviction.

High crimes and misdemeanors are whatever Congress says they are, but that does not mean that Congress should exercise unbounded authority and use impeachment as a means of targeting political enemies.

If Congress is going to impeach and convict a member of the cabinet, it is prudent to do so for concrete, obvious violations of federal law or other forms of extreme misconduct. And there are few abuses of power more extreme than waging war in defiance of the Constitution and Congress.

But first, a bit of background.

The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973 in response to Richard Nixon’s extraordinary use of power during the Vietnam War. Nixon notoriously conducted a secret bombing campaign in Cambodia during the war, for example. The resolution was designed to strike a balance between Congress’s exclusive power to declare war and the president’s exclusive authority to command the armed forces.

Presidents don’t have to wait for Congress to act to order troops into combat when they’re being attacked or when an attack is imminent. American forces, for example, were already engaged in large-scale combat with Japanese forces before Congress declared war on Dec. 8, 1941. They had a right to respond to Japanese attacks.

But the existence of an emergency should not permit the president to circumvent Congress for an indefinite or protracted period of time.

The War Powers Resolution squares that circle. If a president initiates military action, he has 48 hours to inform the speaker of the House and the president pro tempore of the Senate.
That notification then triggers a 60-day clock. If Congress doesn’t authorize the military action, the president has to terminate unauthorized hostilities. If Congress passes a concurrent resolution in both houses, the president still has to terminate hostilities.

As of today, the president hasn’t sought a declaration of war, the 60-day clock has expired and both houses of Congress have passed Concurrent Resolution 86, requiring the president to terminate the war. In other words, the Trump administration is in open defiance of the War Powers Resolution.

Presidents of both parties have long argued that the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. They’ve claimed it encroaches on the president’s inherent authority to command the armed forces. But — and I cannot emphasize this enough — that is not the president’s call to make.

The Supreme Court has not explicitly ruled on the constitutionality of the resolution, and it probably will not. For generations it has avoided deciding interbranch disputes regarding the use of the armed forces. That means it is up to Congress to assert its authority. It cannot rely on voluntary presidential compliance. It cannot rely on Supreme Court intervention.

If Congress wants to enforce its authority, it has two primary levers: funding and impeachment. And between those two, impeachment is the far better remedy. It is better to remove a lawless secretary of defense from office than it is to defund the troops under his command.

In fact, I’d argue that if Congress wants to reclaim its constitutional role as the sole entity that can declare war, it is a constitutional necessity to impeach and convict senior members of the Trump administration (if not Trump himself) for waging war with Iran.

Reserving the power to declare war to Congress was no minor matter. As Abraham Lincoln wrote all the way back in 1848: “Kings had always been involving and impoverishing their people in wars, pretending generally, if not always, that the good of the people was the object. This our convention understood to be the most oppressive of all kingly oppressions and they resolved to so frame the Constitution that no one man should hold the power of bringing this oppression upon us.”

In addition, as I’ve written before, it is simply wrong to say that the Constitution creates three coequal branches of government. In our representative democracy, the most representative branch of government — Congress — is supposed to reign supreme.

Yes, other branches can certainly check it. (No branch of government has unchecked power.) Presidents can veto legislation. Courts exercise the power of judicial review of congressional statutes. But Congress alone possesses the power of the purse. Congress alone possesses the power to declare war. And Congress alone can impeach and remove presidents, cabinet officials and federal judges.

One of the central problems of our democracy is that generations of congressional abdication of power to the executive branch have turned the structure upside down. It is that presidents have reigned supreme. It’s destabilizing our country. Presidents were never intended to be kings — far from it.

I can think of few better ways for Congress to reassert its place in American government than by removing a secretary of defense who shares responsibility for the most outrageous act of constitutional defiance in warmaking in modern American history.

Against these charges, Hegseth can offer two primary defenses. First, that the administration did nothing wrong or unusual. And second, that he was simply following orders. In other words, Congress, you’re going after the wrong guy.

The first defense relies on the argument that the Trump administration was merely following modern precedents set by other presidents. President Barack Obama, for example, did not receive congressional approval before launching airstrikes against Libya in 2011. Nor did he receive specific congressional approval for his anti-ISIS military operations in 2014.

I also think that Obama should have sought congressional approval before ordering both military actions, but there are very substantial legal differences between the Trump administration’s war against Iran and Obama’s campaigns against Libya and ISIS.

In Libya, NATO forces operated under the authority of a United Nations Security Council resolution authorizing the use of force. The U.N. Charter is a Senate-ratified treaty (in much the same way that the North Atlantic Treaty, which created NATO, is Senate ratified) that empowers the use of military force. In addition, Congress never used its authority under the War Powers Resolution to attempt to terminate hostilities in Libya.

The ISIS mission was conducted under the auspices of two congressional authorizations for the use of force, the 2001 authorization for use of military force against Al Qaeda (in 2004, the precursor to ISIS — Al Qaeda in Iraq — essentially merged with Al Qaeda) and the 2002 authorization for use of force in Iraq, which allowed U.S. forces to “defend the national security of the United States against the continuing threat posed by Iraq.”

In reality, presidents have repeatedly sought congressional approval for prolonged military action, and no modern president before Trump has faced — much less defied — a concurrent resolution requiring an end to a war.
President George H.W. Bush notified Congress in accordance with the War Powers Resolution when he ordered the invasion of Panama in 1989 and ended combat operations before the expiration of the 60-day clock.

In fact, in February 1990, the House passed a resolution declaring that Bush had “acted decisively and appropriately in ordering United States forces to intervene in Panama.”

Bush also obtained congressional approval and a U.N. Security Council resolution authorizing Operation Desert Storm.

President George W. Bush received congressional approval for both the Afghanistan and Iraq wars. His decision to obtain congressional approval for the invasion of Iraq was particularly notable. His own Department of Justice told him it was unnecessary, but he disagreed and went to Congress anyway.

What about Hegseth’s claim that he was merely following orders? In a combative news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth said that every operation in Iran, South America, the Caribbean and Yemen was a “lawful operation ordered by the commander in chief, then ordered by myself.”

It is true that Trump bears primary responsibility for the military operations executed under his command. He deserves impeachment and conviction as well. But Trump does not bear exclusive responsibility.

To make this point, I’m going to turn to the Nuremberg trials. But I want to be very clear: I do not believe that Hegseth’s violations of the law are in any way comparable in scope or savagery to the conduct of Nazis in World War II. I am comparing legal principles, not atrocities.

The Nuremberg trials established a legal principle that’s applicable beyond Hitler’s Germany: Powerful subordinates can and should be held accountable for waging war without legal justification. They share responsibility with the leader of the nation for the actions undertaken in its name.

In Count 1, the Nuremberg prosecutors prosecuted multiple senior Nazi leaders who “participated as leaders, organizers, instigators or accomplices” in the “formulation or execution of a common plan or conspiracy to commit, or which involved the commission of, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

Count 2 charged defendants with participating in the “planning, preparation, initiation and waging of wars of aggression, which were also wars in violation of international treaties, agreements and assurances.”

As I said, impeachment isn’t a criminal proceeding, and thankfully, the charges against Hegseth are nowhere near as grave as the charges against the Nazi defendants. But did Hegseth conspire or have a common plan to wage war against Iran without congressional approval and in defiance of the acts of Congress and congressional resolutions? Did he plan, prepare, initiate and wage war in violation of the Constitution, acts of Congress and congressional resolutions?

And consider this: Hegseth had an option unavailable to senior Nazi leaders. He could resign at any time and publicly dissent from the administration’s course of action, without fear for his life.

In addition, American law has long imposed on subordinates an affirmative obligation to refuse to obey clearly unlawful orders.

My focus on the War Powers Resolution should not be taken in any way as a judgment that Hegseth is innocent of the other charges against him. I agree with Andrew McCarthy, my former National Review colleague, who wrote, “I do not believe there is any viable justification for the extrajudicial killings by military force of operators of suspected drug boats.”

If any evidence emerges during impeachment proceedings that Hegseth ordered attacks on sailors who were clinging to the destroyed wreckage of their boat — as The Washington Post reported in 2025 — that’s so clearly illegal that the Department of Defense Law of War Manual uses it as a textbook example of a war crime.

Hegseth’s attempt to punish Senator Kelly for publicly stating that service members have a duty to disobey illegal orders was also laughably unconstitutional. It was a clear abuse of power for which he is individually responsible. If he were impeached on that basis alone, it would be well deserved.

The impeachment charges provide an opportunity for the House and the Senate to think bigger — to recover their power (and, quite frankly, for some of them, their dignity) by at least holding the secretary of defense accountable for his role in waging an unconstitutional war. The president, of course, is primarily responsible — and one day he should face a reckoning for his constitutional crimes — but he is not solely responsible.

Hegseth shares the blame, and no amount of finger-pointing and excuse-making can change the fact that he played his own role in arrogantly leading our nation into an unconstitutional war. Congress must relieve him of his command.

🚩 Iran’s regime should not mistake a pause in American strikes for an escape from American pressure. A regime that uses negotiations to preserve its capabilities must understand that time is not automatically on its side.

President Trump plans to discuss Iran with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen next week. Moscow and Beijing have important relationships with Tehran, but their presence at the table does not mean either has secured protection for the regime.

One possibility is that President Trump could use the wider negotiations with Xi and Putin to seek room for stronger pressure on Iran’s regime in exchange for concessions on other issues. That would depend on what Washington is prepared to offer and whether Moscow and Beijing would accept the trade.

The United States has more than one instrument of pressure. Secretary Rubio says economic pressure is working while military action remains available. Restricting the regime’s revenue matters because money is what allows it to rebuild capabilities and sustain the organizations it finances.

President Trump has told advisers he may hold off further strikes unless Iran or the Houthis launch new provocations. That is not a decision to remove force from the equation. It preserves the option while the regime remains under pressure.

The test is not whether Tehran can prolong another round of talks. It is whether Iran’s regime abandons the nuclear threat. An agreement that leaves that threat intact would not settle the confrontation, it would give the regime more time to prepare for the next one.

On this day in North Carolina history, November 14, 1937.

A mysterious stone discovered in Chowan County may have contained the answer to one of America's greatest historical mysteries: What happened to the Lost Colony of Roanoke?

Earlier that year, a California tourist named Louis Hammond claimed he found a 21-pound rock near the Chowan River while hunting for hickory nuts.

He eventually carried the stone to Emory University in Atlanta, where professors studied its strange markings.

What they deciphered was astonishing.

The inscription appeared to be a message from Eleanor Dare, the mother of Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the New World.

It claimed that Virginia and her father, Ananias Dare, had died in 1591. It also described disease, hardship, attacks and the deaths of other colonists.

The message was supposedly signed EWD, believed to stand for Eleanor White Dare.

On November 14, the professors publicly revealed their transcription. The discovery became a national sensation.

But then things got strange.

Researchers offered a $500 reward for another stone mentioned in the message. Soon, more stones began appearing, supposedly telling the rest of the Lost Colony's story.

Enter Bill Eberhardt, a Georgia stonecutter.

Eberhardt produced 42 additional stones and was paid approximately $2,000 for them. Eventually, investigative reporter Boyden Sparkes exposed the operation as a fraud.

But Eberhardt wasn't finished.

When university professor Haywood Pearce Jr. confronted him, Eberhardt reportedly tried to blackmail him. He produced yet another stone with a message reading:

"Pearce and Dare Historical Hoaxes. We Dare Anything."

He demanded another $200 and threatened to expose the operation.

Pearce refused.

The additional stones were exposed as fakes, but there's still a wrinkle in this story. The original Chowan River Stone was not conclusively proven to be a forgery. Its authenticity remains disputed.

Today, that original stone is held at Brenau University in Georgia.

Nearly 90 years later, North Carolina still has no definitive answer about what happened to the 115 colonists.

A mysterious rock, a national sensation, 42 fake stones and a blackmail attempt.

You couldn't make this stuff up. Except somebody apparently did.

text:
A 1,600-Year-Old Baby Had a Single Eye Socket. Ancient DNA Finally Revealed Why | Tudor Tarita, ZME Science

The infant’s skull had a single eye socket in the centre of her face. Her nose had never developed normally. Yet her teeth suggested something extraordinary: she may have survived for months after birth, despite having a condition that is almost always fatal.

How could this baby have lived, even for a short while?

A Condition Called Cyclopia

The baby lived around 1,600 years ago in what is now southern Peru, among the ancient Nasca people. Archaeologists discovered her remains inside a ceramic urn, buried beneath another infant.

Her unusual skull revealed a rare developmental condition called cyclopia. Cyclopia is an extremely rare birth defect in which the developing brain fails to divide properly, causing the eyes to form within a single central eye socket, often alongside severe abnormalities of the nose and brain. It affects approximately 1 in 100,000 births and is almost always fatal.

As if this find wasn’t weird enough, the infant’s bones told a confusing story.

Her developing teeth suggested an age of two to four months. Her leg bones, however, were no larger than those of a baby approaching birth. Had she somehow survived for months while her body struggled to grow? Or had her condition distorted the normal developmental clues scientists use to estimate age?

Researchers have analyzed her bones and ancient DNA, identifying the genetic disorder responsible for her condition. Their findings also offer a glimpse into how the Nasca treated children born with severe disabilities.

Against All Odds

Archaeologists discovered the infant at Jauranga, in Peru’s Palpa Valley, a region famous for the enormous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines.

She lay at the bottom of a ceramic urn, beneath the skeleton of another infant girl. Both belonged to the Middle Nasca period, between 325 and 440 CE.

The researchers faced an immediate problem when estimating the first infant’s age at death.

Her developing teeth resembled those of a two- to four-month-old baby. But her thigh bones and other long bones matched those of a fetus at approximately 36 to 40 weeks of pregnancy, around the time of birth.

Usually, scientists can use these measurements to estimate how old a child was when they died. Here, the two indicators disagreed.

One possibility is that the infant survived for weeks or months after birth, while her condition severely restricted her skeletal growth. However, the genetic disorder could also have disrupted normal tooth development, making her appear older than she really was.

“We cannot really say how long this individual survived,” Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, and study co-author, told Live Science. “[But] the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants.”

Both infants were placed in the urn during what appears to have been a single burial event. DNA showed that they had different maternal lineages. It’s possible that the infants had the same father, but it’s also possible that they came from different families.

Urn burials were common for Nasca children, accounting for approximately one-quarter of documented graves in Palpa. There were no unusual grave goods or obvious signs that the infant with cyclopia received different funerary treatment.

This suggests that her community included her in its established burial traditions. Whether she received special care while alive remains unknown.

Increasingly, researchers are finding evidence of burial for infants or children suffering from rare, severe conditions. For instance, a 2024 genetic study identified six infants with Down syndrome and one with Edwards syndrome, dating from around 5,000 years ago to the 18th century, from Bulgaria, Greece, Spain, and Finland. Some died before birth, while others survived for months. In Iron Age Spain, people buried an infant with Down syndrome alongside multiple offerings, suggesting that ancient communities sometimes gave children with severe genetic conditions careful funerary treatment.

How One Extra Chromosome Can Change the Entire Face

Cyclopia occurs in approximately one in 100,000 births. Despite its name, the condition does not necessarily produce a single fully formed eye. The eyes may be fused or partially divided within one central socket.

The problem starts early on in pregnancy.

During the first weeks of pregnancy, the developing brain must divide into left and right hemispheres. If this separation fails severely, the result is a condition called alobar holoprosencephaly.

Because the brain and face develop together, the disruption can also prevent the eyes and nasal structures from forming normally. In the most severe cases, the nose is missing or replaced by a small tube-like structure above the eye.

For the Nasca infant, scientists traced the problem back to her chromosomes.

By sequencing ancient DNA recovered from a leg bone, they discovered that she carried three copies of chromosome 13 instead of the usual two. Three separate analytical methods supported the finding.

This genetic condition, called trisomy 13 or Patau syndrome, is a major chromosomal cause of severe holoprosencephaly, although only a minority of affected babies develop cyclopia.

“The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization,” Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, the study’s lead author and an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science. The visible abnormalities developed as the embryo’s brain and face began taking shape.

The discovery adds Patau syndrome to the chromosomal disorders identified in ancient human remains. The aforementioned 2024 investigation of nearly 10,000 ancient genomes found Down and Edwards syndrome but no cases of Patau syndrome.

Archaeologists have learned so much about the infant, but many questions remain.

Her DNA tells us what happened before she was born. Her bones and teeth offer conflicting clues about what happened afterward. We don’t know whether she was born alive, let alone whether she survived for days or months. We don’t know what her brief existence was like, or how the people around her responded to her condition. All we know is that, some 1,600 years ago, she was buried alongside another infant, in much the same way the Nasca buried their other children.

text:
Last week, sexually explicit images of Taylor Swift, one of the world’s biggest pop stars, went viral online. Millions of people viewed nonconsensual deepfake porn of Swift on the social media platform X, formerly known as Twitter. X has since taken the drastic step of blocking all searches for Taylor Swift to try to get the problem under control. 

This is not a new phenomenon: deepfakes have been around for years. However, the rise of generative AI has made it easier than ever to create deepfake pornography and sexually harass people using AI-generated images and videos. 

Of all types of harm related to generative AI, nonconsensual deepfakes affect the largest number of people, with women making up the vast majority of those targeted, says Henry Ajder, an AI expert who specializes in generative AI and synthetic media.

Thankfully, there is some hope. New tools and laws could make it harder for attackers to weaponize people’s photos, and they could help us hold perpetrators accountable. 

Here are three ways we can combat nonconsensual deepfake porn. 

WATERMARKS

Social media platforms sift through the posts that are uploaded onto their sites and take down content that goes against their policies. But this process is patchy at best and misses a lot of harmful content, as the Swift videos on X show. It is also hard to distinguish between authentic and AI-generated content. 

One technical solution could be watermarks. Watermarks hide an invisible signal in images that helps computers identify if they are AI generated. For example, Google has developed a system called SynthID, which uses neural networks to modify pixels in images and adds a watermark that is invisible to the human eye. That mark is designed to be detected even if the image is edited or screenshotted. In theory, these tools could help companies improve their content moderation and make them faster to spot fake content, including nonconsensual deepfakes.

Pros: Watermarks could be a useful tool that makes it easier and quicker to identify AI-generated content and identify toxic posts that should be taken down. Including watermarks in all images by default would also make it harder for attackers to create nonconsensual deepfakes to begin with, says Sasha Luccioni, a researcher at the AI startup Hugging Face who has studied bias in AI systems.

Cons: These systems are still experimental and not widely used. And a determined attacker can still tamper with them. Companies are also not applying the technology to all images across the board. Users of Google’s Imagen AI image generator can choose whether they want their AI-generated images to have the watermark, for example. All these factors limit their usefulness in fighting deepfake porn. 

PROTECTIVE SHIELDS

At the moment, all the images we post online are free game for anyone to use to create a deepfake. And because the latest image-making AI systems are so sophisticated, it is growing harder to prove that AI-generated content is fake. 

But a slew of new defensive tools allow people to protect their images from AI-powered exploitation by making them look warped or distorted in AI systems. 

One such tool, called PhotoGuard, was developed by researchers at MIT. It works like a protective shield by altering the pixels in photos in ways that are invisible to the human eye. When someone uses an AI app like the image generator Stable Diffusion to manipulate an image that has been treated with PhotoGuard, the result will look unrealistic. Fawkes, a similar tool developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, cloaks images with hidden signals that make it harder for facial recognition software to recognize faces. 

Another new tool, called Nightshade, could help people fight back against being used in AI systems. The tool, developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, applies an invisible layer of “poison” to images. The tool was developed to protect artists from having their copyrighted images scraped by tech companies without their consent. However, in theory, it could be used on any image its owner doesn’t want to end up being scraped by AI systems. When tech companies grab training material online without consent, these poisoned images will break the AI model. Images of cats could become dogs, and images of Taylor Swift could also become dogs. 

Pros: These tools make it harder for attackers to use our images to create harmful content. They show some promise in providing private individuals with protection against AI image abuse, especially if dating apps and social media companies apply them by default, says Ajder. 

“We should all be using Nightshade for every image we post on the internet,” says Luccioni. 

Cons: These defensive shields work on the latest generation of AI models. But there is no guarantee future versions won’t be able to override these protective mechanisms. They also don’t work on images that are already online, and they are harder to apply to images of celebrities, as famous people don’t control which photos of them are uploaded online. 

“It’s going to be this giant game of cat and mouse,” says Rumman Chowdhury, who runs the ethical AI consulting and auditing company Parity Consulting. 

REGULATION

Technical fixes go only so far. The only thing that will lead to lasting change is stricter regulation, says Luccioni. 

Taylor Swift’s viral deepfakes have put new momentum behind efforts to clamp down on deepfake porn. The White House said the incident was “alarming” and urged Congress to take legislative action. Thus far, the US has had a piecemeal, state-by-state approach to regulating the technology. For example, California and Virginia have banned the creation of pornographic deepfakes made without consent. New York and Virginia also ban the distribution of this sort of content. 

However, we could finally see action on a federal level. A new bipartisan bill that would make sharing fake nude images a federal crime was recently reintroduced in the US Congress. A deepfake porn scandal at a New Jersey high school has also pushed lawmakers to respond with a bill called the Preventing Deepfakes of Intimate Images Act. The attention Swift’s case has brought to the problem might drum up more bipartisan support. 

Lawmakers around the world are also pushing stricter laws for the technology. The UK’s Online Safety Act, passed last year, outlaws the sharing of deepfake porn material, but not its creation. Perpetrators could face up to six months of jail time. 

In the European Union, a bunch of new bills tackle the problem from different angles. The sweeping AI Act requires deepfake creators to clearly disclose that the material was created by AI, and the Digital Services Act will require tech companies to remove harmful content much more quickly. 

China’s deepfake law, which entered into force in 2023, goes the furthest. In China, deepfake creators need to take steps to prevent the use of their services for illegal or harmful purposes, ask for consent from users before making their images into deepfakes, authenticate people’s identities, and label AI-generated content. 

Pros: Regulation will offer victims recourse, hold creators of nonconsensual deepfake pornography accountable, and create a powerful deterrent. It also sends a clear message that creating nonconsensual deepfakes is not acceptable. Laws and public awareness campaigns making it clear that people who create this sort of deepfake porn are sex offenders could have a real impact, says Ajder. “That would change the slightly blasé attitude that some people have toward this kind of content as not harmful or not a real form of sexual abuse,” he says. 

Cons: It will be difficult to enforce these sorts of laws, says Ajder. With current techniques, it will be hard for victims to identify who has assaulted them and build a case against that person. The person creating the deepfakes might also be in a different jurisdiction, which makes prosecution more difficult.

I think Tesla is offering this early to work out the kinks and learn what works and what doesn't. It's classic build. Measure. Learn. But I also think it's easy to overlook how similar this model will probably end up being to traditional franchises and how they helped build some of the biggest household names.

Take Coca Cola for example. They were able to expand rapidly across the country by selling their concentrate to regional bottlers who already knew their local markets and had established distribution networks. Coke got to focus on the high margin part of the business while letting local partners handle the more labor intensive, lower margin ops.

The same thing happened with companies like McDonald's and Domino's. If you look at how these businesses got started and how they grew, franchising played a huge role. It allowed them to expand much faster, use other people's capital, share the operational burden, and build VERY profitable, asset light businesses.

I think there's a much bigger opportunity here than people realize. Having others help fund and expand the network would be a pretty smart strategy, esp as @Tesla  starts opening up larger geofenced areas. Some of these markets will be nowhere near the existing home base / footprint. Think Idaho, Kentucky, and other places where Tesla doesn't have the same presence it does in Texas or Cali.

Having local owner operators who know their markets, have their own money invested, and are financially motivated to grow the service could be a huge advantage.

I know it might seem strange today that Cybercabs are being sold to the public but are limited to personal use within relatively small geofenced areas. But you have to start somewhere and why not start today? I think we're looking at the early stages of something much bigger. The long lerm vision could very well be the lions share of thr network is directly owned and operated by Tesla with supplementation of owner operators who have a financial stake in the service that help to expand it into new markets.

Tesla gets to test the waters now, work out the operational challenges, and learn from the experience before trying to scale it. By the time they're ready to open things up more broadly, they'll be much better prepared. I think people may be looking at what is being offered today rather than what the final form will look like tomorrow. 

Pushing out it now so Marques will shave his head is just a cherry on top.
