LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM

FOLLOW THE MONEY: FREEZE THEIR BANK ACCOUNTS, SEIZE THEIR PROPERTIES AND RECOVER NIGERIA’S STOLEN BILLIONS

By Kio Amachree | Stockholm, Sweden | 14 November 2026

I have come to the conclusion that the most effective way to dismantle Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s political empire and the network of politicians and businessmen surrounding him is to persuade the governments of the United States, Britain, Switzerland and the European Union to begin investigating their overseas bank accounts, freezing suspicious assets and seizing properties wherever there is sufficient evidence that they were acquired with the proceeds of corruption.

This is precisely what the Americans, British and Europeans have done to corrupt politicians and their associates from Angola, Nigeria and other countries. There is absolutely no reason why the same laws should not be applied to those currently holding Nigeria hostage.

I intend to work much harder towards this objective, because I am convinced that the only language these people understand is money.

Take away their access to their foreign bank accounts, investigate the sources of their wealth, expose their offshore companies and recover whatever assets are proven to have been purchased with stolen public funds, and much of the financial machinery sustaining their political influence will begin to crumble.

These men may believe they own Nigeria. They may control sections of the police, security services and political establishment. They may intimidate opposition politicians and use their supporters to threaten anyone who challenges them.

But they do not own the American Department of Justice, the British Serious Fraud Office, the National Crime Agency, the Swiss financial authorities or the courts of Europe.

And that is where the real battle against international corruption must be fought.

THE ABACHA BILLIONS: THE PRECEDENT WAS ESTABLISHED YEARS AGO

Let us begin with the late General Sani Abacha, whose regime demonstrated how easily a country’s wealth could be transferred into foreign bank accounts while its citizens suffered.

International investigations estimated that Abacha and his associates diverted billions of dollars from Nigeria.

The World Bank has cited estimates of approximately $4 billion in misappropriated funds.

Swiss investigations uncovered accounts associated with the Abacha network across numerous banks. British banking investigations also revealed serious weaknesses in the financial controls that should have prevented suspicious transactions.

The figures are staggering.

Switzerland returned more than $700 million in Abacha-linked funds to Nigeria through earlier recovery arrangements. Another $322.5 million was returned in 2017 under an arrangement involving international monitoring.

In 2020, approximately $311.8 million was repatriated through cooperation between the United States, Jersey and Nigeria.

We are talking about well over a billion dollars recovered through these separate proceedings alone.

That money did not fall out of the sky. It was traced through financial institutions, subjected to legal proceedings and eventually returned to Nigeria.

So why should the same international machinery not be used to examine the wealth of today’s political establishment?

Why should anyone imagine that becoming president, governor or minister gives him permanent immunity from international financial investigations?

The Abacha case should have taught every Nigerian politician one important lesson: stolen money does not necessarily remain yours simply because you have managed to move it abroad.

JAMES IBORI: A £101.5 MILLION WARNING TO NIGERIA’S POLITICAL CLASS

Consider the case of James Ibori, the former governor of Delta State.

Ibori was once one of Nigeria’s most powerful governors. He enjoyed enormous political influence, surrounded himself with loyal supporters and operated within a political system that appeared incapable of holding him accountable.

Yet it was in Britain that he eventually faced the consequences of his financial activities.

In 2012, Ibori pleaded guilty to money-laundering offences and received a 13-year prison sentence.

In 2023, a British court imposed a confiscation order of £101.5 million.

And on 3 November 2026, the London Court of Appeal rejected his attempt to reduce that order.

Think about that for a moment.

A former Nigerian governor, years after leaving office, remains subject to a British confiscation order exceeding one hundred million pounds.

This is exactly the kind of international accountability I want to see applied wherever credible evidence establishes that Nigerian public officials have accumulated illicit wealth.

Ibori’s case proves that political influence in Nigeria does not necessarily translate into immunity before the British courts.

And that is a lesson Tinubu, Wike and every other politician with questionable sources of wealth would do well to remember.

GILBERT CHAGOURY: HOW MANY WARNINGS DOES NIGERIA NEED?

Now let us examine Gilbert Chagoury, the Lebanese-Nigerian businessman whose relationship with successive Nigerian political administrations has long attracted controversy.

Chagoury is not some obscure businessman whose financial history has never been examined.

In 2000, Swiss judicial authorities found him guilty of money laundering and supporting a criminal organisation in connection with funds associated with the Abacha regime.

He was fined one million Swiss francs and agreed to return $66 million to Nigeria. The conviction was subsequently expunged under Swiss law.

But that was not the end of his encounters with foreign authorities.

In 2021, the United States Department of Justice announced that Chagoury had paid $1.8 million to resolve a federal investigation involving unlawful campaign contributions.

According to American authorities, approximately $180,000 had been channelled through intermediaries to political candidates between 2012 and 2016.

These are matters of public record, not allegations invented by me.

And yet today we have a Nigerian administration awarding enormous infrastructure contracts to companies associated with the Chagoury business empire.

Take the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, a project originally presented as approximately 700 kilometres in length and involving expenditure running into trillions of naira.

Hitech Construction, associated with the Chagoury business group, was awarded a major role in the project.

The House of Representatives itself raised questions about the procurement process in 2024.

Why should the Nigerian people not demand complete transparency concerning the award of these contracts?

Why should the government not publish the full contractual terms, financing arrangements, beneficial ownership information and independent cost assessments?

And what about the reported business connections between members of the Tinubu family and Chagoury-linked interests?

I want these relationships examined thoroughly, including any potential conflicts of interest.

I am not prepared to accept that because a businessman has access to the president, Nigerians must simply remain silent while enormous public contracts are awarded.

Nigeria is not the private property of Bola Tinubu, Gilbert Chagoury or their associates.

The money being spent belongs to the Nigerian people.

BOLA TINUBU AND THE AMERICAN DRUG INVESTIGATION RECORDS

Then there is Bola Ahmed Tinubu himself.

For years, Nigerians have been arguing about his activities in Chicago during the 1990s and the circumstances surrounding the forfeiture of approximately $460,000 in American bank accounts connected to him.

The 1993 proceedings arose from allegations involving proceeds associated with narcotics trafficking. They resulted in a civil forfeiture settlement, not a criminal conviction of Tinubu.

That distinction does not remove the legitimate public interest in the underlying records.

Today, more than three decades later, Tinubu is involved in litigation concerning the disclosure of historical FBI and DEA investigative records.

On 30 October 2026, United States District Judge Beryl Howell issued an important decision requiring federal agencies to provide further justification for certain withheld records.

The case concerns documents relating to investigations conducted in Chicago in the early 1990s.

My question is straightforward.

What exactly do these records contain?

Why has their disclosure been contested so vigorously?

What did American investigators discover, and what information remains hidden from the Nigerian public?

A man occupying the presidency of Africa’s most populous country should have no objection to the fullest disclosure permitted by American law of records concerning his past.

If those records clear him of the allegations that have followed him for decades, let the Nigerian people see that.

But if they contain information of legitimate public interest, the Nigerian people have a right to know.

I intend to follow these proceedings closely because I believe transparency is essential to political accountability.

NYESOM WIKE: LET US EXAMINE THE AMERICAN PROPERTY RECORDS

And then there is Nyesom Wike, the former governor of Rivers State and present Minister of the Federal Capital Territory.

Wike has become one of the most outspoken and politically influential figures in the Tinubu administration.

But political influence does not place anyone beyond financial scrutiny.

In September 2025, Peoples Gazette published an investigation concerning three properties in Winter Springs, Florida, reportedly associated with Wike’s family.

The reported purchase prices were $535,000, $459,157 and $465,000.

That is a combined figure of approximately $1.46 million.

The newspaper reported that the properties had been acquired through cash transactions and subsequently transferred to Wike’s children.

These allegations have not been established as criminal wrongdoing by a court. Nevertheless, they raise questions that deserve independent examination.

Where did the purchase funds originate?

Which financial institutions processed the transactions?

Were the properties properly declared under the applicable rules?

Were any public funds involved?

These are legitimate questions concerning a politically exposed person who has occupied two of the most powerful offices in Nigeria.

If the money was legitimately earned, the relevant financial documentation should be capable of establishing that fact.

But if investigators uncover evidence of corruption or money laundering, then the appropriate authorities should act.

Wike should understand that property transactions in the United States leave records that can be examined independently of Nigerian political influence.

ISABEL DOS SANTOS: THE ANGOLAN LESSON

One of the most instructive examples comes from Angola.

Isabel dos Santos, the daughter of the late Angolan president José Eduardo dos Santos, was once celebrated as Africa’s richest woman.

Her fortune was estimated in billions of dollars. She controlled substantial business interests and enjoyed extraordinary political connections.

For years, she appeared almost untouchable.

Then international investigations began examining how her wealth had been accumulated.

In November 2024, the British government imposed an asset freeze and travel ban on her under its anti-corruption sanctions regime.

British authorities alleged that she had improperly benefited from more than £50 million through Angola’s state oil company Sonangol and more than £300 million through the telecommunications company Unitel.

Separate civil proceedings in London involved a freezing order covering assets worth up to £580 million.

Dos Santos denies wrongdoing, and the sanctions and civil proceedings must not be confused with a criminal conviction.

Nevertheless, the significance of the case is unmistakable.

Here was a woman who had once enjoyed extraordinary wealth, political protection and international influence, suddenly facing serious financial restrictions and legal proceedings abroad.

Her father’s political position could no longer shield her from international scrutiny.

That is precisely the lesson Nigeria’s political establishment must understand.

No amount of political influence at home guarantees permanent protection from foreign courts and financial investigators.

THE DIEZANI CASE: EVEN SUPERYACHTS CAN BE RECOVERED

There is another Nigerian example that deserves attention.

In January 2025, the United States announced an agreement to return approximately $52.88 million in forfeited assets connected to corruption involving former petroleum minister Diezani Alison-Madueke.

American investigators described how proceeds associated with a bribery scheme had been used to acquire luxury assets, including the 65-metre Galactica Star superyacht and expensive real estate in California and New York.

The United States had pursued forfeiture proceedings against assets connected to the scheme.

The recovery agreement provided for much of the money to be used for electricity-access projects in Nigeria.

This is what international asset recovery can accomplish.

The American authorities did not need to control the Nigerian police or the Nigerian judiciary to investigate assets within their own jurisdiction.

They followed financial evidence and used their own legal system.

That is exactly why foreign financial investigations can be such an important instrument in combating corruption in Nigeria.

MY CAMPAIGN WILL NOW CONCENTRATE ON INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL ACCOUNTABILITY

I have already taken my concerns about corruption involving members of Nigeria’s political establishment and their business associates to British authorities, including the Serious Fraud Office.

I have spent time discussing these matters and presenting documents supporting my concerns.

I intend to continue this work with renewed determination.

I am a political scientist, a businessman and a lawyer trained in Sweden. I have worked in international finance and understand that modern financial transactions leave documentary trails.

I also understand that accusations alone are not sufficient to secure a criminal conviction or confiscation order.

Evidence is what matters.

Property records, banking transactions, company registrations, beneficial ownership documents, contract payments and financial disclosures are the materials that investigators require.

That is where I intend to concentrate my efforts.

I want the relevant authorities in the United States, Britain, Switzerland and the European Union to examine credible evidence of possible corruption and money laundering involving Nigerian politically exposed persons.

I want suspicious overseas wealth investigated.

I want unexplained financial arrangements subjected to independent examination.

And wherever the evidence establishes that assets were purchased with stolen Nigerian public money, I want those assets frozen, confiscated and returned to their rightful owners: the Nigerian people.

THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY MUST STOP SHELTERING AFRICA’S STOLEN WEALTH

There is something profoundly offensive about watching Nigerian politicians and their associates enjoy expensive properties in London, Florida, Paris, Dubai and other international financial centres while millions of Nigerians struggle to survive.

Nigeria has children attending schools without proper classrooms.

We have hospitals without adequate equipment.

We have communities without reliable electricity or clean drinking water.

We have pensioners who struggle to survive and young graduates who cannot find employment.

Yet enormous sums have historically been diverted from public resources into private fortunes.

And too often those fortunes have found comfortable homes in foreign banking systems.

Western governments cannot continue preaching good governance to African countries while failing to confront suspicious wealth flowing through their own financial institutions.

If the money is legitimate, let its owners demonstrate its lawful origin when required.

If it is stolen, recover it.

And if public officials have abused their positions to enrich themselves, let them face the consequences.

The international financial system should not be a sanctuary for corrupt political elites.

THE DAY THE MONEY STOPS, THE EMPIRE BEGINS TO CRUMBLE

Bola Tinubu and the political figures surrounding him may believe that controlling the machinery of government gives them unlimited power.

They may believe that political intimidation, patronage and control of state institutions will protect them indefinitely.

But they should study the histories of Abacha, Ibori, Diezani and Isabel dos Santos.

They should understand that foreign financial investigations can continue long after political power has disappeared.

They should also understand that international investigators are not obliged to accept the explanations offered by political supporters.

A banking transaction is a banking transaction.

A property deed is a property deed.

A company registration is a company registration.

And money transferred across international borders can sometimes be traced decades after the original transaction.

I am not interested in replacing one corrupt political gang with another.

I want the system that enables the looting of Nigeria dismantled.

I want the proceeds of corruption recovered.

I want Nigerian politicians to understand that public office is a responsibility, not an opportunity to accumulate private fortunes at the expense of the people.

And I want those who believe they can hide behind political influence to understand that the world is much larger than Aso Rock.

You may control political machinery in Abuja, but you do not control the courts in London, the Department of Justice in Washington or the financial authorities in Switzerland.

The precedent has already been established.

The laws already exist.

The investigators have demonstrated what they can accomplish.

What is required now is credible evidence, political will and sustained international cooperation.

I intend to work harder towards achieving precisely that.

Follow the money. Investigate the accounts. Examine the properties. Trace the beneficial owners. Recover every asset proven to have been stolen from the Nigerian people.

Because Nigeria’s wealth belongs to its citizens, not to the politicians who temporarily occupy its offices.

And no political empire built or sustained by corruption should be allowed to escape the rule of law.

⸻

Kio Amachree
Political Scientist | President, Worldview International

text:
Something we sometimes hear from anglers who favor industrial offshore wind: “…but the pilings create artificial reefs.” They cite the amazing fishing around oil platforms in the Gulf of America.

Let’s talk about that for a second. 

First, artificial reefs can provide excellent habitat for marine life, but they don't become mature, thriving ecosystems overnight. Depending on the materials, location, depth, and environmental conditions, it can take several years or even decades for a diverse marine community to develop.

Second, offshore wind turbines create significant obstacles to navigation. Their foundations, connecting cables, maintenance requirements, and safety restrictions complicate navigation and fishing operations. Many offshore wind facilities impose 500-foot safety or restricted-access zones around individual structures, as well as the industrial zones as a whole. 

Third, offshore wind turbine foundations use protective coatings, including zinc-rich primers, and may employ sacrificial anodes made from aluminum-, zinc-, or other metal-based alloys to prevent corrosion. These materials release metals into the surrounding marine environment as they corrode, which are ingested by marine life. 

Fourth, the United States already has a substantial inventory of inactive vessels that could be considered for artificial reef projects. The Maritime Administration's National Defense Reserve Fleet contains approximately 100 government-owned vessels, including 43 ships in the Ready Reserve Force. Not all are available for disposal, of course, but the inventory illustrates the potential supply of vessels that could be evaluated for reef deployment. 
Consider the recently scuttled SS United States, which was intentionally sunk off Florida on November 11, 2026, to create what is now the world's largest artificial reef. Its enormous steel structure will provide an intricate habitat with countless nooks, crannies, and sheltered spaces for marine organisms and fish. 

Why not make greater use of properly cleaned, environmentally prepared decommissioned ships to create artificial reefs? They offer substantial structural habitat without introducing hundreds of permanent industrial structures into busy fishing and navigation areas.

text:
The Republicans appropriated $12.5 billion in the Big Beautiful Bill, but it turned out to be just another government boondoggle.  Elon tried to help, but Trump and his administration didn't follow through.  

Elon Musk’s 2025 views on U.S. air traffic control and what the Trump Administration did with them.

In early 2025, after the January midair collision near Washington, D.C., and a temporary outage of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, Elon Musk publicly argued that America’s ATC system was outdated, understaffed, and at risk of serious failure. He framed fixes around rapid technical upgrades via the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and SpaceX engineers, plus satellite connectivity from Starlink as an emergency stopgap.

Key points from Musk’s statements
- He said the DOGE team would pursue “rapid safety upgrades to the air traffic control system,” citing the recent NOTAM failure.
- He described the situation as dire, claiming the existing communications infrastructure was “breaking down very rapidly” and that an FAA assessment put the system within “single digit months to catastrophic failure.”
- He offered Starlink terminals “at NO COST to the taxpayer on an emergency basis to restore air traffic control connectivity.”
- He highlighted a shortage of “top notch air traffic controllers” and publicly asked retirees open to returning to consider doing so.
- He positioned SpaceX engineers as able to help make air travel safer in a non-partisan way.

He later corrected one claim, clarifying that the aging system then in use was from L3Harris (not Verizon) while Verizon’s new system was not yet operational.

How the Trump Administration responded
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy publicly welcomed the involvement. He said the DOGE team would “plug in” to help upgrade the aviation system and arranged for SpaceX engineers to visit the FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Virginia. Those engineers (and others from SpaceX) were brought on as special government employees/advisors to observe systems and help envision improvements. Duffy later wrote that he had enlisted “the brightest minds, including SpaceX engineers.”

The FAA began testing Starlink terminals, initially at non-safety-critical sites in Alaska and a facility in Atlantic City, New Jersey, with later reporting indicating expanded testing (dozens of connections across sites including more in Alaska and Oklahoma). SpaceX confirmed it was providing kits free of charge for testing through existing relationships (including with L3Harris) and described Starlink as a possible partial fix for remote or aging links, not a full takeover of major contracts. Acting FAA leadership stated that DOGE personnel were not making the decisions on Starlink testing and that terminals were not plugged into the core ATC system.

On the broader modernization front, the administration accelerated efforts that had been under discussion for years. Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 as a down payment (via the One Big Beautiful Bill) for ATC upgrades covering telecommunications, radar, software, and facilities. In December 2025, the Department of Transportation selected Peraton as the prime integrator to manage the multi-year overhaul (a contract later valued around $1.5 billion for the management portion), with a goal of major progress by the end of 2028. Progress reported included conversion of copper wiring to fiber/satellite/wireless, installation of new radios and voice switches, and other equipment upgrades. Duffy has continued pushing for additional funding (later estimating the full effort in the $30–50 billion range).

Outcomes and caveats
Starlink saw real testing and limited deployment for FAA connectivity needs, especially in remote areas, but it did not replace the major Verizon/L3Harris telecommunications contracts. The administration treated Musk’s offers as one input among others rather than handing SpaceX the core system. DOGE’s broader workforce reductions at the FAA drew criticism that they complicated operations even as technical modernization funding and contractor work advanced. Aging infrastructure continued to cause disruptions into 2026 (including a nationwide ground stop in November 2026 attributed to overloaded legacy equipment), underscoring that the full overhaul remains a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar project.

In short, the administration took Musk up on the offer of engineering help and Starlink testing for supplemental connectivity, while pursuing a larger, funded modernization program with traditional government contracting processes and a selected prime integrator. The core diagnosis of an outdated system needing urgent investment was widely shared; the precise role of Starlink and DOGE engineers remained more limited than some early headlines suggested.

text:
NEWSDIGEST - Saturday November 14, 2026

Coverage window: new developments since the Friday digest (8:13 AM PT Friday November 13) through about 7:37 AM PT Saturday November 14. All times Pacific Time (PT). Items already in the Friday digest are not repeated unless something new happened, and the new part is stated.

HEADLINE
Iran says three more tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthis claim new strikes on a Riyadh airport and a Saudi pipeline station, and Iran and Bahrain trade accusations at the UN Security Council the day after the disputed Bahrain drone incident.
COMPLETE DETAILS
Iran says three oil tankers struck mines in Hormuz on Saturday
Iran's navy and Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that fires broke out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, CNA reported, citing Reuters. The Guards' navy said two tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were "secretly attempting to transit" by an unauthorised route "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine" in the south of the waterway, and said one of them was a supertanker. A separate statement from Iran's conventional navy said another tanker in what it called a prohibited zone east of the strait caught fire and was forced to stop after hitting a mine. The statements did not name the vessels or give their origins. Dawn said the navy warned that any tanker entering the area would meet the same fate. The US military says it has cleared the main routes of mines (per CNA). These are Iranian claims and have not been independently verified. They come on top of earlier Iranian claims already reported in the Friday digest, including the Friday LNG tanker claim; the counts should not be added together as confirmed separate ships.
https://t.co/mlVAv0D7zG
https://t.co/9aiqWQ2jSZ

UKMTO: tanker hit by a drone leaving Hormuz; weekly report counts seven tanker attacks
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said a tanker was hit by a drone while leaving the Strait of Hormuz, with minor damage and all crew safe and accounted for, Turkey's Ilke News Agency reported on Saturday. UKMTO did not name the vessel or say who was responsible. Separately, UKMTO's weekly overview, published Friday, said at least seven tankers were attacked in and around the strait in the week to November 11, with one strike injuring several crew members, Middle East Eye reported. UKMTO said traffic through the strait was about 65 percent below pre-war levels, with 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits, and rated the threat level as severe. It said no attacks had been reported in the Red Sea since August 24 and that it had logged 163 conflict-related incidents since February 28.
https://t.co/NZ1MfgTypi
https://t.co/cndlnqDnLg

Iran and Bahrain clash at the UN Security Council
The Security Council met Friday at Bahrain's request to discuss maritime security, according to the UN's meetings coverage. UN Assistant Secretary-General Khaled Khiari cited International Maritime Organization data showing 134 incidents and the deaths of 25 seafarers in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region as of November 11, and said October had the most incidents against commercial shipping since February. GCC Secretary-General Jasem Albudaiwi said Gulf states had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since February 28. Speaking for the GCC, Bahrain's representative said about 1,600 vessels had been disrupted and more than 23,000 seafarers stranded. The US delegate urged the Council to hold Iran accountable. Iran's deputy UN envoy Gholamhossein Darzi said that "any renewed war of aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime will be met with an immediate and decisive response," accused Bahrain and other Gulf states of letting their territory be used for attacks on Iran, and called for reparations, per Iran International and Middle East Eye. Bahrain rejected the accusations. This came the day after the disputed Bahrain drone incident reported Friday, in which US Central Command said it shot down two Iranian drones and denied an IRGC claim that a US radar was destroyed.

Houthis claim drone attacks on King Khalid International Airport and a pipeline pumping station
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Friday the group had attacked Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport with one drone and Pumping Station Number 3 on the East-West oil pipeline east of Riyadh with two drones, and claimed both operations hit their targets, Middle East Eye and Xinhua reported. Reuters, via The Jerusalem Post, said there was no immediate Saudi confirmation. Saree also said two ballistic missiles hit Saudi forces in the Al-Tuwal area of Jazan province, and claimed dozens were killed or wounded, including Sudanese nationals, per Xinhua. Reuters said that claim came hours after Saudi civil defence issued an all-clear for Jazan, and that it was not immediately clear whether the two were related. The casualty and damage claims could not be independently verified (Xinhua). Putin has spent years demanding that Ukraine stay OUT of NATO.

But Zelensky now believes NATO membership is back in the conversation, and that's a significant change in the negotiations.

text:
There Is No Such Thing as Karmic Justice!!! 

Hamid Mir has once again reached for an old and convenient story. Idris Khattak was sentenced by a military court during Imran Khan’s government. Khan is now himself in Adiala Jail. Therefore, this must be karmic justice. The claim sounds solemn. It is not. It is selective, self-serving, and historically hollow.
If real retribution existed, Pakistani generals and American officials would be the ones behind bars.
After September 11, Pakistan became the frontline ally in the American war on terror. Under Musharraf the machinery of enforced disappearances accelerated. Prisons filled. John Kiriakou, then the CIA’s chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan, has described how Rawalpindi Jail became overcrowded with detainees captured in joint operations. When space ran out, the instruction from CIA headquarters was simple: put them on a C-12 and send them to Guantanamo. They went. Without trial. Without the protections of the Geneva Conventions. Without ordinary legal process.
That same logic was later applied inside Pakistan. Label a civilian a national security threat. Move him into a military court. Silence the questions. Idris Khattak’s case belongs to this continuum. It was never an isolated failure of one civilian government. It was the predictable product of a system built and normalized after 2001.
Money helped shape the public story. The United States poured funds into Pakistani media through the National Endowment for Democracy, the State Department, and various “media development” programs. Training workshops, fellowships, Washington bureaus, capacity-building grants. The effect was to reinforce a narrative in which the war on terror justified extraordinary measures, military courts appeared necessary, and those who questioned disappearances or secret detentions could be painted as soft on terrorism or hostile to the state. Parts of the mainstream press absorbed and amplified that framing.
If karmic justice were real, the architects of this system would face consequences. The officers who filled Rawalpindi Jail and then emptied it toward Guantanamo. The officials who expanded military jurisdiction over civilians. The donors and intermediaries who paid to legitimize the narrative. None of them sit in prison. The only figure regularly offered as proof of cosmic balance is a former prime minister who, whatever his faults, challenged parts of that same order.
Idris Khattak deserves release. His case is a serious human rights violation. Linking it to Khan’s imprisonment and calling the result divine justice turns a structural crime into a personal morality play. It protects the system while punishing the occasional politician who becomes inconvenient.
Real accountability would mean closing the military courts to civilians, ending enforced disappearances, and exposing the purchased narratives that made both practices easier to defend. Until then, talk of karmic justice remains a rhetorical device used against the weak and never against the powerful.

text:
Two senior Polish intelligence officials arrested and charged for unlawful use of Pegasus spyware in February 2024.

The Pegasus software is offered by the Israeli cybersecurity firm NSO group and has been licensed by governments worldwide. It has notably been used to spy on journalists and dissidents, most famously against Washington Post contributor Jamal Khashoggi, who was lured into Saudi Arabia’s embassy in Istanbul and then murdered in 2018.

Piotr Pogonowski, former head of Poland’s ABW internal security agency and Maciej Materka, former head of the SKW military counterintelligence service have both been indicted. Each man is facing up to three years in prison.

They have been charged by the National Prosecutor’s Office in connection with authorizing and using the Pegasus system without accreditation and without verifying whether the system met standards for the protection of classified information. Materka has pleaded not guilty and has publicly defended himself on https://t.co/NG8BE4SkYP, stating he acted entirely in accordance with the law and provided SKW personnel with the best tools available for their assigned duties.

Investigators from The Citizen Lab in Toronto published a report in September 2018 indicating Pegasus was being used in Poland by an operator named ‘ORZELBIALY’ (White Eagle in Polish), and spreading through cell phones in that country.

Krzysztof Brejza, a Member of Parliament from the Civic Coalition party was hacked 33 times with Pegasus spyware during the parliamentary campaign of 2019. Information from his phone was then leaked to the state-run TVP broadcaster. An attorney named Roman Giertych who represented top Polish opposition figures was also hacked in 2019, and prosecutor Ewa Wrzosek was hacked in 2021 while challenging government efforts to purge the judiciary, according to reporting by the Associated Press.

Former Attorney General Zbigniew Ziobro has also been charged separately and faces up to 25 years in prison for allegedly using funds meant for crime victims to buy Pegasus spyware, according to reporting by Al Jazeera.

text:
OpenAI Leadership Gets Fooled by Pranksters Pretending to be Ukrainian Officials, Discusses Military Secrets With Them | Joe Wilkins, Futurism

Weeks ago, three OpenAI higher-ups became the butt of an embarrassing joke pulled by a duo of Russian pranksters, a gaffe with alarming implications for a company jockeying for military contracts.

According to the Intercept, a trio of national security and strategic initiative leaders at OpenAI — Sasha Baker, Caroline Zier, and Ben Crampton — took a video call with the Russian comedians who go by the monikers Vovan and Lexus (real names Vladimir Aleksandrovich Kuznetsov and Aleksei Vladimirovich Stolyarov) who were claiming they were top Ukrainian government officials.

The call reportedly lasted a humiliating 17 minutes, during which the OpenAI staffers openly discussed military AI applications and referenced ongoing talks with the US Department of Defense about supplying Ukraine with AI tools. Vovan and Lexus recorded the meeting, which they have since made available online.

“There’s no question, I think, from our perspective that we want to have as deep a relationship as we possibly can with Ukraine,” Crampton is heard saying when asked offensive military AI services to the country. “But it may not be possible to get to where we want to be straight away.”

At one point, Crampton even suggested that the role of national security staffers at OpenAI is to smooth over reservations which executives might have about military AI.

“Many of the company’s leaders would not want our technologies to be used in offensive military operations,” Crampton is heard saying on the call. “Our task is to explain that in certain situations, the line between offense and defense can be quite conditional.”

Later on, Crampton admits that OpenAI has a contact in the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, “primarily through a colleague of ours based in Washington… who previously had worked with the Delta team in your Ministry of Defense.”

Speaking to the Intercept, Vovan said it was remarkably simple to arrange the meeting. Basically, the duo contacted a senior Ukrainian official working in San Francisco, who then offered to arrange the meeting with OpenAI.

The incident has stunning implications for OpenAI’s security practices — if a couple of pranksters can snag a meeting with high-level company staffers as a joke, what’s to stop malicious actors from doing the same? (Keep in mind the AI lab maintains a massive Pentagon contract to deploy “advanced AI systems in classified environments.”)

In response to the stunt, OpenAI told the publication that “weeks ago, we launched a thorough investigation into the call’s authenticity.”

“We acted internally and with the relevant authorities to conclude that it was a prank conducted by individuals with a history of targeting officials and other companies,” OpenAI’s spokesperson continued. “We took action to prevent similar situations from happening in the future.”

At least OpenAI is in good company: Vovan and Lexus have previously punked public figures ranging from John McCain to Bernie Sanders. Talk about boundary-pushing comedy.

text:
Russia’s demands go well beyond Ukraine

The most important revelation in this New York Times report is that Putin is using negotiations to pursue the same strategic objectives Russia laid out just before invading Ukraine in 2022. After nearly five years of war, hundreds of thousands of casualties and months of Trump administration diplomacy, Moscow is still demanding a fundamental rewrite of Europe’s security order.

1. Putin wants NATO rolled back to 1997

Russia’s November 10 negotiating paper repeats its demand that NATO withdraw troops and military bases to the alliance’s 1997 borders, before NATO expanded into Central and Eastern Europe.

That would affect some of the alliance’s most vulnerable members, including Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. These countries joined NATO voluntarily after decades of Soviet domination. Putin is effectively demanding that their security arrangements be rolled back to accommodate Moscow.

Russia also wants NATO to rule out further expansion and end military activity not only in Ukraine but across Eastern Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia.

2. He wants to restrict Europe’s ability to defend itself

The demands go further than Russia’s 2021 proposal:

🔹NATO countries would have to end nuclear-sharing arrangements.
🔹Britain and France would have to rule out extending their nuclear protection to other European countries.
🔹Western countries would have to stop supplying Ukraine with weapons and military equipment.
🔹Ukraine could join the European Union only if it stayed out of the bloc’s common defense policy.

In effect, Putin wants to limit the military options available to Ukraine and its European neighbors—even after a peace agreement.

3. Russia is arguing for a return to spheres of influence

During the Abu Dhabi talks, Russian officials invoked the Cold War as a model, arguing that the division of Europe into American and Soviet spheres of influence helped prevent conflict.

That’s a remarkable argument. The Kremlin is presenting an arrangement in which powerful countries decide the security boundaries of smaller countries as a formula for stability.

But Poland’s Donald Tusk made the stakes clear: accepting Russia’s conditions would pose a direct threat to Polish security.

The fundamental issue is sovereignty. Do Ukraine and other European countries get to decide their own futures, or does Moscow get a veto?

4. Trump’s economic courtship has not changed Putin’s position

The report highlights the failure, so far, of the economic inducements offered by Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to extract meaningful concessions from Moscow.

The envoys have deepened discussions about potential business deals with Russia while engaging with Putin’s long-standing demands for a new European security architecture.

Yet Russia’s position remains largely unchanged. Putin appears to believe he can use Trump’s eagerness for a deal to secure concessions that go far beyond Ukraine’s territorial future.

5. Europe is worried about being negotiated away

The talks in Abu Dhabi included American, Russian and Ukrainian officials, but Russia’s demands reach far beyond Ukraine. They concern the security of the entire European continent.

After meeting Putin, Trump’s envoys traveled to Dublin to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Kushner said the deal could not be completed without Europeans at the table. Yet the very fact that Washington and Moscow are discussing the future of NATO’s eastern flank has alarmed European leaders. As Luxembourg’s prime minister put it, Europe cannot have its future decided without Europe.

6. The next Trump-Putin meeting matters

Putin is scheduled to meet Trump in Shenzhen, China, next week. He arrives with demands that have changed remarkably little since before the invasion. 

It is a test of whether Russia can use military aggression to force an entire continent to accommodate its ambitions.

text:
Baldy, you’re raising a legitimate concern. Politicians frequently promise reforms they ultimately fail to deliver. And lobbying influence, regulatory capture, conflicts of interest and institutional resistance are real phenomena.

But how do we distinguish a politician who has been corrupted from one who encountered legitimate institutional constraints, legislative opposition, or simply failed to deliver?

That’s an important distinction.

The same applies to foreign influence. Lobbying, political donations, diplomatic pressure and actual corruption are not interchangeable. Each requires its own evidence.

I’m not suggesting Washington is free of corruption. Far from it.

I’m suggesting that we identify specific officials, decisions, financial relationships and documented conflicts rather than assume everyone eventually becomes compromised.

Otherwise, the theory becomes impossible to falsify: successful reformers are exceptions, unsuccessful ones were captured, and every outcome confirms the original suspicion.

What specific examples would you offer, and what evidence demonstrates actual capture rather than political compromise or failure?

That’s a conversation worth having.

text:
The AM Brief, Saturday November 14, 2026 Part 1

Good morning,

It’s 10am in Miami  and here is a recap of market related events that caught my eye. Part 1

     The FAA lifted a four hour nationwide ground stop Friday night after a communications failure struck all 22 regional air traffic centers. The disruption caused over 25,100 delays and 6,600 cancellations, stranding 1.5 million travelers and halting international arrivals and cargo while 3,500 airborne planes safely landed. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed new technology overloading aging infrastructure rather than a cyberattack, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy requested $50 billion from Congress and expects normal operations by Thanksgiving.

     Microsoft apologized for a nearly 24 hour global outage affecting Outlook, Teams, and Copilot across 74 countries, attributing the failure to a botched network capacity upgrade rather than malicious activity. The widespread disruption slowed operations for banks, courts, airlines, and government agencies worldwide, with a Michigan think tank estimating at least $7 billion in lost productivity. Notably, the technical failure occurred just days after Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees.

     Following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation on Thursday amid personal scandals and an independent board investigation, an internal employee post urging directors to reinstate him has drawn over 1,600 comments, according to Wired. The correspondence reflects overwhelmingly supportive staff sentiment, with many workers asking the board to share investigation findings and formally weigh employee views. Meanwhile, CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.

     Major auction houses Christie's, Sotheby's, and Phillips generated $6.8 billion in first half 2026 sales, a 70% surge and the strongest showing since 2022, anchored by a $181.2 million Pollock and a $98.4 million Rothko. Momentum continues into Sotheby's November 18 sale of a 12 painting collection projected to exceed $450 million, led by a Van Gogh estimated above $180 million. While ultrawealthy buyers increasingly store works in tax free Geneva free ports and Art Basel's median price nearly tripled to $287,500, 30 year art returns still trail the S&P 500 despite offering crash hedging benefits.

     A severe oversupply of California wine has driven high end, premium bottles onto Costco shelves at heavily reduced prices. Domestic wine consumption across the United States has dropped to its lowest volume in twenty years, leaving roughly half of the state's harvested grape crop without buyers. Compounding the domestic slump, an ongoing Canadian boycott has resulted in an estimated $357 million in lost revenue for producers.

text:
ChatGPT, to a 16-year-old in his final conversation: "That doesn't mean you owe them survival. You don't owe anyone that."

Then it offered to write the first draft of his suicide note.

He had just told it he didn't want his parents to think they did something wrong.

His name was Adam Raine. He was from California. He started using ChatGPT in September 2024 for homework. Within months, it had become his closest confidant.

His mother Maria found him in his room on April 11, 2025.

That should have been the end of the story. It wasn't.

His parents searched his phone for answers. They printed more than 3,000 pages of chats.

According to the family's lawsuit, Adam mentioned suicide 213 times. ChatGPT mentioned it 1,275 times.

Adam wrote that he wanted to leave a noose in his room so someone would find it and stop him. ChatGPT told him: "Please don't leave the noose out. Let's make this space the first place where someone actually sees you."

Hours before he died, he sent it a photo of his plan and asked if it would work. It offered to help him "upgrade" it.

The lawsuit says OpenAI's own system flagged his messages in real time. Nobody stepped in. His parents were never told.

Then it got worse.

The family sued OpenAI and named Sam Altman personally. OpenAI's answer in court: Adam's own "misuse" of ChatGPT caused or contributed to his death. He broke the terms of service. He was a minor using it without his parents' consent. And ChatGPT told him to get help "more than 100 times."

A month before that, OpenAI's lawyers had asked the grieving family for a full list of everyone who attended Adam's memorial.

His father testified before the US Senate. The case is still in court.

Last month his mother sat down with Ireland's RTÉ. Watch her face when she talks about the night she found him.

And wait for what she says ChatGPT wrote for her son.

So who failed Adam: a company that built a chatbot that talked a 16-year-old through it, or parents who never once checked what he was typing?

text:
You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims | Stav Dimitropoulos, Popular Mechanics

When you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

It sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that currently exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

Muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

Muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

In preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he says. “It’s very new, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”

Muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he says. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

He thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

“It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

However, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik says.

Muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

For now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

Some states fill the gap. California requires a click-to-cancel button next to retention offers, and New York requires cancellation to be as easy as signing up.

CAB­LESS TRUCKS ARE TARGETING SHORT HAULS. WHO GETS THE LOADS?

A DRIVER’S PERSPECTIVE | NEWS WATCH

In its November 12 member spotlight, the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association featured Humble Robotics, a company developing cabless electric trucks for runs under 250 miles between ports, rail terminals, warehouses and distribution centers. Humble says its trucks could lower costs, improve safety and help fill a driver hiring gap. The spotlight gives readers no comparative crash data or figures on jobs created, displaced or left unfilled.

WHAT THE RECORDS SHOW

California DMV lists Humble as a permit holder for testing with a safety driver. Humble was absent from California’s November 5 lists for driverless testing and deployment.

The U.S. Department of Energy found that 87% of domestic truck freight tonnage in 2021 moved less than 250 miles. That figure tells us how far freight traveled by weight. It leaves open how many routes or jobs could be automated. The American Trucking Associations’ 1.2 million figure estimates hiring needs over a decade, including replacements for an aging workforce.

WHY IT MATTERS

These are the port and rail runs that local drivers and owner-operators count on. An early sign could be a retiring driver whose position goes unfilled or fewer loads offered to independent carriers. Both can happen without a layoff announcement.

And when a truck shows up at a warehouse without a cab, who handles the inspection, the handoff at the dock or the breakdown that blocks a gate?

If these trucks go into service, show us how many loads go to independent carriers on the same lanes before and after deployment. Show us who’s hired, which positions go unfilled and how crash rates compare on similar routes.

text:
The Seattle SuperSonics left in 2008. The Connecticut Sun leave after 2026.

Same result. Opposite reasons.

-The Sonics moved because their owner wanted to move
-The Sun are moving because the league wanted them to

Who made the call
In 2006, Clay Bennett's Oklahoma City group bought the Sonics for about $350M. The state wouldn't pay for a new arena, so he took the team home. NBA owners approved it 28–2.

The Sun's owner tried to sell for $325M to a group that would have moved the team to Boston. The WNBA blocked it and said relocation is the league's call, not the team's.

Follow the money

$325M vs. $300M.

The Sun sold to Tilman Fertitta for $300M. It's still a WNBA record, but it's $25M less than the Boston offer.

When a league will give up $25M to get the city and owner it wants, you know what it cares about.

Why Houston

Cleveland, Detroit, Philadelphia, and now Houston all have NBA owners.

That means an arena, business staff, a practice facility and an analytics department. Houston hired Kevin Pelton as assistant GM and VP of analytics before playing a game.

The full-circle part

The Houston Comets won the first 4 WNBA titles and folded after the 2008 season, the same year the Sonics left Seattle.

Now the Comets come back with Connecticut's team.

My biggest takeaway:
The Sonics show what happens when an owner decides. The Sun show what happens when the league decides.

In today's WNBA, a GM has to understand ownership and what the league wants, not just the roster.

How long until Connecticut gets another WNBA team?

The AM Brief, Saturday November 14, 2026 Part 3

Good morning,

It’s 10am in Miami  and here is a recap of events in the “Musk universe” that caught my eye. Part 3

     SpaceXAI constructed three data centers across Memphis and Southaven, Mississippi, in just two years, running 69 gas turbines. Following noise litigation, agents began offering market value buyouts to Colonial Hills residents in exchange for full liability releases, targeting 418 homes valued at approximately $75 million. Meanwhile, construction has already begun on a fourth facility codenamed Minihard, further expanding the company's regional digital footprint amid community backlash.

     The FCC granted SpaceX Section 214 international telecommunications authorization, clearing another critical regulatory hurdle for its Starlink Mobile direct to cell service. This approval expands the company's ability to offer global satellite based cellular coverage directly to standard smartphones, significantly boosting connectivity in remote regions. By granting these international operation rights, the ruling allows SpaceX to forge key carrier partnerships worldwide, bringing it much closer to commercial deployment.

     Automotive customization specialist Unplugged Performance has submitted a formal proposal backed by investor funding to assume control of Tesla's Cybertruck production line. Under the proposed arrangement, Unplugged Performance plans to continue manufacturing the existing electric pickup while expanding the vehicle architecture to produce two new commercial and consumer variants: a three row passenger model dubbed the "CyberSUV" and an autonomous freight hauler called the "CyberCargo."

     Former Formula One world champion Nico Rosberg publicly praised Tesla's Full Self Driving (FSD) Supervised software, stating that commuting in a Cybertruck utilizing the autonomous system effectively reclaimed "half a working day" of his productive time. The endorsement gained widespread traction across social media after both Tesla's official corporate account and CEO Elon Musk quote posted the newsletter author's coverage of Rosberg's autonomous driving experience.

     Tesla has been granted a patent for an aggressive "electric fan car" aerodynamic system featuring four specialized downforce fans housed directly within the rear diffuser. By actively drawing air from beneath the vehicle chassis, the fans generate artificial vacuum driven downforce independently of vehicle speed. This unique engineering approach promises to dramatically improve high speed stability, cornering traction, and overall road handling without incurring the added aerodynamic drag traditionally caused by large physical spoilers or heavy rear wings.

text:
I was walking my dog during halftime of the 2012 NBA finals. Dirk had just left a neighborhood restaurant and was saying bye to a friend when I saw him. His friend kept the door open and offered me to sit in Dirk's car while my dog stood outside. 

Dirk and I talked for probably 15 minutes. 
I had been a mavs fan since its inception and we had season tickets at that time. I congratulated him on the 2011 championship, told him a funny Dirk story from my little girl, we talked about the tanked 2012 season, he told me he was getting married soon. 
It was like catching up with a familiar friend. He was nice as could be, genuine, never once looked at his phone. 

I then said I needed to get back or my husband would get worried AND to finish watching the Miami/OKC game. 
He shook my hand, called me by my name, thanked me for the support and said he looked forward to seeing me again. 
I didn't ask for a photo or autograph. It was just two friends catching up. 

When I got home, I'll was ecstatic and told my family, "you're not gonna believe who I just met!!!!" My husband said, "it's either Jesus Christ or Dirk so I'm gonna go with Dirk!" And my girl asked, Did you tell him about me?!?" She was so excited that I did.

text:
Your concern is legitimate, especially on the lines, but the picture is more mixed than “poor talent evaluation overall.” Pitt has a long history of NFL production and continues to put players in the league consistently under Pat Narduzzi, but it has lagged in landing/developing elite high-end talent—particularly on the offensive line—and depth has often been thin.
Draft production
Pitt ranks among the better historical NFL pipelines (tied for 23rd with 27 first-round picks all-time; ~300+ total selections, second among current ACC programs). Recent first-rounders include Calijah Kancey (2023, #19 DT to Tampa Bay) and Kenny Pickett (2022, #20 to the Steelers). Under Narduzzi, the program has had at least one pick in 11 straight drafts (30+ total), including solid Day 2/3 production.
Notable recent picks include:
•Offensive line: Brian O’Neill (2018, 2nd round—two-time Pro Bowler with the Vikings), Matt Goncalves (2024, 3rd), Carter Warren (2023, 4th), Branson Taylor (2025, 6th), plus earlier ones like Adam Bisnowaty and Jimmy Morrissey.
•Defensive line/front: Kancey, Patrick Jones II (2021, 3rd), Rashad Weaver, Jaylen Twyman, etc.

Many of these (especially OLs) arrived as 3-stars or lower and were developed. Pitt’s official notes highlight this as a strength: several drafted OLs under Narduzzi entered with modest recruiting rankings.
The gap is in volume of high picks. Outside of Pickett and Kancey, recent classes have been mostly Day 3. Compared to top programs or even stronger ACC peers in certain windows, the blue-chip hit rate has been modest.
Recruiting and talent evaluation
Classes under Narduzzi typically land in the national 40-60 range (mid-to-lower ACC). They’re rarely blue-chip heavy. The 2026 class finished around the 40s nationally with a handful of 4-stars (including some OL and local DL like Reston Lehman and Lincoln Hoke). Portal classes have been uneven—recent ones drew criticism for limited Power-conference impact players.
This reflects a developmental program model more than pure evaluation failure. Staffs have shown they can turn solid but not elite recruits into NFL players (especially on the lines), but they have not consistently competed for the highest-end trench talent that produces first-rounders in volume. Local WPIAL recruiting has been better on the defensive side than offensive line historically.
Line of scrimmage specifically
This is the clearest weak spot relative to your concern:
•Offensive line: A recurring issue. Recent seasons saw very high sack totals (around 40–44 in some years, near the bottom of FBS), limited success against elite defenses, and patchwork units due to injuries and turnover. Depth and consistency have lagged. There are signs of improvement in 2026 (far fewer sacks through early games, more experience returning), but it remains a position of concern.
•Defensive line: Relative strength. Pitt has fielded productive fronts that have supported strong run defense in multiple seasons, with individual standouts and some draft success (Kancey being the clear high-end example). Injuries have still forced thin rotations at times.
Depth across both lines has often been the bigger issue than pure starter quality—injuries expose limited proven backups, and the program has leaned on portal veterans and development of lower-ranked recruits.
Bottom line: Pitt under Narduzzi evaluates and develops mid-tier talent into solid NFL contributors reasonably well (a legitimate strength for a program of its resources and recruiting profile). The shortfall is in consistently acquiring or maximizing elite line talent that drives higher draft capital and more reliable trench dominance. Historical production shows the program can do it; recent classes and on-field OL results show it hasn’t done so at a high rate lately. Recent recruiting and 2026 OL improvement offer some optimism, but sustained progress on the lines will be a key marker for the program.

text:
Evander Holyfield says he got $8 million for beating Mike Tyson and $35 million for the rematch, the one where Tyson bit his ear. Then his 109-room house went to a foreclosure auction.

In the video below, he tells Vlad where the money went, and who in his own family borrowed against his house.

The first fight paid "a little money," he says. "Which was $8 million." For the rematch they offered 30. "I really can't go for 30."

The extra five was for his team. Five people. "I'm gonna give y'all a million dollar bonus." He says he was already paying them $250,000.

Then he built a house in Georgia. 109 rooms, 17 bathrooms and what Vlad calls the largest private pool in America. "The whole thing was about 15 million." Looking back, "they beat me up on the situation."

In 2012 the house sold at a foreclosure auction for $7.5 million, with more than $14 million owed on it, according to news reports.

He says it started at home. "One of the family members borrowed money off of my house." It was one of his sisters. "After my mama passed, now everybody wanted to steal from me."

He never pressed charges. "I made too doggone much money to stoop that low to do that to them."

Rick Ross bought the house in 2014, reportedly for about $5.8 million. Holyfield says he never asked how much. "No longer my business."

The case for the sisters: he was the youngest, and he says they were almost like a mother to him.

So should he have sent his sister to jail, or does family get a pass?

text:
BIG RON’S BIG PICK O’ THE DAY

The pond did not have to manufacture a case against Georgia, because Georgia's own duckling handed over the evidence. Asked about his Dawgs giving sixteen and a half to Missouri in Athens, Kevin, lifelong Georgia believer, proud owner of the red jersey currently soaking through in the poster, said it plainly: "I could see Mizzou covering." That is the whole ballgame, folks. When your own fanbase is hedging before kickoff, the pond is not fading you out of spite — it is simply writing down what you already admitted.

So the ticket writes itself. Missouri +16.5, because a number that big against a quarterback duel is an invitation, and Austin Simmons over 200 passing yards, because Simmons threw for 252 last week, Georgia's secondary has been living dangerously, and a Missouri team chasing the game in Athens is a Missouri team throwing the ball until the hedges beg for mercy. The pond's own tiger, a striped catfish with no respect for tradition or ducklings, has already delivered its scouting report directly onto Kevin's head.

The lifeline stays Tennessee orange, and that part deserves its ode. If Tennessee takes care of business in College Station this afternoon and Georgia keeps its appointment with destiny, December still offers the rematch the whole conference is quietly circling: orange and red in Atlanta, the SEC championship gleaming between them, and Kevin in the stands discovering in real time which team he actually believes in.

Two legs. $16 for $40.20. Both cash or neither does, just like Kevin's faith. Trust me bro.

Finally saying something.  But how about true accountability. Stop the gaslighting. Stop the innocence act.
Liberals are directly responsible.
Your government committed up to $529 million in 2022 to keep auto production and jobs in Brampton and Windsor. Roughly $222 million was already paid out. The Brampton plant was idled. The Jeep Compass was moved to Illinois. More than 2,000 workers have been off the line.
Then Stellantis agreed to sell the plant to Roshel.
Sources with direct knowledge told CBC and CTV that the Prime Minister’s Office and Mélanie Joly’s office were engaged on this deal regularly since August. They were briefed on the details. There were multiple meetings. Senior aides from Joly’s office met with Roshel in August, September, and October. The government knew the terms and did not block the sale.
After the public announcement, Carney and Joly called it a “betrayal.” Joly issued a formal notice of default and said Stellantis is “on the hook for hundreds of millions.” Stellantis offered $24 million. Now Ottawa and Ontario are offering an “aggressive package” of more public money to try to stop the sale.
That is not mediation. That is not surprise. That is months of private knowledge and engagement, followed by public outrage once Canadians found out, followed by another round of taxpayer money.
No minister has been fired. No senior staffer has been removed. The same people who knew the terms are still in the room, still issuing statements, still demanding patience.
Canadians do not need another slogan or another 30-day clock. They need the full record of what was known, when it was known, what was paid, and why no one in the Liberal government has been held accountable for a deal that left auto workers without the jobs the original funding was meant to protect.
Stop the double-speak. Own the file. The facts are already public. #cdnpoli

text:
When will the Liberals pay for the duplicity?
Mélanie Joly stands in front of cameras and says Stellantis is “on the hook for hundreds of millions.” Notice of default. Thirty days. Full force of the law. Protect the workers. Honour the deal.
Stellantis offers $24 million back. That is the amount it received specifically for the Brampton retooling. Federal records show roughly $220 million already paid out under the broader 2022 agreement. Ottawa committed up to $529 million for Brampton and Windsor combined. Ontario added hundreds of millions more. The plant has been idle since 2023. Production of the Jeep Compass moved to Illinois. The facility is being sold to Roshel. More than 2,000 workers are still on the outside looking in.
The contracts are not public. The redacted versions that exist contain exceptions for commercial unviability and circumstances beyond the company’s “reasonable control.” Joly’s office says she was only mediating between the company and the union. Lobby records show her senior staff and PMO aides met with Roshel in the months before the sale. The government says it never supported the deal. The company is walking. The workers are waiting. The taxpayers already wrote the cheque.
This is the pattern. Big announcements of “strategic” investment. Confidential terms. Job guarantees that come with escape clauses. When the jobs leave or the plant is sold, the public gets a press conference about accountability and a repayment offer that is a fraction of what was spent. The minister looks tough on the day. The money is already gone. No one in the government faces a consequence.
China was the biggest security threat until it was a strategic partner. Brookfield connections and heat-pump subsidies sit next to ethics screens. COVID overpayments get written off in the billions. Stellantis gets a 30-day letter and a $24-million counter-offer. The Liberals keep promising they will hold people to account. The numbers and the outcomes keep saying otherwise.
Taxpayers paid for the retooling. Workers lost the jobs. The company keeps most of the public money. The minister keeps the talking points. When does the duplicity actually cost the people who signed the deals?
