text:
BREAKING UPDATE: MULTIPLE BOMBS REPORTED IN PEORIA, ILLINOIS

A massive emergency response is underway in Peoria and East Peoria, Illinois, where thousands of residents have been told to evacuate following a credible bomb threat at the BioUrja Renewables facility, formerly known as the ADM plant, on Friday evening, November 13.

According to The Daily Dossier on Facebook, reports are circulating that as many as 6 explosive devices have been located, with the page reporting that 4 have been confirmed. Information shared from a reported 10:50 p.m. press briefing indicates that at least 1 device was identified as a bomb, that it may have been deactivated, and that authorities were concerned additional devices could exist.

The situation has prompted evacuations within approximately a 1-mile radius of the BioUrja facility at 1 Edmund Street. The evacuation area includes portions of downtown Peoria, the Warehouse District, South Peoria, and areas across the Illinois River in East Peoria. Officials have released a map showing the affected areas highlighted in green and are urging everyone within that perimeter to leave immediately.

The FBI, Illinois State Police, local law enforcement agencies, fire departments, and bomb disposal personnel are involved in the emergency response. According to the information shared from the late-night briefing, restrictions have also been placed on barge traffic along the Illinois River, while Interstate 74 access and downtown bridges have been affected. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker is monitoring the situation.

The evacuations have created significant disruptions throughout the area. Numerous ramps leading from I-74 into Peoria have been closed, along with streets throughout the evacuation zone. Downtown access is severely restricted, and motorists are being directed away from the affected areas.

Emergency shelters have been established at Manual Academy, located at 811 S. Griswold Street in Peoria, and EastSide Centre in East Peoria. Friday night’s Jon Pardi concert at the Peoria Civic Center was canceled, and Caterpillar instructed employees not to report for their third shift.

The situation is also bringing out some remarkable kindness from local residents. In a Facebook group called Citizens of East Peoria, a woman in Morton offered to open her home to displaced mothers and children who needed somewhere to rest, watch movies, or spend the night. Other residents reported that nearby hotels were evacuating guests as well, adding to the number of families searching for accommodations.

The evacuation orders remain in effect according to the latest information available to me, and authorities have urged residents not to return until an official all-clear is issued.

This remains an active and developing investigation. The reported number of explosive devices has not been independently confirmed, and additional information is expected as law enforcement continues its work.

Sources: Peoria Police Department, City of East Peoria, 25News Now, WMBD, WCBU, CBS Chicago, The Daily Dossier, and screenshots shared with True Crime Mama.

text:
Japanese garage doors have one setting.

Closed.

In America, a garage door is a language. Nobody teaches it. Everybody speaks it.

Iida, who sits across from me at work, spent two years on a dead-end street outside Louisville, Kentucky, learning it the hard way.

Some context. Iida lived in the same Tokyo apartment building for eleven years. He never learned the name of the man next door. That's not rude in Japan. That's privacy. That's a good neighbor.

His first week in Kentucky, every evening at six, the neighbor across the street opened his garage, turned on a radio, and sat down. On a church pew. Facing the street. For three hours.

His name is Haskell. 68. Retired lineman. Hands like catcher's mitts.

In Japan, a man sitting alone facing the street every night is one of two things. Locked out by his wife. Or employed by the city.

Iida's wife said locked out. Iida said security. They argued about it for a week, through the curtains, very politely not staring.

The second week, Iida couldn't take it anymore. He brought Haskell a gift box of green tea and bowed deeply. The way you visit a man in trouble.

Haskell looked at the tea. Then at Iida. Then he slid over on the pew.

"Well, come on in."

They sat for three hours. Haskell talked about Kentucky basketball. Iida understood maybe nine words. He nodded in all the correct places. Nodding in the correct places is the national sport of Japan.

When it got dark, Haskell explained the law.

DOOR CLOSED: Nobody's home. Or somebody's mad.

DOOR HALF OPEN: Somebody's teenager is in trouble. Keep walking.

DOOR OPEN, NOBODY IN IT: Borrow what you need. Bring it back.
("Even the lawn mower?" "Especially the lawn mower.")

DOOR OPEN, MAN UNDER A TRUCK: Hand him things. Do not ask what's wrong with the truck. He doesn't know either.

DOOR OPEN, TWO MEN, ARMS CROSSED, STARING AT A LAWN MOWER: That's a meeting. You may attend. You may not help.

DOOR OPEN, MAN, RADIO: Come over. Don't talk during free throws.

DOOR OPEN, MAN, RADIO, COOLER: You're staying.

TWO MEN, NOBODY TALKING FOR AN HOUR: That's the best kind of night there is.

Iida wrote it all down, in a notebook with colored tabs. In Japan, when someone explains a rule, you write it down.

The next evening, Iida opened his own garage. First time ever.

He had no pew. He sat on his wife's yoga ball. Facing the street. With a radio. Very proud. Very still, because the ball rolled.

Nobody came.

A teenager on a bike stopped and asked if he was locked out.

The third night, Haskell walked across the street carrying a second church pew.

"Where do you get two church pews?"

"Methodists."

By the fourth night, there were three men in Iida's garage. By October, there were nine. It became the street's garage. Mostly because Iida's wife kept putting out Japanese snacks. The dried squid scared everybody. Then nobody could stop eating it. A man from four streets over came to ask, very seriously, if this was "the Japanese garage."

Haskell's wife came over once. She looked at her husband, on Iida's pew, eating dried squid.

"I haven't seen him since September," she said. "I know exactly where he is. I can see him from my kitchen."

In November, Iida attended his first meeting. Four men, arms crossed, around a lawn mower that would not start. Forty minutes. Nobody touched it. Nobody fixed it. Everybody left happy.

Iida has attended four thousand meetings in Japan. He calls this one the best of his career.

That was the street for two years.

Then the company called him home.

On their last night, the whole street came to his garage one last time. Hugs. Back slaps. Somebody's mother cried.

Haskell offered a handshake. And one word.

"Well."

Iida was a little hurt. He didn't say so.

On Saturday, before six a.m., Iida and his wife loaded the last suitcase into the car. In Japan, you leave quietly. You don't make anyone get up for you.

He backed out. The street was still dark.

Haskell's garage door was open.

Haskell was on his pew. Next to him was the second pew. Empty. Somebody had burned four letters into the end of it with a wood-burning pen.

IIDA.

Iida rolled the window down. Haskell didn't get up. He just lifted his chin toward the empty pew.

"Door's open," he said. "Whenever."

Iida drove on. The next garage was open. And the next.

Every garage on that dead-end street was open. Fourteen of them. Lights on. A man in every one. Coffee mugs instead of coolers. Every radio on the same station, turned down low, so nobody would wake the babies.

A man under a truck rolled out on his creeper and raised a wrench. Two men standing over a dead lawn mower uncrossed their arms and raised their mugs. And in the last garage, in his dad's camping chair, wrapped in a blanket, sat the teenager from the bike. Awake. Before six. On a Saturday.

"That one," Iida told me, "is the one that broke me."

Iida didn't know the word for this. So he used the law. He rolled every window down, found their station, and turned his radio all the way up.

Man. Radio. Windows down. Close enough.

Behind him, garage after garage, back up the dead-end street, fourteen radios went up with it.

So much for the babies.

He had to stop the car twice. A baby woke up. Nobody minded.

Back in Tokyo, his apartment doesn't have a garage. It has a steel front door and a hallway.

But this summer, on hot nights, Iida propped that door wide open, sat in the doorway on a folding stool, and listened to the baseball on the radio.

His Japanese neighbors were confused for three weeks.

On the twenty-third night, the old man from next door came out holding two cans of beer. He sat down beside Iida. Not one word.

His name is Mr. Ota. It took Iida eleven years and one street in Kentucky to find that out.

Best kind of night there is.

Under @UKYpres’s and @UKYmonday’s leadership, UK has investigated a tenured professor over speech outside the classroom, faced litigation over academic freedom and due process, and now proposes sweeping authority to monitor university technology, including personal devices accessing its networks or data.

George Orwell wrote 1984 as a warning about institutional surveillance and control. Eli Capilouto and Eric Monday apparently read it as an instruction guide.

Prospective employees should ask themselves whether they want their careers, personal communications, and academic freedom subject to that kind of administrative discretion.

UK’s leadership has given them plenty of reasons to reconsider.

UNIVERSITY OF KENTUCKY — 15 YEARS OF FACULTY AND STUDENT RIGHTS LITIGATION

SETTLEMENTS AND PAYMENTS

1. Mullins v. Kyrkanides (2018) — $620,000 settlement.

Dentistry professor Raynor Mullins alleged First Amendment retaliation after criticizing proposed Medicaid changes. UK settled before trial and agreed to reemploy him.

https://t.co/8gjpqbMMcU

2. Buck Ryan litigation (2025) — $500,000 settlement.

Journalism professor Buck Ryan brought defamation lawsuits concerning university investigations and accusations about his teaching practices. UK settled two state-court lawsuits and agreed to end its investigation.

https://t.co/NIj3bf2bsK

Former University Senate Council chair DeShana Collett opposed changes to faculty governance. Her agreement required the withdrawal of pending open records requests and restricted future requests.

https://t.co/UibK6VRzBf

Documented payments — $1,495,000.

The total includes two litigation settlements and one employment separation agreement.

ADVERSE COURT RULINGS AND STUDENT DUE PROCESS

4. Doe v. University of Kentucky (2016) — UK lost a motion to dismiss.

A student who reported sexual assault challenged UK’s handling of disciplinary proceedings. A federal court allowed her Title IX lawsuit to proceed. No damages awarded in that ruling.

https://t.co/ZdhPTVzYzY

5. Doe v. University of Kentucky (2017) — UK lost part of a federal appeal.

UK’s own appeals board twice reversed disciplinary decisions against a male student because of due process violations, including withheld evidence and improper communications. The Sixth Circuit reinstated his claim against a university administrator. No damages established.

https://t.co/rTFkvVz5NQ

6. Doe v. University of Kentucky (2020) — UK lost a Title IX appeal.

The Sixth Circuit ruled that a community college student participating in UK programs and living in university housing could pursue Title IX claims against UK. No damages established.

https://t.co/tWmC3qzBqv

7. Doe v. University of Kentucky (2024) — UK lost a Title IX retaliation appeal.

Following allegations involving a student-athlete, UK conducted four disciplinary hearings. Its appeals board overturned the first three decisions because of procedural errors. The Sixth Circuit reversed summary judgment for UK on the reporting student’s retaliation claim. No damages established.

https://t.co/QVaNYkH416

FACULTY SPEECH, ACADEMIC FREEDOM AND DUE PROCESS

8. Woodcock v. University of Kentucky (2026) — UK lost a federal appeal.

UK placed tenured law professor Ramsi Woodcock on administrative leave while investigating controversial political speech. The Sixth Circuit rejected the district court’s abstention ruling and remanded the case. No damages awarded by that ruling.

text:
My Dearest Darlings,

I sure do love @universityofky’s bullshit. 

A word of warning to the University of Kentucky. If UK adopts its proposed technology surveillance policy, President @UKYpres, @UKYmonday, and @UKYprovost had better be prepared to live under the same rules they’re imposing on faculty and staff.

Especially when it comes to their text messages with legislators. Here’s where things get interesting.

In April 2026, the Kentucky Supreme Court ruled in Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources Commission v. Kentucky Open Government Coalition that communications held exclusively on personal devices and accounts, outside an agency’s ownership and control, were not public records under the Kentucky Open Records Act.

UK’s proposed policy attacks the very foundation of that defense. Under KRS 61.870(2), public records include electronic communications prepared, owned, used, possessed, or retained by a public agency. Once UK obtains or uses those communications in conducting university business, the argument that they remain exclusively private falls apart.

And here’s where Eli and Eric should pay close attention. If UK imposes this policy on faculty and staff while exempting its own administrators, selective enforcement opens another avenue for litigation. A court could be asked to compel uniform enforcement, including through a writ of mandamus if the regulation creates a mandatory duty UK refuses to perform.

If enforcement results in UK obtaining or using administrators’ communications, those records become potential targets under the Open Records Act, with KRS 61.882 providing a means to seek judicial enforcement of disclosure.

And for legislators, heads up:  legislative privilege isn’t a blanket shield for records held by UK. The university’s possession and use of communications triggers its own obligations under the Open Records Act. Legislative correspondence does not automatically become exempt simply because a legislator participated in the conversation.

Apply the policy equally to Capilouto, Monday, and the rest of UK’s administration, and suddenly their text messages concerning legislative floor seats, political donations, performance funding, university policy, asking for friends kids to be considered, holding press releases during elections, or requests for helmets, tailgating  or signed basketballs are all could be on the table for open records requests.

Imagine the discovery process when UK has to explain why it monitored faculty and staff while protecting its own leadership from the same scrutiny…I dare their General Counsel to make that argument. If the admin is protected by some miracle from hell, I’m sure we can find staff they’ve been communicating with via message, ping, chat or the like.

Eli and Eric should think carefully about what they’re proposing. UK is giving itself the authority to reach into personal devices while creating the very legal arguments that could expose its own leadership’s communications.

I suspect their messages with legislators would make for some fascinating reading. All it takes  are records produced and an exchange with 1 non protected staff/admin. 

Be careful what you wish for, darling @universityofky and @UK_HealthCare. 

Transparency works both ways, my dearest darlings. Ain’t it delicious? 😋 🤤

Conditioning is just one of the changes Rocky undergoes in the story's five-week span.

text:
🔭 ASTRONOMY PICTURE OF THE DAY (APOD) 🌌

Discover the cosmos, one extraordinary image at a time. Every day, explore a different corner of our fascinating universe through a remarkable astronomical image, accompanied by insights from a professional astronomer.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌌 NOVEMBER 14, 2026

🚀 APOLLO 12 AND SURVEYOR 3

More than half a century ago, a human explorer walked across the lunar surface to visit a robotic pioneer. Their remarkable encounter remains a testament to humanity's determination to explore the unknown.

📸 IMAGE CREDIT: Apollo 12, Alan Bean — Stereo Image Copyright: Kevin Frank

✨ THE COSMIC STORY

Put on your red-and-blue glasses and prepare to take a remarkable journey across the western Ocean of Storms on the Moon.

Today's extraordinary three-dimensional photograph takes us back to November 1969, when Apollo 12 astronaut Pete Conrad approached an unusual visitor on the lunar surface: Surveyor 3, a robotic spacecraft that had arrived there more than two years earlier.

Surveyor 3 had landed in April 1967, settling onto the inside slope of a small lunar crater. Its mission was to examine the lunar landscape and help prepare the way for future human exploration.

And that preparation would soon prove invaluable.

In November 1969, Apollo 12 became the second crewed mission to land on the Moon. Astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean touched down in the Lunar Module Intrepid, bringing humanity back to the lunar surface just four months after the historic Apollo 11 landing.

But Apollo 12 had a particularly interesting destination.

The mission was deliberately targeted near Surveyor 3, allowing the astronauts to examine the spacecraft, photograph it, and retrieve components for examination back on Earth.

The distance between the two spacecraft was remarkably small.

Intrepid landed less than 200 meters (approximately 650 feet) away from Surveyor 3.

In other words, the astronauts were within comfortable moonwalking distance of their robotic predecessor.

Imagine the extraordinary sight: a spacecraft that had spent more than two years alone on the Moon, suddenly receiving a visit from human explorers.

Surveyor 3 had been designed to investigate the lunar environment. Now, its own surroundings were being examined by astronauts who had traveled nearly a quarter of a million miles from Earth.

The photograph presented here offers something particularly special.

It is not an ordinary photograph but a stereo anaglyph, a technique that creates the illusion of three-dimensional depth when viewed through red-and-blue glasses.

The image was carefully constructed from two separate photographs taken on the lunar surface: AS12-48-7133 and AS12-48-7134.

Each photograph captures nearly the same scene from a slightly different viewpoint, approximating the separation between human eyes. When combined, they allow our brains to perceive depth, bringing the lunar landscape to life.

Beyond the far crater wall, the Lunar Module Intrepid can be seen on the horizon, marking the location where Conrad and Bean had arrived.

More than a beautiful lunar photograph, this image preserves a remarkable meeting between two generations of exploration: one robotic, the other human.

🌀 THE WONDER BENEATH THE STARS

There is something profoundly moving about this encounter.

Surveyor 3 arrived on the Moon as a pioneer, sent ahead to investigate a world humanity had never walked upon. More than two years later, human explorers arrived to examine the very landscape it had helped us understand.

One mission prepared the way for another.

Today, we can look back at this photograph and see more than a lunar crater, a spacecraft, and two astronauts carrying out their mission.

We see the extraordinary progression of discovery: machines venturing into the unknown, humans following their paths, and each achievement making the next one possible.

The Moon may be our nearest celestial neighbor, but its surface preserves some of humanity's most remarkable stories.

And sometimes, the most extraordinary encounters are not between distant worlds, but between the explorers who make it possible to reach them.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔭 TOMORROW'S PICTURE: WHAT'S NEXT?

🌠 Meteors Through Orion

The night sky has another spectacular performance waiting for us. Tomorrow, we'll turn our attention toward the constellation Orion, where meteors streak across the darkness in a dazzling celestial display.

Keep looking up. The universe never runs out of wonders.

你考上了一所顶尖大学的计算机专业。
父母给你买了一台高配电脑，叮嘱你大学四年好好学技术。
但你刚上大一，大模型就彻底爆发了。
你没有把它当成替自己写作业的工具，而是第一次意识到——这个时代，真正的程序员可能拥有了一台前所未有的“第二大脑”。
大一，你加入了ACM校队。
别人还在苦苦研究暴力枚举，你让AI帮你分析题解、寻找规律，然后自己重新推导一遍。
不会的算法，你就去学。
不会的数据结构，你就去补。
一道题不会，就再写十遍。
第一次参加校赛，你连铜牌都没拿到。
第二次，拿到了银牌。
第三次，你们开始冲击ICPC区域赛。
你逐渐发现，AI并没有让算法变得没有意义。
恰恰相反。
当别人还在花几个小时查一个模板的时候，你已经可以把时间全部投入到更困难的问题本身。
你让AI解释源码、检查思路、寻找反例、模拟面试官。
但最终敲下代码、调通程序、在比赛结束前提交Accepted的人，依然是你。
大二，你一手抓学业，一手抓竞赛。
白天上课，晚上训练。
数据库、操作系统、计算机网络、编译原理，一门都没落下。
周末泡在机房。
有时候凌晨两点走出实验楼，校园里已经没有多少人。
你也不是没有想过放弃。
毕竟隔壁宿舍的人正在打游戏，朋友圈里的人正在旅游。
但你知道，真正决定一个人几年后站在哪里的，从来不是某一个晚上多睡了两个小时。
而是四年下来，你究竟积累了什么。
大三，你开始参加科研和开源项目。
你不再满足于“会调用API”。
你开始研究Transformer、RAG、Agent、推理优化、分布式系统。
看不懂论文，就让AI陪你啃。
看不懂源码，就让AI陪你拆。
实验跑不通，就让AI帮你定位问题。
但每一个实验结果、每一次失败、每一行最终进入项目的代码，都经过你的手。
你逐渐发现：
AI并没有让真正优秀的人失去价值。
它只是把优秀的人，变得更加可怕。
别人一天写五百行代码。
你借助AI可以写五千行。
别人三天读完一个项目。
你可以一天读完十个。
但前提是——你知道什么值得读，什么值得写，什么是对的，什么是错的。
大三暑假，你拿到了第一份大厂实习。
第一次走进真正的研发团队，你才发现大学里学的那些东西并没有白学。
操作系统、网络、数据库、算法、工程能力，终于全部变成了现实世界里的生产力。
你开始真正理解什么叫工程。
什么叫性能。
什么叫稳定性。
什么叫一个系统上线之后，凌晨三点突然挂掉，而你必须把它修好。
实习结束，你拿到了留用意向。
但你没有停下来。
大四，你继续准备ICPC，继续做科研，继续写论文，继续实习。
一手抓学业，一手抓科研。
一手抓竞赛，一手抓工程。
你的简历开始变得越来越长。
ACM/ICPC奖项、科研论文、开源项目、大厂实习、GitHub贡献、技术博客……
毕业的时候，你发现自己甚至不知道应该选哪一家公司的Offer。
国内头部互联网公司给了你Offer。
AI独角兽给了你Offer。
海外科技公司也给你发来了面试邀请。
你最终选择继续深造。
因为你发现，比起立刻拿到一份不错的工资，你更想看看人工智能这个领域的边界究竟在哪里。
于是你进入顶尖实验室。
硕士期间，你继续研究Agent、RAG和AI系统。
你第一次作为一作发表论文。
第一次参加国际顶会。
第一次在论文里写下自己的名字。
第一次发现，自己几年前在机房里熬夜刷过的那些题、读过的那些论文、写过的那些代码，正在一点一点变成真正属于自己的东西。
毕业之后，你没有停下。
你通过人才计划、科研合作、海外访问、顶级实验室招聘等各种机会，进入了世界顶尖的AI研究机构攻读博士学位。
在那里，你每天面对的已经不是课堂作业。
而是下一代模型。
下一代Agent。
下一代AI基础设施。
你的同事来自世界各地。
有人来自MIT，有人来自Stanford，有人曾经在Google DeepMind、OpenAI、Anthropic、Meta等顶级机构工作。
你第一次感觉到，自己真正进入了这个行业的最前沿。
而这一切，并不是因为你比所有人聪明。
只是因为很多年前，当所有人都在问：
“AI以后会不会取代程序员？”
你问的是：
“如果AI真的这么强，我怎样才能成为最会使用它的人？”
后来，你真的做到了。
某一天，你坐在办公室里，看着HR把最终Offer递到你面前。
年薪超过一百万美元。
你没有立刻签字。
只是突然想起很多年前的那个晚上。
那时候你还只是一个刚进入大学的学生。
你坐在机房里，第一次打开大模型。

10,932 signatures on the petition from Preservation Thurmond as I type this update, and it’s looking like we’re going to lose. 

The National Park Service is tearing down structures and it begins next week. Equipment is being moved in tomorrow. 

They have released RFP’s for some structures literally yesterday. The Dun Glen Ark, Mini Ark, and Boat Storage Rack request for proposals are open and offers are due January 15, 2027. 

In my belief, this wouldn’t have happened without you all. They have felt the media pressure and it has taken forever it seems to get to that win, even. 

I’m at a loss for the lack of care or concern for our important history that could have been restored and sustainably ran if someone who owned it cared. A majority of these structures are not beyond repair and have had work completed to them recently including roofing. It just makes no sense to do this now. 

The NPS owns 80% of Thurmond, and they claim they have “big plans” for saving Commercial Row and such. 

But they also claimed to have “big plans” for what they’re now tearing down. So I guess we’ll see. I do know ALL of our Federal Politicians have been silent and they for sure know what’s going on. 

So what’s evident is they do not care. 

I assure you I care and always will, but we’re in a time in West Virginia where money talks and controls the big ideas that happen here.

Including the demolition of our soul, building by building.

text:
"Not yet. I wanted to discuss our situation first before reaching out to them."

"But we need to give them an answer soon."

"I know." His response came out a little sharper than he intended. He immediately sighed and leaned back in his chair.

"Sorry. I know. I'll handle it."

The girls exchanged glances.

They knew their manager was under just as much pressure as everyone else. He had been running between the hospital, the company, and their schedules for the past week. He was also the one who had to communicate with Ning's family and keep the company updated about her condition.

Diana felt a little guilty for snapping earlier.

"P’Sun..." she began.

Their manager looked at her. "We're not trying to make things harder for you."

"I know, Diana."

"We just don't want to debut without Ning."

"I understand."

March nodded. "We'll wait for her. However long it takes."

Kmar crossed her arms. "We're four. Not three."

Their manager offered them a tired smile. "I know, girls."

He gathered the documents in front of him and stood. "Give me some time. I'll speak with the management and see what we can do. For now, I want the three of you to focus on yourselves and continue preparing. I'll talk to you again once we have a clearer direction."

"Okay, P’Sun," March answered.

"Thank you," Diana added.

Their manager nodded before excusing himself from the conference room. As the door closed behind him, the three girls remained seated, each lost in her own thoughts.

"There's no way we're actually debuting without her, right?" Kmar finally asked.

Diana shook her head. "We won't."

March looked down at the photograph of the four of them sitting on the table. It had been taken during one of their first evaluation days, back when their debut still felt like a distant dream.

She gently ran her thumb over Ning's face.

"We'll wait for you, Ning," she whispered. "Just wake up soon, okay?"

Why Ljungby? 🇸🇪

Because it offers the best of both worlds!

It’s within easy reach of Tylösand and Halmstad, Växjö, Jönköping, Kristianstad, the beautiful Äspet beach, and the charming coastal towns of Ystad and Karlskrona. We love exploring all these places!

The climate is relatively close to what we’re used to in the Netherlands, and there’s something we really value: plenty of space, peace, nature and freedom.

We are buying a secluded house with lots of space and privacy, yet still close to the town centre. Being able to walk or cycle to ICA or Willys for our daily shopping is a big plus!

And with the upcoming Fehmarnbelt Tunnel, travelling by car between Sweden and the Netherlands will become even more convenient.

But perhaps the biggest reason is that we’ve stepped out of the Matrix. We’ve left the rat race behind and no longer have to work for a living. Now it’s time to enjoy life, freedom, nature, travelling and doing what makes us happy.

For us, Ljungby ticks so many boxes. It’s the perfect balance between countryside living and everyday convenience.

So more living. On our own terms. ❤️

She's on track to finish with about 86k more votes than Scott Jensen received in 2022.

But when you look at Wisconsin right next door, the weaknesses become apparent. Tom Tiffany kept his race to single digits in a bad wave without fraud as a glaring issue because he had personality. Tiffany's ads were upbeat and a bit folksy. Very different from the corporate bio look the Demuth campaign tried to sell their girl.

Demuth felt like a living incarnation of "Generic R." Although the double digit beatdown could've been worse, it could've been better too with a more relatable personality. This election showed how much Amy Klobuchar's unsinkable brand has fallen off.

She would've won in 2026 no matter what, but Klob could've been pinned down to single digits if we'd had a better messenger, and downballot damage perhaps mitigated.

This was a tough year for the GOP and I won't condemn Demuth as a "bad" candidate. There was no perfect option. The two alternatives to her in the primary would've performed worse. Still, Minnesota Rs need to look at their shortcomings and refine their top of the ticket next time.

text:
Dallas Stars vs Buffalo Sabres — Oettinger's Stars at home against a leaky Buffalo defence

Preview · NHL · Regular season · Saturday 14 November 2026

Last season these two finished almost level in the table, so it offers little. This season is clearer: Dallas have 22 points from 18 games and have conceded 49 goals, while Buffalo have 20 points from 19 games and have let in 68. Dallas also won the last meeting 4-0 in Buffalo. Dallas at medium confidence.

THE MATCHUP

Dallas finished 2025-26 with 112 points (50-20-12), 7-2-1 over their last ten and five straight wins to end the season, but went out 4-2 to Minnesota in the first round. Buffalo were right behind on 109 points (50-23-9), finished 6-3-1, then beat Boston 4-2 before losing 4-3 to Montréal in the second round.

The meetings lean Dallas. Buffalo won 4-1 in Dallas in December 2025, Dallas won 4-3 in a shootout in Buffalo in April 2026, and on Thursday 8 October Dallas won 4-0 in Buffalo. That makes it 2-1 to the Stars.

Mikko Rantanen leads Dallas with 21 points (nine goals, 12 assists), with Jason Robertson on 20 and Roope Hintz on 17. Buffalo's main threat is Tage Thompson, who has 12 goals and 21 points, followed by Jack Quinn with nine goals and 19 points.

FORM & CONTEXT

Dallas are 10-6-2, 6-3-1 over their last ten, with 52 goals for and 49 against. The last result was a bad one: an 8-3 home defeat to Winnipeg on Thursday. Before that they had won 4-3 at home to San Jose on 7 November. At home they are 6-5-0, on the road 4-1-2.

Buffalo are 8-7-4, 4-4-2 over their last ten, with 55 goals for and 68 against. Their last three games brought a 4-1 home defeat to Vegas on 8 November, an 8-3 home loss to Tampa Bay on Wednesday and a 3-2 overtime loss in Chicago on Thursday. They have been better away (4-1-4) than at home (4-6-0).

The goaltending numbers are the clearest split. Jake Oettinger is 9-4-1 with a .895 save percentage in 14 starts for Dallas. Buffalo's Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen is 5-4-3 at .867 in 11 starts and Colten Ellis 3-3-0 at .873 in seven.

Both teams last played on Thursday, so rest is level.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Goals against. Dallas concede far less often, and Oettinger's numbers are well clear of anything Buffalo have used in net. Buffalo's road record and Thompson's scoring are what keep them in it, and the Stars need to show the Winnipeg game was a one-off.

THE CALL

The table is too close to count, but this season's form, the head-to-head and the goaltending all point to Dallas. With last season's finish essentially level, this stays at medium.

Dallas Stars to win, medium confidence.

    Minnesota Taxpayers are Paying to Train Somalis to Run for Office

    How Rep Ilhan Omar got her start in politics

    By: Daniel Greenfield, November 11, 2026:

    There are 10 Somali elected officials in Minnesota: including Rep. Ilhan Omar. The latest Somali elected official is Abdi Daisane, whose day center received $7.2 million in taxpayer money despite repeated violations, and whose wife reportedly said, “I smuggled myself and jumped over the wall”, and who has just flipped a Minnesota State House seat in St. Cloud.

    The Somali day care center owner joins fellow Somali Minnesota House members Mohamud Noor, Samakab Hussein, and Anquam Mahamoud in the Minnesota State House.

    And Somali activists Zaynab Mohamed and Omar Fateh in the Minnesota State Senate.

    There are now 4 Somali Minnesota State House and 2 State Senate members, and while there isn’t a single African American woman in the Minnesota State Senate, there are multiple African immigrants, even though African Americans make up 8% of Minnesota and Somalis only 1%.

    Other Somali elected officials in the state include Minneapolis Councilman Jamal Osman, St. Louis Park Mayor Nadia Mohamed, and St. Cloud Councilwoman Hudda Ibrahim, whose husband was accused of intimidating voters and who, according to a news story, was caught using an ID with a completely different name during a voter fraud investigation in which a woman in a burka had submitted two absentee ballots.

    There are now more Somalis, Kenyans and Nigerians in the Minnesota State House than African Americans. Nevertheless, taxpayers have been funding an organization that trains Somalis to run for political office.

    Ayada Leads, formerly headed by Minnesota Sen. Zaynab Mohamed, claims that its mission is to “equip New Americans, particularly African Diaspora Women, to excel in leadership positions”. In reality, Ayada is a Somali word, the directors of Ayada Leads are two Somali women with the last name ‘Abdulle’, its program coordinator is another Somali woman named Sagal Ali, and its elected alumni are Somalis.

    Ayada Leads offers to train Somali Muslim candidates in “campaign planning & strategizing”, “fundraising”, “endorsements” and “ground game and field game”.

    The site states that, “Congresswoman Ilhan Omar is the first woman Ayada Leads recruited to run for office” and Habon Abdulle, a Somali immigrant from Mogadishu who heads Ayada Leads was honored by Rep. Omar on the House floor and invited as her guest to the State of the Union address in 2020. Ayada has also taken credit for State Sen. Zaynab Mohamed, State Rep. Hodan Hassan, and Mayor Nadia Mohamed of St. Louis Park, MN whom the Somali political training group describes as “the youngest elected official trained by Ayada Leads”.

    Ayada Leads is a 501(c)(3) non-profit which means its involvement in electoral politics is already legally problematic, but the Somali training group for political candidates has actually been funded by taxpayers through the Minnesota Department of Employment and Economic Development.

    In 2023, Propel Nonprofits, a leftist non-profit hub, announced $3.2M in “infrastructure funding” for “56 culturally led nonprofit organizations” including Ayada Leads so that the Somali campaign training group could hire a “Development Manager and a Community Outreach Coordinator to alleviate their current workload”. Under Naima Farah, a Somali Propel leader, and board member at Reviving the Islamic Sisterhood for Empowerment (RISE), the leftist non-profit had also moved money to Ayada Leads as a “Family Engagement Grant”.

    That funding round had included not only Ayada Leads, but also the Advancing Equity Coalition, of which Ayada is a member, and two other Somali groups: one named “Somali Success”.

    Non-profit money and even taxpayer money has flowed to Ayada Leads despite the fact that the first activity that the Somali organization lists is “Ayada Political Campaign Training.”

    “Our Ayada Political Campaign Training is a must for anyone who has the intention to run for public office,” its website states. “It can give you some much-needed clarity on how the political and electoral processes operate, and how you can fit into them. Before throwing your hat in the ring, it is essential that you know what kind of hat you need, and where the ring is located.”

    The non-profit’s “campaign school curriculum” has “been developed to support budding political leaders in developing the confidence and skills needed to launch winning campaigns” and promises to introduce students to “top political strategists and trainers” who “will share culturally competent expertise on critical elements of campaigning” including “campaign planning & strategizing”, “fundraising”, “endorsements” and “ground and field game”.

    Ayada Leads recruits Somali women looking to get “trained to run for office” or working on a political campaign. And it’s flouting the law by doing it as a 501(c)(3) and taking taxpayer money.

    Despite getting a “Family Engagement Grant” through Propel, Ayada’s Engaged Parent Program features photos of Somali women in hijabs and is yet another political activism training program that “provides participants with knowledge, skills, and motivation to take part in decision-making in their cities and states” complete with “voter education programs”.

    There is a “Born to Lead Program” featuring photos of Rep. Ilhan Omar with Somali women which once again emphasizes “leadership” and “advocacy”.

    Should taxpayers be funding a Somali political training and advocacy program?

    Ayada Leads tries to pretend that it has educational programs and is for women in general, but constantly pivots back to political activism and Somali identity. For example, it promotes “Bashaal Events” which it advertises as, “Bashaal gatherings create spaces for women of all backgrounds and identities to come together and share critical information on leadership opportunities and challenges.” Bashaal, like Ayada, is a Somali word and a Somali concept.

what is indias and Pakistans stance on the fallout of a nuclear strike on Iran?

Summarized India and Pakistan nuclear stances

￼
￼
￼
￼
+6
Pakistan has firmly rejected any role in a nuclear response on Iran's behalf, calling Iranian claims of a "tit-for-tat" nuclear guarantee "fabricated and irresponsible." Its nuclear doctrine is explicitly India-centric and defensive, and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar stated that striking nuclear installations "is a violation of international law." Pakistan condemned US/Israeli strikes on Iran as sovereignty violations and offered "unequivocal" diplomatic support to Tehran, but stopped short of any military commitment. 

 Its core concerns are the precedent of attacks on nuclear infrastructure (given its own status as a nuclear state bordering India), economic fallout from disrupted Gulf energy supplies, and the risk of radioactive contamination crossing its borders. Pakistan has positioned itself as a mediator between Iran and the Gulf states. 

India has taken a measured, non-aligned stance, urging restraint while prioritizing its own strategic interests. 

 Its primary concerns are energy security (over 80% of crude imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz), the safety of 8+ million Indian expatriates in Gulf states, and the viability of its Chabahar Portinvestment. On the fallout question specifically, experts note that while a nuclear strike on Iran's Pickaxe Mountain could send lower concentrations of radioactive particles to northwestern India (Punjab, Rajasthan, J&K, Gujarat) under certain wind conditions, the direct radiation threat is considered minimal due to dilution over distance. India is also wary of the precedent set by strikes on nuclear facilities, given its 1991 agreement with Pakistan not to target each other's nuclear installations. Unlike Pakistan, India has explicitly declined a mediator role, with External Affairs Minister Jaishankar stating India would not act as a "go-between."

text:
Let’s clear your little retarded mind… Ole Miss charters via JetBlue operating out of Tupelo Regional Airport, an hour bus trip from Oxford. KTUP is a small airport with little scheduled commercial traffic, it is uncontrolled after 10pm, and is not a hub or base of operations for JetBlue.

Due to the nationwide ground stop, the JetBlue crew operating the Ole Miss charter certainly would have timed out their duty day before the aircraft could depart. 

Since it isn't a hub or base of operations, no relief crew would have been available to operate the charter tonight and no commercial flights departed from or arrived at KTUP after the ground stop was lifted so none could be flown in.

That means the earliest Ole Miss can depart would be when the rest period for the assigned crew is up, 10 hours, which only begins after the duty day ends. Depending on when that occurred, it is possible their next duty day couldn't even begin until after 8am. Add in an hour to bus/pre-flight, an hour to board, an hour and a half flight into Oklahoma City, an hour to load onto buses and half an hour to bus to Norman it would have been early afternoon before Ole Miss could get to OU.

Even if kick was delayed until evening, that would be pushing it in terms of player safety and it is also unclear if the SEC even offered a late Saturday kick time as an option.

Could an all-out last ditch effort made it work? Sure. But is an Ole Miss-Oklahoma game in mid-November worth making that all-out last ditch effort at the risk of player safety? I would personally say no. Unfortunately that means Oklahoma fans, through no fault of their own, get screwed. Knowing OU fans as I do, they'll find a way to make it hell on Ole Miss Sunday.

text:
A recent study from Trinity College Dublin published in the Journal of Dental Research examined whether lifelong exposure to community water fluoridation is associated with cognitive decline in older adults. 

Researchers analyzed data from 2495 participants in the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing who averaged 65 years of age. 

Lifetime fluoride exposure was carefully reconstructed by linking detailed residential histories to national water fluoride concentration records dating back to the 1964 introduction of fluoridation in Ireland. 

Participants were grouped by the proportion of their lives spent drinking fluoridated water ranging from low to high exposure. 

Cognitive function was measured using the Mini-Mental State Examination and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. 

After adjustment for relevant confounders no significant differences in scores appeared across the exposure groups. 

Cumulative lifetime exposure showed no association with cognitive errors and early-life fluoride exposure did not modify the outcomes. 

The results offer reassurance that Irish fluoridation levels do not relate to poorer cognition in later life among older adults.

Source: Sharma et al., Journal of Dental Research (2026), 

DOI: 10.1177/00220345261490925.

This is long and I apologize but it's definitely why civics get removed meanwhile history repeats itself:

The Machine and the Ballot Box: Why Boss Tweed’s Warning Still Matters Today
In the mid-1800s, New York City was growing faster than it could handle. Hundreds of thousands of poor immigrants, many fleeing the Irish Potato Famine, stepped off boats onto Manhattan’s docks with almost no money and zero safety net. Into that gap walked William "Boss" Tweed and the Tammany Hall political machine.
Tweed understood a simple truth about politics long before modern strategists gave it a name: if you take care of people’s immediate survival needs, they will repay you at the ballot box. Back when cities offered no welfare, unemployment checks, or housing aid, Tammany Hall acted as an unofficial relief agency. Ward bosses met newcomers at the docks with food, temporary shelter, and coal for the winter. If a family faced eviction, a Tweed operative paid the landlord. If a young man got arrested, a friendly judge quietly tossed the case. Most importantly, Tweed controlled tens of thousands of city jobs on the police force, in the fire department, and on public construction crews. Handing out those paychecks created an army of people whose livelihoods depended on keeping Tammany Hall in power.
Tweed genuinely had massive support among working-class New Yorkers, yet he refused to leave any election to chance. To guarantee total control, his inner circle turned the voting system itself into a tool of the machine. In the weeks before major elections, Tammany-controlled local judges ran what critics called "naturalization mills," cranking out tens of thousands of fraudulent citizenship papers—sometimes more than a thousand a day—without checking residency or requiring witnesses. Newly minted citizens were handed pre-filled ballots and walked straight to the voting booth. Meanwhile, paid street gangs traveled from precinct to precinct casting dozens of ballots under fake names, and hand-picked election inspectors stuffed ballot boxes and cooked the final counts. In several Manhattan wards during the 1868 election, Tammany recorded more votes than there were legal residents. Rival poll watchers who tried to object were beaten or arrested on trumped-up charges by Tweed’s police.
Whenever modern debates flare up over voting laws, automatic registration, and immigration policy, people still point back to Tammany Hall as a warning about what happens when political power gets too concentrated. In Colorado, which has become a national focal point for universal mail-in voting and sharp legal battles over election oversight, many critics see echoes of how institutional alignment affects public trust.
Opponents of Colorado’s current direction point to the overlapping roles of Jena Griswold, who oversaw the state’s election system as Secretary of State before winning the Attorney General’s office in 2026, and Phil Weiser, who served as Attorney General before winning the governorship. Critics argue that pairing automatic DMV voter registration and universal mail ballots with state-funded migrant programs and sanctuary-style limits on federal immigration enforcement creates a system that naturally favors the ruling coalition. Those concerns grew louder during court fights in which state leaders pushed back against outside federal reviews of voter registration rolls and opposed ballot measures requiring voter ID for mail-in ballots—moves critics compare to insulating political machinery from independent scrutiny.
Griswold, Weiser, and state election officials reject any comparison to 19th-century machine politics, and there are real structural differences. Unlike Tammany Hall, where party bosses printed their own ballots and hand-counted stuffed boxes with no paper trail, Colorado runs on auditable paper ballots, signature verification, bipartisan election judges, and mandatory post-election audits.

text:
Ole Miss charters via JetBlue operating out of Tupelo Regional Airport, an hour bus trip from Oxford. KTUP is a small airport with little scheduled commercial traffic, it is uncontrolled after 10pm, and is not a hub or base of operations for JetBlue.

Due to the nationwide ground stop, the JetBlue crew operating the Ole Miss charter certainly would have timed out their duty day before the aircraft could depart. 

Since it isn't a hub or base of operations, no relief crew would have been available to operate the charter tonight and no commercial flights departed from or arrived at KTUP after the ground stop was lifted so none could be flown in.

That means the earliest Ole Miss can depart would be when the rest period for the assigned crew is up, 10 hours, which only begins after the duty day ends. Depending on when that occurred, it is possible their next duty day couldn't even begin until after 8am. Add in an hour to bus/pre-flight, an hour to board, an hour and a half flight into Oklahoma City, an hour to load onto buses and half an hour to bus to Norman it would have been early afternoon before Ole Miss could get to OU.

Even if kick was delayed until evening, that would be pushing it in terms of player safety and it is also unclear if the SEC even offered a late Saturday kick time as an option.

Could an all-out last ditch effort made it work? Sure. But is an Ole Miss-Oklahoma game in mid-November worth making that all-out last ditch effort at the risk of player safety? I would personally say no. Unfortunately that means Oklahoma fans, through no fault of their own, get screwed. Knowing OU fans as I do, they'll find a way to make it hell on Ole Miss Sunday.

text:
Val-Tricia Garrett’s life was worth far more than the horrific way it ended. She was a mother, a grandmother, and someone her family should still have beside them.

According to Vicksburg, Mississippi, police, the 53-year-old was killed by her husband of 16 years, 40-year-old Cedric Garrett. Around 7 a.m. Friday, he went live on Facebook discussing what he had done while she lay motionless in the passenger seat.

Her brother learned what happened through a devastating phone call: a friend told him her husband was online saying he had killed his sister.

Around 9 a.m., officers responded to a welfare check behind the Vicksburg Convalescent Home following a report of an armed man inside a vehicle. Police say they spent approximately 20 minutes trying to persuade him to surrender before he killed himself.

Authorities also say the couple had a documented history of domestic violence. That history demands scrutiny. What was reported? What protection was offered? What opportunities existed to intervene?

Val deserved safety, protection, and the chance to grow old with her family.

When domestic violence is already documented, what more must be done to protect victims before another family receives that devastating call?

text:
November Week 2 CNBC Morning Squawk Weekly Wrap

1. Squawk this week centered on the Jensen Huang affair. Huang admitted a relationship with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence has suspected of being a Chinese spy, and apologized. Alice Huang works at Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud firm that is an Nvidia customer and has been accused of helping sanctioned Chinese companies obtain AI chips. The board opened an investigation. President Trump said he spoke with Huang, who denied knowing the woman was a spy, and said the FBI was looking into the matter. On Thursday Huang resigned immediately as president, CEO, and director, and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO.

2. The board hired Wachtell Lipton to examine whether secrets were compromised. A Los Angeles firm filed a shareholder class action against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose. Sen. Chuck Schumer accused Trump of defending Huang at the expense of national security after being briefed more than a year ago. Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office asked the administration to preserve documents on advanced AI chip exports to China, and Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer called for Huang to resign.

3. Analysts cut targets. Bernstein lowered its target to $200 from $400 and downgraded to market perform. Baird cut its target to $200 from $500 and moved to neutral. Morgan Stanley removed Nvidia from its top-picks list. Wells Fargo cut its target to $300 from $315, and Citi to $285 from $315. Dan Ives put Nvidia at $300 a share with Huang as CEO and $225 without him.

4. The stock fell early in the week, bounced in Wednesday premarket, then slid again on reports the board was weighing a removal. On Monday the S&P 500 had its best daily gain since April even without Nvidia leading, as Broadcom and AMD led the chip rally.

5. CoreWeave reported a 168% jump in third-quarter revenue and raised 2026 guidance, sending the stock up more than 16% premarket and lifting other neoclouds. Shares were still down 65% from the May high and more than 40% over the past month. Its 2031 bond yield was above 16%, and five-year CDS exceeded 1,240 bp. Some of Wednesday's gain was given back the next day.

6. Anthropic planned to offer 825 million shares at $70-78, with pricing on 11/18 and trading on 11/19. About 20% of the offering could go to retail investors through platforms including Robinhood, Schwab, and Fidelity.

7. The House voted 211-204 to send an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, leaving little time to act before January. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, lifting Democrats to at least 55 Senate seats. Colom campaigned on pausing new data centers until they pay their own power and water costs.

text:
Computer vision systems are everywhere. They help classify and tag images on social media feeds, detect objects and faces in pictures and videos, and highlight relevant elements of an image. However, they are riddled with biases, and they’re less accurate when the images show Black or brown people and women. And there’s another problem: the current ways researchers find biases in these systems are themselves biased, sorting people into broad categories that don’t properly account for the complexity that exists among human beings. 

Two new papers by researchers at Sony and Meta propose ways to measure biases in computer vision systems so as to more fully capture the rich diversity of humanity. Both papers will be presented at the computer vision conference ICCV in October. Developers could use these tools to check the diversity of their data sets, helping lead to better, more diverse training data for AI. The tools could also be used to measure diversity in the human images produced by generative AI.

Traditionally, skin-tone bias in computer vision is measured using the Fitzpatrick scale, which measures from light to dark. The scale was originally developed to measure tanning of white skin but has since been adopted widely as a tool to determine ethnicity, says William Thong, an AI ethics researcher at Sony. It is used to measure bias in computer systems by, for example, comparing how accurate AI models are for people with light and dark skin. 

But describing people’s skin with a one-dimensional scale is misleading, says Alice Xiang, the global head of AI ethics at Sony. By classifying people into groups based on this coarse scale, researchers are missing out on biases that affect, for example, Asian people, who are underrepresented in Western AI data sets and can fall into both light-skinned and dark-skinned categories. And it also doesn’t take into account the fact that people’s skin tones change. For example, Asian skin becomes darker and more yellow with age while white skin becomes darker and redder, the researchers point out.  

Thong and Xiang’s team developed a tool—shared exclusively with MIT Technology Review—that expands the skin-tone scale into two dimensions, measuring both skin color (from light to dark) and skin hue (from red to yellow). Sony is making the tool freely available online. 

Thong says he was inspired by the Brazilian artist Angélica Dass, whose work shows that people who come from similar backgrounds can have a huge variety of skin tones. But representing the full range of skin tones is not a novel idea. The cosmetics industry has been using the same technique for years. 

“For anyone who has had to select a foundation shade … you know the importance of not just whether someone’s skin tone is light or dark, but also whether it’s warm toned or cool toned,” says Xiang. 

Sony’s work on skin hue “offers an insight into a missing component that people have been overlooking,” says Guha Balakrishnan, an assistant professor at Rice University, who has studied biases in computer vision models. 

Measuring bias

Right now, there is no one standard way for researchers to measure bias in computer vision, which makes it harder to compare systems against each other. 

To make bias evaluations more streamlined, Meta has developed a new way to measure fairness in computer vision models, called Fairness in Computer Vision Evaluation (FACET), which can be used across a range of common tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation. Laura Gustafson, an AI researcher at Meta, says FACET is the first fairness evaluation to include many different computer vision tasks, and that it incorporates a broader range of fairness metrics than other bias tools. 

To create FACET, Meta put together a freely available data set of 32,000 human images and hired annotators from across the world to label them. The annotators were asked to label the images with 13 different visual attributes, such as their perceived age, skin tone, gender representation, hair color and texture, and so on. They also asked the annotators to label people based on what they were doing or what their profession seemed to be, such as hairdresser, skateboarder, student, musician, or gymnast. This, the researchers say, adds nuance and accuracy to bias evaluation.  

Meta then used FACET to evaluate how state-of-the-art vision models performed on different groups of people; the results pointed to big disparities. For example, the models were better at detecting people with lighter skin, even if they have dreadlocks or coily hair. 

Because people around the world bring their own biases to the way they evaluate images of other people, Meta’s efforts to recruit geographically diverse annotators are positive, says Angelina Wang, a PhD researcher at Princeton, who has studied bias in computer vision models. 

The fact that Meta has made its data freely available online will also help researchers. Annotating data is very expensive, so it’s only really accessible to big tech companies at a large scale. “This is a welcome addition,” says Balakrishnan. 

But Wang warns it’s wise to be realistic about how much impact these systems can have. They will likely lead to small improvements rather than transformations in AI. 

“I think we’re still far from nearing something that actually captures how humans represent themselves, and likely we will never reach it,” she says.

text:
“We’ll start marketing again when sales pick up.” I’d love to know where those sales are supposed to come from.

When the Great Depression hit, Kellogg doubled its advertising budget. The average business owner cuts theirs after one slow month.

Kellogg almost got it wrong.

When the Depression started, the company's own directors voted to cut advertising. W.K. Kellogg came back from his home in California and called another meeting. They voted again and added $1 million to the budget.

The company moved into radio and pushed a new cereal called Rice Krispies.

Post was the other big name in cereal.

Post cut.

By the early 1930s Kellogg's profits had gone from about $4.3 million a year to $5.7 million, and it came out of the Depression as the leader in cereal.

Economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi had workers commit ahead of time to putting part of every future raise into savings.

The decision was made once, before the money showed up.

Most of the workers who were offered the plan took it, and 80% of them were still in it four raises later.

In 40 months their savings rate went from 3.5% to 13.6%.

One decision.

Google set its split early. 70% of its resources went to the core business, 20% to businesses close to the core, and 10% to new ideas. Eric Schmidt called it their rule for resource allocation.

Yale sets its endowment spending with a formula. 80% is based on what it spent the year before, and 20% on a fixed rate applied to what the endowment is worth. A great year in the market can't blow the budget up, and a terrible one can't gut it.

Every one of them took the decision away from the month.

Most business owners run a mood budget.

In a good month the money goes to whatever is exciting.

In a bad month growth is the first thing cut.

It feels like judgment. It is a reaction to last month.

Growth spending pays you back months later.

So the decision gets made with the wrong information every time.

You cut in the slow month, right before the spending from a few months back was about to pay off.

Cutting also feels good, because profit goes up right away. A few months later you're wondering where the leads went, and you don't connect it to the cut.

Growth is the one line that can't argue back.

Payroll and rent have to be paid, and nobody sends you a late notice for the marketing you didn't do.

A fixed share also puts a number on paper, so at the end of the year you can see whether it worked.

Set the share once, before the year starts.

1. Pick a share of profit, not a dollar amount. A share shrinks in a bad month and grows in a good one without you deciding anything.

2. Start from your real number. Take what you put back into growth last year as a share of what you made. That was your rate, whether you chose it or not. Now choose it on purpose.

3. Define what counts. Growth is spending meant to bring in new revenue. Replacing a laptop is the cost of staying open.

4. Keep it small enough to keep. A small share you hold all year beats a big one you cut in the first slow month.

5. Decide what it pays for before January. Which channels and which hires. Growth money with no assignment turns back into a mood budget.

6. Move the money on a schedule. Mike Michalowicz built Profit First on this. The percentages are set ahead of time and the money moves on the 10th and 25th of every month.

7. Put one review on the calendar each quarter. That is the only time the share can change, and it changes because of a number you can point to.

8. Leave it alone at both ends. In a month with no profit, the share of nothing is nothing, and the rule already made the cut for you. In a great month the share stays the same and the dollars go up by themselves.

Stop asking how you feel about spending this month.

Set the share once and let the year run on it.

text:
Anytime Barcelona fans want to gaslight people in midfield debates, they bring out the word "technically."

That was how they pushed the Xavi and Iniesta superiority narrative over players like Gerrard, Pirlo, Scholes, Lampard and Vieira. Now they're using the same playbook to push Pedri above Bellingham, Cherki, Bruno Fernandes, Palmer, Ødegaard, Güler and Declan Rice.

The funny thing is that they've never actually come out to define what they mean by "technical."

What exactly makes a midfielder technical? First touch? Ball control? Passing range? Vision? Dribbling? Press resistance?

The irony is that most of the players they dismiss possess those same technical qualities. The difference is that they also offer other dimensions to their game: goals, assists, creativity, physicality, defensive contribution, work rate, leadership and match-winning influence.

Why should technical ability be treated as the ultimate measure of a midfielder while every other quality is treated as secondary?

Being technically gifted doesn't automatically make you the better overall midfielder. Football is not played on a technicality.

text:
Ambassador  Ham, fusion will one day deliver heat in abundance, and Korea's coasts already have heat to spare today. One tower beside a steelworks turns it into 365 million m³ of fresh water and 6–9 TWh a year. The concept was written in Graz by an independent concept developer and is offered to Korea as open prior art, with respect.

HCTGS v49 Korea describes that tower. It takes in seawater by gravity at Pohang, Gwangyang, Ulsan, Yeosu or Daesan and turns industrial heat into fresh water, electricity and dry minerals: magnesia, magnesium, potash, bromine and lithium. One tower delivers €0.7–1.1 bn of output a year on 0.1–0.2 km². The same ladder takes the heat of any future fusion plant.

What one pilot tower changes for Korea:
→ Regions: each host city gains its own water, power and industrial jobs, a local project ready to grow into national policy.
→ AI transformation: the heat of data centres becomes water and power, so every new AI campus arrives with its cooling and supply secured.
→ SMEs: about €5 bn a year in orders for pumps, heat exchangers, ceramics and steel, ready for Korean suppliers to fill.
→ Pensions: the National Pension Service holds 20–30 % of every tower, and the dividend returns to Korean pensions for forty years.
→ Minerals: magnesium and lithium from Korea's own sea for batteries, cars and chips.
→ Climate: 148 towers secure twice today's water for a world 3 °C warmer.

10 towers by 2040, 74 by 2050: €55–82 bn of output a year and 150,000–220,000 jobs.

The Name That Stays
Byeokgolje at Gimje has watered the rice fields of Jeolla since its first record in the year 330, and its embankment still crosses the plain after seventeen centuries. King Sejong gave Korea its alphabet and, in 1441, the rain gauge that measured every drop across the kingdom; today a city and a great avenue carry his name. King Jeongjo built Hwaseong and, in 1795, the Manseokgeo reservoir that watered the new fields around Suwon; two centuries later both still stand, and Suwon remembers him as the king who built for his people.

Some decisions outgrow the calendar of those who take them. They happen when a country recognises that a condition it managed season by season has become a structure. The machine is steel, salt and steam. The signature is the immortal part, and every great work also remembers the envoys who carried the idea home.

What could Korean industry gain if Austrian partners such as RHI Magnesita, Andritz, voestalpine, Montanuniversität Leoben and TU Graz joined the first pilot tower?

text:
The parents are Rob and Angel Burnside. Rob had spent thirty-one years in education and was the principal of Lakota East High School outside Cincinnati. The young man's name is Landerius “DeDe” Hayes... 

During DeDe’s junior year, his home life fell apart. 

He says living with his mother wasn’t safe, his father was dealing with problems of his own, and there were nights when DeDe was sleeping in a car with the heater running because the mobile home where his father was staying was too cold. 

And yet, every morning, he kept showing up to school. 

Eventually the school learned DeDe’s mother had moved outside the district. 

Without a qualifying address, DeDe was withdrawn from Lakota East. 

That’s when Principal Burnside realized this wasn’t just an enrollment problem. 

This kid didn’t have a home. 

Rob went home and told Angel what was happening. 

Her response was: If he needs somewhere to live, he can live with us. 

Rob and Angel already had six children, including two they had adopted, but there was a sixteen-year-old boy out there without a stable place to sleep, and they couldn’t ignore that. 

The couple prayed about whether they should take DeDe in. 

Rob has said that just minutes after praying, their phone rang. 

It was DeDe. “Hey, Mr. Burnside.” 

Rob looked at his wife and knew they had their answer. 

DeDe moved in with the Burnsides and suddenly had something he desperately needed: 

A warm house, food, stability and people who were going to show up for him. 

While DeDe’s custody and residency situation were being worked out, Burnside allowed him to continue attending classes even though he’d been withdrawn. 

The district investigated Rob for insubordination and raised concerns about enrollment, lunches and liability. 

He was eventually placed on administrative leave. 

After thirty-one years in education, Rob says he was given a choice to step down or go through the termination process. 

The sixteen year old, DeDe, realized Rob’s career was on the line and offered to leave their home so Burnside could keep his job. 

Rob wouldn’t allow it. He hugged DeDe and told him: 

"You’re part of this family. We’re not gonna turn our back on you.” 

So Burnside stepped away from the career he’d spent three decades building and DeDe stayed. 

The Burnsides eventually became his legal family. 

DeDe started calling Rob and Angel “Pops and Ma.” 

Then this past May, Rob Burnside sat in the stands at DeDe’s high school graduation. 

Not as the principal. He was there as a dad, watching the kid he refused to abandon walk across the stage. 

DeDe is eighteen now and pursuing a career in aviation mechanics. 

When asked if he regretted what happened, Rob simplly said: 

“What value can we put on the life of a young person?” 

When Rob and Angel Burnside had to choose, they chose the kid.

text:
The NFL could close a trade loophole after multiple deals fell apart or had their terms changed at the last minute.

Several NFL execs have complained about the situation, and ESPN reports the league will investigate. 

Recent trades have raised concerns:

🔶 Broncos and Chargers: Denver backed out of a deal for LB Daiyan Henley after medical concerns surfaced and couldn't agree on revised compensation.

🔶 Lions and Jets: Detroit's trade for S Andre Cisco went through with different draft compensation than originally agreed upon.

🔶 Bengals and Eagles: Cincinnati backed out of a deal for EDGE Arnold Ebiketie after discovering it could cost the team a 3rd-round compensatory pick.

Some execs are concerned teams could exploit the system to lower their offers after the deadline, backing the other team into a corner.

text:
A major development in Texas could have important implications for Nashville's Music City Loop.

The Boring Company is preparing to tunnel beneath the Colorado River at Tesla's Gigafactory in Austin. Its Prufrock 3 cutting head is now positioned for launch, with tunnel liners already on site.

Why does this matter for Nashville?

The proposed Music City Loop expansion to the East Bank and Nissan Stadium would require a similar crossing beneath the Cumberland River.

A successful Colorado River crossing would provide an important proof of concept for The Boring Company's ability to construct vehicle tunnels beneath major waterways.

While Nashville's limestone geology presents different engineering considerations, this Texas project could offer valuable evidence of how the company approaches underwater crossings.

It's worth watching closely. The technology being tested in Austin could eventually help connect downtown Nashville to the East Bank.

text:
Whenever I visit Chennai from the US, I make it a point to visit Vedanta Desikar Temple, Mylapore, at least a couple of times. This visit was no different. Had the anugraha of Srinivasa Perumal and a wonderful dharshan. 🙏

After such a wonderful darshan, I thought of treating myself to dinner at the iconic Ratna Cafe, Mylapore.

I have fond memories of Ratna Cafe, both at Mylapore and during my visits to Triplicane after visiting Parthasarathy Temple. Unfortunately, today's experience was quite disappointing.

Finding a seat was easy. Getting someone's attention to take the order was not!

Ordered sambar idli. No one bothered to offer even a glass of water. The manager (?) came by and asked whether I had ordered. I politely said yes.

The idli arrived after a while, but the chutney was missing. Had to remind the server, who seemed more occupied blaming someone else in Hindi. Interestingly, almost all conversations among the servers were in Hindi, not Tamil.

The chutney eventually arrived after I had finished my first idli. The water followed!

The idli was soft, but the sambar was watery and excessively hot. Couldn't really enjoy the taste.

Then came the second order, a ghee roast. More waiting!

The manager noticed my rather disappointed face and somehow managed to get the dosa served. But one small cup of sambar and a little chutney, barely enough for a couple of bites!

Had to chase them again for more sambar. Even after the manager nodded and went inside, someone else had to remind him!

By now, the excitement of enjoying my dinner had completely vanished.

Finished the dosa. Nobody bothered to ask whether I wanted anything else. Finally, I had to ask for the bill.

The bill came to ₹263 (₹90 for sambar idli and ₹160 for ghee roast, plus taxes).

A little pricey for the idli, particularly considering the food and service. But that's fine, as long as it helps bring back the taste buds and memories of what I experienced at Ratna Cafe earlier!

One more thing. I usually tip generously whenever I dine out. I believe good service deserves appreciation. But today, I decided not to leave a tip. Somehow, I genuinely felt it wasn't deserved.

What has happened to Ratna Cafe?

I have visited a couple of times earlier and the experience wasn't this bad. Hopefully, this was just an exceptionally poor evening and not a reflection of what the place has become.

An iconic name deserves much better service.

Attaching today's bill for reference.

Ratna Cafe, hope you are listening!

#Srinivega #RatnaCafe #Mylapore #Chennai #ServiceMatters

text:
In Christian reality, not this guy's fantasy...

Here's a breakdown how the early Church Fathers and New Testament texts specifically framed the Church as the continuation of Israel.

From an Orthodox perspective, the Church is not a "Plan B" or a separate Gentile entity running parallel to Israel; it is the historical continuation, restoration, and fulfillment of Israel in the Messiah.

Both the New Testament apostles and the earliest Church Fathers were unanimous on this point, arguing directly from the Hebrew Scriptures that covenant membership was always defined by faithfulness to God rather than mere physical descent.

1. The New Testament Foundation
The apostles systematically dismantled the idea of a dual-covenant system by redefining Israel around Christ Himself.

Christ as the True Israel:
In Matthew 2:15, the Evangelist applies Hosea 11:1 ("Out of Egypt I called my son") directly to Jesus. Throughout the Gospels, Jesus recapitulates Israel's history—passing through the waters (baptism), enduring forty days in the wilderness, and appointing twelve apostles (Luke 22:30) specifically to reconstitute the twelve tribes of Israel.

The Olive Tree (Romans 9–11):
St. Paul explicitly states that "not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel" (Romans 9:6). In Romans 11, he uses the image of a single cultivated olive tree: unbelieving branches were broken off, and believing Gentiles were grafted into the existing root of Israel. There is only one tree, not two.

Children of Abraham by Faith (Galatians 3 & 6):
Paul argues that God's promises were made to Abraham and his singular "offspring"—Christ (Galatians 3:16). Therefore, "if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise" (Galatians 3:29), concluding his epistle by calling the Church "the Israel of God" (Galatians 6:16).

Old Covenant Titles Transferred (1 Peter 2:9):
St. Peter takes the exact covenant titles bestowed upon Israel at Mount Sinai in Exodus 19:5–6 and applies them directly to the Church: "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession."

The Synagogue of Satan (Revelation 2:9 & 3:9):
St. John writes to the churches in Smyrna and Philadelphia regarding those "who say that they are Jews and are not," establishing that rejecting the Messiah forfeits the spiritual claim to the covenant name.

In St. Paul's agricultural metaphor, wild Gentile branches do not form a separate orchard; they draw their life directly from the ancient patriarchs' rootstock.

2. The Early Church Fathers
Within a single generation of the apostles, the Fathers defended this exact ecclesiology against both Roman pagans and non-Christian Jewish polemicists, leaving zero room for modern dispensationalist distinctions.

St. Justin Martyr c. 160 AD Dialogue with Trypho
Explicitly calls the Church "the true spiritual Israel" and descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham (Ch. 11).

St. Irenaeus of Lyons c. 180 AD Against Heresies
Teaches that the Church is the true seed of Abraham, inheriting the promises because the patriarchs rejoiced to see Christ's day (Book 4.8).

Tertullian c. 200 AD An Answer to the Jews
Argues from Rebecca's twins (Esau and Jacob) that the "older" people (Israel according to the flesh) now serve the "younger" people (the Church).

St. Cyprian of Carthage c. 250 AD Three Books of Testimonies
Compiles dozens of Old Testament prophecies demonstrating that the Gentiles were foretold to inherit the vineyard and covenant of Israel.

Eusebius of Caesarea c. 324 AD Church History
Traces the Church back to Abraham and the righteous pre-Mosaic patriarchs, showing Christianity is the original religion of Israel restored.

St. John Chrysostom c. 387 AD Homilies on Galatians
Emphasizes that the "Israel of God" consists of those who walk by the rule of the Cross, whether Jew or Gentile by birth.

Key Patristic Arguments Against Sola Scriptura Proof-Texting
When modern Christian Zionists cite Old Testament land or blessing promises as unfulfilled guarantees for a modern secular state, they bypass how the Fathers read Scripture:

Typology and Fulfillment:
The Fathers read the Old Testament Christologically. The earthly Jerusalem, the Temple, and the land of Canaan were types (foreshadowings) pointing toward the Heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), the Body of Christ as the true Temple (John 2:21), and the entire cosmos redeemed in the Resurrection.

The "Remnant" Theology:
Drawing on Isaiah 10:22 and Romans 11:5, the Fathers pointed out that Israel was never completely cast off; rather, the faithful remnant of Israel—the Virgin Mary, the Twelve Apostles, the 3,000 baptized at Pentecost—became the foundation stones of the Church, into which the nations were then gathered.

Eucharistic Continuity:
Even the earliest liturgical manuals, such as the Didache (late 1st century), apply Malachi 1:11's prophecy of a "pure sacrifice" offered by the Gentiles directly to the Christian Eucharist, demonstrating that the Church understood itself from day one as offering the true, fulfilled worship of Israel.
