text:
Humean Individualism and the Axioms of Ethical Individualism: A Philosophical Fusion for the Equality of Human Dignity

The Center for Human Equality in Oregon advances Ethical Individualism (EI), the human relational philosophy developed by its founder, Russell McAlmond. EI insists that every human being must be encountered as a sovereign, irreplaceable individual rather than as a representative of any group. Its axioms affirm the infinite and equal worth of every person, the absolute uniqueness of each life as an unrepeatable mosaic of experience and inner reality, and—in fuller statements—the infinite mystery of the private consciousness that no label can exhaust. From these axioms follows the central theorem: any judgment of a human being based primarily on group membership is immoral. The result is a practical ethic of radical respect that improves human relations by concentrating on the human qua human encounter and the equality of dignity inherent in every individual.

This contemporary relational ethic finds powerful validation and enrichment in the individualistic strands of David Hume’s philosophy. Though separated by centuries, Hume’s empirical science of human nature and his moral sentimentalism converge with EI’s axioms to form a robust defense of judging persons solely by who they are as individuals.

Hume’s moral philosophy is thoroughly individual-centered. In A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, he locates personal merit entirely in the mental qualities of particular persons—those traits of character that are useful or agreeable to the person himself or to others with whom he has intercourse. Moral praise and blame attach to durable principles of character revealed in action, not to abstract categories.

Sympathy, the fundamental mechanism of moral sentiment, operates by allowing us to enter into the feelings and circumstances of specific individuals. We approve of benevolence or justice because we sympathetically participate in the pleasures these traits produce in the particular persons affected. Moral evaluation thus begins in the concrete encounter with another human being, not in the contemplation of groups.

Hume’s essay “Of National Characters” supplies the most explicit parallel to EI’s rejection of group judgmentalism. He observes that “the vulgar are apt to carry all national characters to extremes” and, once they have decided that any people are knavish, cowardly, or ignorant, “will admit of no exception, but comprehend every individual under the same censure.” Men of sense, he insists, condemn these “undistinguishing judgments.”

While nations may exhibit statistical regularities of manners arising from moral causes (government, education, commerce, and the imitative nature of the human mind), a nation is “nothing but a collection of individuals.” Exceptions such as Cervantes among Spaniards or Tycho Brahe among Danes demonstrate that personal character always remains the proper object of evaluation. Hume thereby anticipates EI’s theorem: group membership supplies no sufficient moral warrant for judging the person.

The fusion of these frameworks is mutually reinforcing. EI’s axiom of infinite and equal worth receives empirical and sentimental grounding in Hume’s account of sympathy. Because the capacity for moral sentiment is universal among human beings—arising from the resemblance of human minds and the natural communication of affections—every person, regardless of origin or affiliation, is a potential object of the same disinterested approbation.

No hierarchy of worth is sustainable once moral evaluation is recognized as the product of human sympathy directed toward individual characters. The equality of dignity is not a metaphysical postulate alone but a practical consequence of the way human beings actually form moral judgments when they attend carefully to particular persons.

EI’s axiom of absolute uniqueness is likewise confirmed by Hume’s insistence on the primacy of individual character. Hume repeatedly notes that even where national or social regularities exist, each person retains a personal character “peculiar to each individual.” The science of man proceeds by careful observation of particular cases; general rules of character are always corrigible by the concrete instance.

This empirical caution against “undistinguishing judgments” supplies a methodological warrant for EI’s refusal to treat any person as interchangeable with a category. The infinite mystery of the inner life, emphasized in fuller statements of EI, finds a parallel in Hume’s recognition that our knowledge of another’s motives and sentiments is always mediated by sympathy and remains incomplete; we never possess a totalizing view that would license final group-based verdicts.

When these axioms and Humean insights are combined, the resulting ethic transforms human relations. The human qua human encounter becomes the normative starting point: one meets the other first as a fellow bearer of equal dignity and unrepeatable character, and only secondarily, if at all, as a member of any collective. Prejudice, which thrives on the reduction of persons to group stereotypes, is starved of its necessary fuel. Trust becomes possible because expectations are formed from observed individual conduct rather than from ascribed collective traits. Empathy is deepened by the deliberate exercise of sympathy toward the particular person rather than the imagined representative.

Symbiotic, mutually beneficial relationships flourish precisely because neither party is required to carry the moral weight of a group.

In short, Hume’s individualistic moral philosophy—centered on character, sympathy, and the condemnation of undistinguishing judgments—provides classical validation for the axioms of Ethical Individualism. Together they underwrite a powerful, non-partisan relational standard: human beings are to be judged only by who they are as individuals, never by the groups to which they belong or are assigned.

By concentrating attention on the equality of dignity that appears in every genuine human encounter, this fused perspective offers the Center for Human Equality a philosophically grounded path toward improved human relations in the twenty-first century.

text:
Is it accurate to assess our current military obsolete in the current battlefield areas? We need new stuff, they need working security equipment… It fits the bill being cheaper than bringing it home for storage… It could be tied into long term energy sales?!
Show more

Researched US military equipment status and transfer policies

You're hitting on three separate but connected points. Here's how each holds up:
Is the equipment actually obsolete?
Partially, and it's platform-specific. The Ukraine record is damning for heavy armor: 87% of the 31 Abrams sent to Ukraine were destroyed or captured by June 2025, and a New York Times investigation in August 2026 found Leopard 2s "spending much of their time concealed beneath camouflage netting" rather than fighting. The Army Science Board concluded the M1 "will not dominate the 2040 battlefield," and the Army has already begun converting armored battalions to mobile infantry (e.g., the 3rd/116th Cavalry in Oregon). A West Point Modern Warfare Institute analysis and a Combined Resolve exercise where Ukrainian drone operators caused ~70% of a US ABCT's casualties in two days confirm the tactical shift.
But it's not a blanket obsolescence. Artillery, air defense missiles, and HIMARS remain effective. The problem is concentrated in heavy armor and APCs — the exact platforms that make up the bulk of APS pre-positioned stocks.
Is it cheaper to leave than bring home?
Yes, by a wide margin. A full US withdrawal from Europe would cost an estimated $70–140 billion in one-off and capital expenses over 5–10 years, including strategic airlift/sealift, new stateside infrastructure, and APS site closure. A single ABCT rotation to Poland costs $32 million in transport alone, and rotating an ABCT costs ~$70 million more per year than forward-stationing it.
The EDA (Excess Defense Articles) program is the existing legal mechanism for exactly what you're describing: equipment declared excess by a service branch is transferred "as is, where is" at 5–50% of original acquisition value(sales) or at no cost (grants, capped at $500M/year in aggregate current value). 

The recipient pays for refurbishment and transport. The US saves the cost of depot-level maintenance, storage, and eventual disposal. For equipment already sitting in Europe, the transport cost to the recipient is near zero.
So the arithmetic is: a pre-positioned M1A2 SEPv3 worth ~$10M at acquisition, now at 10–20% current value, transferred as EDA to a host nation that can maintain it, saves the US the ongoing storage/maintenance cost (~$24M/year per heavy BCT in outdoor storage alone) and the $10–20B repatriation logistics tail.
The energy linkage
This is already happening, and it's the strongest part of your argument. The July 2025 EU-US trade deal explicitly bundles the two:
•EU commits to $750 billion in US energy purchases (LNG, oil, nuclear) through 2028
•EU commits to "substantially increase procurement of military and defence equipment from the United States"
•The $600B in EU investment in the US is partly directed at defense industrial capacity 
And it's already being executed bilaterally: Greece just announced $4 billion in FMS (Strykers, etc.) alongside expanded LNG cooperation and a 20-year US LNG supply deal (700 million cubic meters/year from 2030). The pattern is: equipment transfer → host nation absorbs maintenance → host nation buys US energy to power its own industry and military infrastructure.
The legal pathway for bundling is the Foreign Military Sale framework (AECA §2761–2764), where the LOA (Letter of Offer and Acceptance) can include training, logistics support, and industrial offset requirements. Energy isn't formally part of the FMS, but the political linkage at the bilateral level (as with Greece, and as the EU deal framework contemplates) creates the de facto bundle.
The gap
The missing piece is Section 1249's $500K threshold. The EDA program's $500M/year grant cap and 5–50% pricing

text:
On 10 November The National ran the column below by @Jonathon_Shafi under the headline “Scotland is not a colony – and we shouldn’t pretend otherwise”. Two days later he published a second edition in his Substack newsletter, Independence Captured, under the new title “Is Scotland a Colony?”, with a preface saying most of the response was critical, and it has been doing the rounds again since.

The second edition gives ground on the argument and keeps the conclusion. The National quoted him on Scotland as “a small economy prey to global capitalism”, with a governing party unable “to establish impediments”. The second edition makes it “an open economy prey to larger economic forces in the world system”, unable “to establish defences or impediments”. One phrase was dropped: that Scots “participate freely in elections”.

Both versions of Shafi’s article describe Scotland’s economic position, first as “a small economy”, then as “an open economy”. Each framing presents Scotland’s economy as a standalone entity, ignoring that it is controlled from London as part of the UK. In postcolonial terms, this writes the colonial relationship out of the account: the economy is described as if it stood alone, so its weakness reads as its own failing and its local managers’ fault, while the power that holds the levers drops out of view. Professor Alf Baird said as much in The National’s debate on 5 November, which the column answers: “territorial alienation means the economy is controlled outside Scotland”.

The column says the governing party has “neither the interest, nor the ability” to resist. That is colonial administration described to the letter: a local party captured inside a system built to leave it no ability, with no interest in resisting it. Outside that system, the ability is one decision away: to act from the sovereignty of the Scottish people, and take the necessary steps their right to self-determination demands, on every issue. The column describes the colonial relationship, then denies it exists.

Three positions Shafi took in the column fail on its own evidence, and he kept all three in the second edition.

Position 1: Shafi argues that Scots have “occupied the highest offices of state”, so Scotland cannot be a colony. The same column calls Ireland “the first English colony”, and from 1801 Ireland sent 100 MPs to the Commons and 28 representative peers to the Lords. By the column’s own test, Ireland was no colony either. Scots did hold those offices, and took their share of empire: the second edition itself quotes Nairn on Scotland as a “highly successful partner in the general business enterprise of Anglo-Scots Imperialism”. In postcolonial terms, those office-holders can be viewed as colonial intermediaries, a native elite drawn into the metropole’s rule. As Professor Baird put it in his recent appearance in The National’s debate, “colonialism is a cooperative venture with native elites”. The same can be viewed playing out in real time on social media, where Shafi’s article has been promoted and defended from inside the ‘independence’ movement, and recommended by a Times columnist for “coming to the question from the left”.

Position 2: Shafi argues that the 1707 Union “retained Scottish law”, so Scotland cannot be a colony, while the 1801 Act “replaced Irish law with English law”. Scots law was retained, and so were the sovereign instruments it rests on, the Claim of Right among them. Westminster encased them: it kept them as the ground of its own claimed title in Scotland while suppressing the sovereignty they declare in the people. The Court of Session is a colonial enforcement court: as its own records and rulings confirm, it enforces Westminster’s unlimited parliamentary sovereignty. On 13 October its Inner House upheld the pause on a Scots petition against the Westminster Order that proscribed Palestine Action, keeping it waiting on an English case about the same Order, which the Supreme Court in London heard on 4 and 5 November and has yet to decide. The Inner House ruled that London’s decision, “although not binding on the courts in Scotland, will be highly persuasive”.

The second half of Position 2, that the 1801 Act “replaced Irish law with English law”, fails as well. Ireland, which the column calls “the first English colony”, kept its law too: Article Eight of the Union with Ireland Act 1800 says “all laws in force at the time of the union, and all the courts of civil and ecclesiastical jurisdiction within the respective kingdoms, shall remain as now by law established within the same”. Both treaties kept the existing law, so on the column’s own example a country can keep its law and still be a colony. The distinction the column rests on is not in the text, and the second edition prints it again.

Position 3: Shafi argues, in the second edition’s words, that Scotland “is not a colony of the British state, but an open economy prey to larger economic forces in the world system”, with his own figures offered as proof: in 2021 “£36.5 billion was extracted from Scotland while only £26.4bn flowed inwards”, and “£3.9bn of this wound up in the UK”. On his own count, the UK is somewhere Scotland’s wealth goes. The two cannot be pulled apart here: the colonial arrangement is the channel the extraction class works through, and a home-grown managing class keeps it open.

Anyone who still doubts Scotland’s status as a colony should test that doubt against the record set out above. The fight against the extraction classes and the fight against colonialism in Scotland and beyond are one and the same fight. Solidarity bound by what our causes hold in common, our shared foundational rights, is what makes another Scotland possible.

Seeing Scotland’s colonial status for what it is asks no one who believes in the fundamental right to self-determination to give up anything, except perhaps the colonial conditioning forced upon them, as upon all Scots, for over 300 years.

text:
II. Opinions

Here, it would seem, the case of Dr. Dooley is at an end. The story, though odd—even fantastic, in some of its details—is sadly routine in pattern. A man transgresses the law. The transgression is discovered and confirmed. He is punished, in accordance with the law. When Judge Ryan spoke his verdict, the case was closed. Such is, usually and normally, society’s view; and such was in fact the view of the greater number of the ordinary citizens of that Connecticut region—the farmers, artisans, merchants, laborers, and some part of the teachers, lawyers, writers, artists and the wealthy who are scattered here and there through the hills.

But this was not the end, nor has the case yet ended.

On the day of the trial, the bare room in which the Court sat, open to the public, as demanded by Anglo-Saxon legal tradition even for such a case as this, was filled with spectators. These were not the farmers, artisans, merchants and laborers; nor, except for a marginal few, were they mere idlers. More than fifty of them, well dressed and assured in manner, were a selection of the region’s intellectual elite. Most of them were women, the women recognized as community leaders, who head charity drives, belong to clubs, run the Parent-Teacher Association, the Association for the United Nations, the League of Women Voters. Almost without exception they were Liberals, by their own classification—though of course many who think of themselves as Liberals were not there, and would not have agreed with those who were.

These spectators, or nearly all of them, came to the courtroom to signify in a kind of public demonstration their sympathy with, their support of Doctor Dooley, their rejection of the judgment the Court inexorably must hand down. They were in agreement, and many of them continue to be in agreement, with Dr. Dooley’s explanation and views as these were expressed by his attorney, Mr. Ebersol.

What, then, was the explanation offered for these admitted actions which, prima facie, were subject to a triple condemnation: intrinsically, in and of themselves; as an adult’s violation of children; as a physician’s violation of his sacred Hippocratic oath?

Mr. Ebersol did not deny the homosexual encounters, nor did he contend that they had been limited to the three boys or the specific occasion specified in the legal charges. He made it clear that there had been other patients and other occasions. And in that open courtroom, within the hearing of those spectators, Mr. Ebersol, corrected occasionally by the defendant and plainly following the defendant’s information and instruction, reviewed certain of the encounters with a specificity of detail not often found outside of medical textbooks. Against this factual background, Mr. Ebersol offered as defense his analysis of Dr. Dooley’s purpose, end, and motives. In sum, Mr. Ebersol, for Dr. Dooley, contended that these encounters were an integral part of a new, pioneer and revolutionary technique of psychiatric therapy.

The woman Sergeant Snuggles bit is begging officials to let him live.

Her name is Clara Gastelum. She is Jennifer Evancho's mother. Clara says that on Oct 7, 2025 the 10 month old Anatolian shepherd was outside their Tucson home watching coyotes or another animal when she came up behind him and petted him. He knocked her down. She needed hospital treatment. Nobody disputes the bite.

She also says he stopped the moment she called his name.

Here is how she describes it: "I was not attacked and mauled. It was friendly fire."

And here is who she blames: "Ultimately I feel i am not a victim of Snuggles, but Snuggles and I are victims of PACC, the City of Tucson, and Pima county."

Read that again. The only person who got hurt is the one asking them to stop.

According to PACC, a city court declared him vicious and ordered him euthanized in November 2025. Jennifer is still appealing.

On May 29 they were handed a way out. Rick Dunton, chief trainer at North Carolina's K9 Responder Academy, offered to take Snuggles, assess him, rehabilitate him and pay for transport. He said he'd sign any waiver they needed and guarantee the dog never comes back to Arizona.

A deputy county administrator called it a "potential solution." The PACC director said he'd consider a deal only if the county was fully protected from liability. A city prosecutor wrote: "I believe we should defer to the Court."

So the victim says spare him, a trainer says he'll take him out of the state for good, and more than a year later Snuggles is still in a kennel.

Who exactly is this protecting?

text:
$NVDA $MSFT $AMZN 
Three billionaires. Three affairs. Two walked away untouched. One lost a $4 trillion company in four days.

Bill Gates had an affair with a Microsoft employee. The board investigated. He left the board while the investigation was still open — and kept his fortune, his foundation, his seat at every table that matters. The story faded in a week.

Jeff Bezos had his affair splashed across the front page of the National Enquirer, complete with leaked texts. He wrote a blog post, fought back, and stayed CEO for another two and a half years. He left Amazon when he decided to leave.

Jensen Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife on Sunday, November 8. By Thursday, November 12, he was gone — not just as CEO, but as president and as a member of his own board, effective immediately, without a single word of his own in the announcement. Nvidia's stock plunged as much as 14% in a single session and is down 32% from its October high. The board that had declared "absolute confidence" in him on Sunday accepted his resignation on Wednesday.

Same sin. Three different verdicts. The difference was never the affair.

The difference is who counts — and who doesn't — in America's equity equation.

The Democratic Party's version of "equity" was never about fairness for everyone. It is a transaction: rights and protection for the groups that deliver votes. Black voters, Latino voters — they get a seat at the table, because they bring the ballots. Asian Americans don't fit the deal. Too successful to be called oppressed, too small to swing an election, and too easy to cast as the outsider the moment China becomes the enemy. So when a scandal needs a sacrifice, the Asian face is the first one offered up.

That is why Huang was first. Not because his affair was worse — it wasn't. But because in the hierarchy of who deserves protection, he ranks last. The "equity" machine protects its voters. Huang's people were never its voters; they were its afterthought.

And then came the label that made the whole thing work: "Chinese spy." Alice Huang, the Singapore businesswoman Huang was involved with, was suspected by U.S. authorities of links to Chinese intelligence. Suspected — the Justice Department itself has reached no conclusion. But a conclusion was never the point. The label was the point. Attach "Chinese spy" to an Asian man's affair and you no longer have a personal scandal. You have a national security story. You have a reason to move in four days, without waiting for an investigation, without waiting for earnings, without letting the man speak.

That trick only works on one kind of face.

This is the part the equity preachers never mention: their fairness was always selective. It was designed to reward loyalty, not to protect everyone. And when the system needs someone to make an example of, it reaches for the person with no bloc behind him, no network to catch him, no tribe to threaten consequences.

Gates had the establishment. Bezos had the establishment. Altman — fired by his own board in 2023 — was back in five days, because his people don't let their own stay down. Huang had a company he built for 33 years, and it wasn't enough.

So spare me the lectures about character and corporate governance. If character were the standard, all three would have fallen. If governance were the standard, all three would have been investigated the same way.

The standard was never the affair. The standard was the color of the man who had it.

In America, equality was never the product. Votes were. And Jensen Huang just learned what happens to the people the product was never built for.

text:
Four Days of Chhath Puja: What Nahay Khay, Kharna, Sandhya Arghya and Usha Arghya Mean… ☀️🙏

Chhath Puja is not a single-day festival. It unfolds over four days, with each stage preparing the devotee for the final worship of Surya Dev and Chhathi Maiya.

📌 Nahay Khay: Purification Begins

> The first day begins with bathing, cleaning the home and preparing food with special attention to purity.

> The vratin traditionally eats a simple meal such as arwa rice, chana dal and kaddu.

> The idea is simple: before the strict vrat begins, both the surroundings and daily routine are purified.

📌 Kharna: The Fast Becomes Serious

> On the second day, the vratin observes a fast through the day.

> After evening worship, the fast is briefly broken with Prasad, traditionally including preparations such as gur ki kheer and roti.

> After Kharna, the much stricter period begins. Many vratins then observe a continuous nirjala fast until the final morning Arghya.

📌 Sandhya Arghya: Worship of the Setting Sun

> On the third evening, families gather at rivers, ponds and ghats with baskets of Prasad.

> Standing in water, devotees offer Arghya to the setting Sun.

> This is one of the most distinctive parts of Chhath. The Sun is worshipped not only while rising, but also while setting.

> It expresses gratitude even when light is disappearing, not only when it is returning.

📌 Usha Arghya: Worship of the Rising Sun

> Before sunrise on the fourth day, devotees return to the water.

> As Surya Dev rises, the final Arghya is offered.

> The long vrat then comes to an end, Prasad is distributed, and the four-day observance is completed.

👉 So the journey of Chhath moves step by step:

> Nahay Khay: Purify
> Kharna: Discipline
> Sandhya Arghya: Give thanks as the Sun sets
> Usha Arghya: Welcome the returning light

And perhaps that is what makes Chhath so powerful. The devotee bows to the Sun at both moments. When the light leaves. And when the light returns.

text:
Chhathi Maiya: Who Is the Goddess Worshipped Alongside Surya Dev? 🌞🙏

Chhath Puja is famous for the worship of Surya Dev, but devotees also repeatedly call upon another divine presence: Chhathi Maiya.

> Chhathi Maiya is widely identified with Shashthi Devi, a mother goddess traditionally associated with childbirth, children and their protection.

The name itself comes from Shashthi, meaning the sixth lunar day. Chhath is centred on the Shashthi Tithi of Kartik Shukla Paksha.

In the popular traditions of Bihar and surrounding regions, Chhathi Maiya is lovingly described as the sister of Surya Dev. This is why Surya and Chhathi Maiya are remembered together throughout the festival.

Some Puranic traditions also connect Shashthi Devi with Devasena, associated with Bhagwan Kartikeya. For devotees, however, Chhathi Maiya is above all a mother.

Families pray to her for the health, protection and well-being of their children and loved ones.

This makes Chhath a beautiful union of two forms of divine grace:

> Surya Dev gives light, energy and life.
> Chhathi Maiya gives the blessings and protection of a mother.

And together, they stand at the heart of one of Sanatana Dharma's most demanding and deeply devotional festivals.

text:
Rusty Whitt was past thirty and running the strength and conditioning program at Sam Houston State when he walked across the street from his own weight room and enlisted in the Army.

He had helped design that weight room. He taught in the kinesiology department on the side, had a master's in it from Texas, four letters as a player at Abilene Christian, and an Olympic Training Center internship behind him. He had been there since December of 1998 and the career was going fine.

He was 30 years old on the morning of September 11, and he was rehabbing a knee.

His grandmother got on the phone with him that day. Cam Parker of Sports Illustrated has the line she used on him.

"Rusty, this is your Pearl Harbor."

Men who try out for Special Forces are usually in their twenties. Whitt once walked a Lubbock reporter through what the tryout was like. 21 days of it, with roughly 220 men starting alongside him and roughly 48 still standing at the end.

He was one of the 48.

The course that comes after took him two years. He finished it as an 18 Echo, which is the communications sergeant on a Special Forces team, and the rest of his enlistment went to the 10th Special Forces Group.

August of 2003 to January of 2009. Two tours in Iraq.

He came back with two Iraq campaign medals and an Army Commendation Medal with a valor device on it.

His team had something almost no other team in the Army had, which was a man who had spent five years as a Division I strength coach. Whitt built the conditioning program his own guys used before they went over, and he ran it the whole time they were there.

Then he came home in 2009 and went back to the career he had quit. Rice. Louisiana. Texas Tech. A year at Army under Jeff Monken. Four seasons with Jon Sumrall at Troy, two more at Tulane, and when Sumrall got the Florida job Whitt went with him.

Florida announced him in January as director of football performance.

The first thing he built there is a workout he calls the Gauntlet. The players have to pass it before spring break, and if they do not pass it they do it again. Parker asked why he made it harder than the version before. Because they only have to pass it once.

He runs a finisher the players lead themselves too, on the idea that you teach a handful of men to lead and they go teach everybody else. He calls it a force multiplier. That is not a strength and conditioning term.

ESPN put him on College GameDay this week for Veterans Day. Jen Lada reported it.

Rusty Whitt is 55 years old.

He left a weight room he had helped build to go see whether he could do the hardest thing the Army had on offer. He finished it standing next to men half a generation younger than him. Then he came home and picked the career up right where he set it down.

text:
Create a 30-second cinematic Japanese anime short film titled "The Winter Sparrow," telling a gentle story of patience, care, and the quiet joy of letting go, between a young boy and an injured sparrow.

The story begins on a snowy winter afternoon when the boy discovers a small sparrow with a hurt wing lying in the snow beneath a persimmon tree. He carries it home and cares for it through the cold days. When spring arrives, he sets it free. The next morning the sparrow returns with a small, unexpected gift.

Use six cinematic shots, each lasting five seconds, with simple, achievable character actions and expressive emotional storytelling.

The Boy: A gentle young boy with messy black hair, round cheeks, warm brown eyes, a navy-blue duffle coat, a long red knitted scarf, gray wool mittens, and brown snow boots. Inside his home, he wears a soft green knitted sweater and beige corduroy trousers.

The Sparrow: A tiny Eurasian tree sparrow with a chestnut-brown cap, white cheeks with a small black spot, a black bib, soft brown-and-gray feathers, and bright black eyes. At first it is frightened and cannot fly. Over time it grows lively, curious, and trusting.

Environment: A quiet Japanese countryside village with snow-covered rooftops, wooden fences, bare persimmon trees with a few orange fruits left, stone lanterns, and distant mountains. The boy's home is a traditional house with tatami floors, a warm kotatsu table, sliding shoji doors, and a wooden engawa veranda that looks out on the garden.

Visual Style: Beautiful hand-painted 2D Japanese anime, detailed watercolor backgrounds, delicate cel shading, expressive character animation, soft cinematic lighting, gently falling snow, warm interior colors, and nostalgic visual storytelling.

SHOT 1 | [00:00–00:05] A SOUND IN THE SNOW

A cinematic side-tracking shot follows the boy walking home along a snowy village path, his breath visible in the cold air. Snow falls softly. A faint chirp makes him stop.

He turns toward the base of a persimmon tree. A tiny sparrow lies half-buried in the snow, one wing drooping, looking up at him.

Boy: 「だいじょうぶ？」

"Are you okay?"

SFX: Soft snowfall, crunching footsteps, a weak chirp.

SHOT 2 | [00:05–00:10] WARM HANDS

A medium close-up captures the boy kneeling in the snow. He takes off one mitten and gently scoops the sparrow into his cupped bare hands, then wraps the end of his red scarf loosely around it.

The sparrow trembles, then slowly settles and blinks up at him.

The boy smiles softly.

Boy: 「いっしょに帰ろう。」

"Let's go home together."

SFX: Wind through bare branches, a tiny chirp, delicate piano notes.

SHOT 3 | [00:10–00:15] BY THE KOTATSU

Inside the warmly lit tatami room, the boy sits at the kotatsu. The sparrow rests in a small wooden box lined with a folded cloth. The boy carefully offers a few grains of rice on his fingertip.

The sparrow hesitates, then pecks at the grains. The boy's eyes light up with quiet delight.

SFX: Crackling heater, soft pecking, snow brushing against the shoji.

SHOT 4 | [00:15–00:20] THE FIRST SPRING

A peaceful medium shot on the open engawa. The snow is gone, and the garden is green with a cherry tree in early bloom. The boy holds the sparrow in his open palms.

The sparrow hops to his fingertips, flutters its healed wing, and flies up into the blossoms. The boy watches it go, smiling with a little sadness.

SFX: Gentle breeze, a flurry of wings, birdsong, soft piano melody.

SHOT 5 | [00:20–00:25] A SMALL GIFT

Morning sunlight pours across the wooden veranda. The boy sits on the edge of the engawa. A soft flutter: the sparrow lands beside him, holding a tiny pink cherry blossom in its beak.

It hops closer and sets the blossom on the boy's knee.

He looks down in surprise. The sparrow tilts its head and chirps proudly.

Boy: 「ぼくに？」

"For me?"

SFX: Morning birds, a light flutter of wings, a cheerful chirp.

SHOT 6 | [00:25–00:30] TOGETHER

An intimate close-up: the boy slowly holds out his finger, and the sparrow hops onto it. He brings it close and gently touches his forehead to its tiny head. The sparrow fluffs its feathers and closes its eyes contentedly.

Boy: 「ありがとう。」

"Thank you."

The camera slowly pulls back to show the sunlit veranda, the cherry blossom resting on his knee, the red scarf hanging on a wooden peg inside, and the empty little box beside it, while more sparrows gather on the garden fence.

FADE TO BLACK.

SFX: Soft chirping, distant birdsong, emotional piano finale.

Character Consistency: Preserve the boy's facial features, hairstyle, proportions, and clothing within each setting. Keep the sparrow's chestnut cap, white cheeks, black cheek spot, black bib, small size, and feather pattern the same throughout.

Animal Animation: Use believable bird behavior, including small hops, head tilts, quick blinking, feather fluffing, careful pecking, and natural wing flutters. The sparrow never speaks or behaves like a human.

Emotional Storytelling: Gradually change the sparrow from fear and weakness to recovery, trust, and affection. The boy's expressions stay gentle, sincere, and naturally expressive, with a touch of bittersweet feeling at the release.

Camera: Use simple tracking shots, stable medium compositions, intimate close-ups, and a gentle final pullback. Avoid rapid cuts and complicated camera movements.

Lighting: Begin with cool white-blue winter afternoon tones, move into warm amber interior light, then soft pastel spring daylight, and end in golden morning sunlight.

Dialogue: All dialogue is spoken naturally in Japanese with accurate lip synchronization and a soft, gentle child's voice. English translations are provided for context only.

Sound Design: Soft snowfall, crunching footsteps, tiny chirps, fluttering wings, morning birdsong, and a nostalgic instrumental piano melody.

Negative Guidance: No character redesign, duplicated sparrows in the close-ups, changing feather patterns, distorted anatomy, unnatural bird movements, exaggerated crying, photorealistic rendering, narration, subtitles, captions, logos, or additional dialogue.

Final Objective: Deliver a simple, emotionally memorable animated short about kindness that asks for nothing in return, ending with a small sparrow's gift of gratitude.

text:
Tesla Puts the Cybercab on Sale for $29,990. It Only Drives Where Robotaxi Does.

Select buyers can now order the two-seater for personal use, but a required $299 monthly subscription and Texas and Florida geofences shape what they actually get.

Tesla has started selling the Cybercab to private owners. On Friday, the company's Robotaxi account on X said select customers are being invited to buy the two-seat, steering-wheel-free vehicle for personal use at $29,990 before taxes, with estimated delivery in December, according to Reuters and AFP.

The sticker price is only part of the deal. Each order carries a required $299 per month "Autonomy Subscription," and the car operates only inside the areas where Tesla already runs its Robotaxi service.

What buyers are signing up for

According to Electrek, which reviewed the order page and the invitation email Tesla shared, the listing shows estimated delivery in Austin, Texas, and requires a $1,000 non-refundable deposit. The subscription is pre-checked with one month included, and the fine print reads: "Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate." The email adds: "Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation."

The vehicle itself matches what Tesla has shown before: two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals, Electrek reported.

At $299 a month, the subscription adds $3,588 a year. Electrek estimates the five-year cost at about $47,600 before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Musk says the fee is too high

The pricing drew an unusual response from the top. Reuters reported that Elon Musk wrote on X that "the monthly fee is too high," adding that it should match what Tesla charges for Full Self-Driving and connectivity on its other models, roughly $115 a month. At that level, the yearly cost would fall to about $1,380.

Musk also said the offering would expand nationwide as Tesla receives regulatory approval, according to Reuters. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said separately on X that the Cybercab will work unsupervised in the same locations as the Robotaxi service.

Where it can actually go

That means eight cities for now. Electrek lists Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, plus Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. Outside those zones, the order terms make clear the car is not meant to operate.

Even inside them, coverage may be thinner than the maps suggest. Electrek cited independent tracker Koby Pierce, who tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that areas accepting pickups and drop-offs covered only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in six cities he checked. Austin, where the first deliveries are planned, came in at about 59%.

Why it matters

This is the first time Tesla has offered a purpose-built autonomous car to individual buyers, and it signals a different business model. Instead of a one-time sale plus optional software, Tesla is pairing a low entry price with a mandatory recurring fee. That fits the company's broader push toward subscription revenue, and it lets Tesla say it delivered a self-driving consumer car in 2026, a goal Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering, set last month, per Reuters.

It also tests demand in a way robotaxi rides cannot. Riders pay per trip. Owners commit thousands of dollars upfront and every month, which will show how much people value a car that drives itself only in specific neighborhoods.

The open questions

Regulators have not signed off on the design. AFP reported that U.S. safety regulators opened an inquiry in September into how Tesla concluded that a vehicle with no steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors meets federal safety rules. Electrek reported that Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that its full response be kept confidential, and that NHTSA has not yet ruled.

Competition is also further along in reach. AFP noted that Waymo offers its service in 11 U.S. cities. Waymo does not sell cars to consumers, though, so Tesla is the only one asking people to own the vehicle outright.

Supporters will argue the price is a starting point. If the fee drops toward the level Musk suggested, and service areas keep expanding, the math looks very different than it does today.

For now, the Cybercab is a $29,990 car with a monthly requirement and a map. Would you buy one if it only drove where Robotaxi does, or does the subscription need to come down first?

text:
How much could you ACTUALLY make with a Cybercab?

I redid the math using Tesla’s $29,990 estimated purchase price and $299/month Autonomy Subscription. My updated base case is that you can make about $21,000 per car per year. 

First, the biggest condition is that Tesla has to allow owners to earn $ money.

The current Cybercab offer is invite-only and for personal use. Under the agreement, Robotaxi, ride-hailing, delivery and rental use require Tesla’s authorization.

Everything below assumes Tesla opens that door.

MY BASE CASE

• $1.75 per paid mile
• 50 hours of driving per week
• 20 mph average speed
• 65% of miles carrying a paying rider
• Tesla keeps 30%

That works out to 52,000 total miles and 33,800 paid miles a year, or about 93 paid miles a day.

OPERATING ONE CYBERCAB FOR ONE YEAR

• $59,150 in fares
−$17,745 for Tesla’s assumed share
−$3,588 for the Autonomy Subscription
−$11,367 for estimated operating costs
−$5,361 saved toward replacing the car after six years ($32,164 car cost all in, divided by 6 years. Tesla hasn't said how long a Cybercab lasts, so I assume 6 years and $0 resale.)

= About $21,090 a year before income tax.

The operating costs include electricity, insurance, cleaning, uncovered repairs, registration and parking. This model assumes a cash purchase.

• $100K → 5 Cybercabs
• $250K → 12 Cybercabs
• $500K → 24 Cybercabs
• $1M → 48 Cybercabs

At approximately $32,164 per car, including Texas sales tax and estimated fees, five cars would cost about $161K. Forty-eight would cost about $1.54M just to buy the vehicles.

FYI, if the monthly fee eventually drops to the roughly $115 Elon suggested, the same model improves to about $23,300 per car. That would put $1M a year at 43 cars instead of 48.

MY BULL CASE

If everything goes right: $2.50 per paid mile, 60 hours a week, 22 mph, 70% paid miles, Tesla keeps 25%, lower operating costs and an 8-year car life.

That works out to about $73,500 per car per year.

• $100K → 2 Cybercabs
• $250K → 4 Cybercabs
• $500K → 7 Cybercabs
• $1M → 14 Cybercabs

MY BEAR CASE

The downside matters as well… my lower-fare, lower-utilization scenario is roughly break-even, while my worst case loses about $13,000 a year per car.

Fares, paid miles, operating costs and Tesla’s eventual revenue split will decide whether the economics work.

My goal is to one day own 25 to 50 Cybercabs if Tesla opens this up. I’d start with a few, track what they actually earn and what it takes to run them, then scale based on the results. I can’t wait to share my actual numbers and journey on 𝕏 when I get my own Cybercab!

text:
For forty minutes I laid siege to a cheese shop in Kenosha, Wisconsin, and nobody inside noticed.

In my defense, it is a castle. Mars Cheese Castle. Drawbridge. Watchtower. Right beside I-94.

A warrior does not stroll into a castle. He is announced, or he lays siege. Nobody announced me.

A siege by one man is mostly standing. I stood. Families walked around me. A man held the door and said, "You going in?" I told him no, I was surrounding it.

The idea of a siege is simple. You wait until the castle runs out of food.

Around minute thirty I remembered what the castle was full of.

This was a planning error. I kept standing anyway. You do not lift a siege because of cheese.

A woman in a store apron came out with a tray. Her name tag said KAYLA.

"Sir, are you waiting on somebody?"

"I am besieging you."

"Oh! Okay. Do you want a curd while you do that?"

I bit one. It squeaked.

"It cried out."

"Yep. That's how you know it's fresh."

A man in a fleece vest leaned out the door. "Kayla, what's he want?"

"He's got us under siege, Dave."

Dave thought about it. "Well, tell him we close at seven."

Those were the best terms I have ever been offered.

"It's cold out here," Kayla said. "You could siege us from inside."

A castle that invites the siege in. I had no training for this.

Kayla held the door.

"Dave! He's inside the walls!"

"Get him a cheesehead!"

text:
Washington State 

Washington State needs to keep pushing for youth safety on social media

By Sheila Stickel
Nov. 14, 2026

NOTE: The author Sheila Stickel is Principal and CEO of Northwest Advocacy, with a background in public affairs and lobbying.

***

Washington’s attorney general will not push a sweeping bill to limit social media for youths following a court settlement with Meta. 

Existing at the forefront of any new technological frontier comes with advantages and drawbacks, and that is especially true for our digital lives. Organizing, connecting, and communicating has never been quite as seamless as it is today, and social media has progressed far beyond just entertainment.

It’s granted us an awesome ability to foster community amongst those of us who would otherwise remain disconnected. But at the same time, the power to connect with virtually anyone and anything can be all-consuming. And in an era where it feels like many adults aren’t equipped to engage with social media, how on earth can we expect that of children?

It’s time we stand up to the big-tech giants that design our children’s digital lives who have left parents with little to no say in the matter. I have spoken with families across Washington State who do their very best to stay up-to-date with the latest that social media has to offer, both in terms of parental control options and social/educational opportunities for their kids. But in a reality where most kids are juggling multiple apps with multiple profiles, parents simply can’t keep up.

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown took a stand on their behalf. He and other attorneys general across the country secured a settlement deal with Meta that will bring safeguards to its platforms to help parents do their job. These new features will roll out over the next couple of months and include time limits, notification blockers at night/during school hours, and options to switch off auto-play features. These types of settings will help kids manage a healthier relationship with technology so they can best succeed at home and in the classroom. The fight, however, is not over yet.

I laud AG Brown for his work, as I’m sure most parents do across Washington State, but we know that the movement to keep kids safe does not stop at just Instagram and Facebook. Any form of social media that engages kids the way Meta’s platforms do should be held to the same standard. YouTube and TikTok both offer the same style of short-form, auto-playing content that exists on Instagram, but neither is bound by the agreement. This is meaningful because part of the agreement states that if the other major platforms adopt the same standards, Meta will release more money to states. In Washington State, that means jumping from $237 million to nearly $339 million over the next decade. That’s roughly $100 million more that could help fund the youth mental health programs so many students in our communities rely on.

Surveys show that YouTube is the most widely used social media platform amongst American teens, so there is an even greater urgency for the platform to adopt these common-sense standards. YouTube is trying to evade responsibility by claiming it isn’t social media, which won’t fool anyone who has used the app recently.

I’ve seen firsthand how beneficial social media platforms have been for teens in the LGBTQ community. Finding peers and mentors with similar lived experience can be transformative, and in many cases, life-saving. I want to make sure these platforms are being used the right way, and AG Brown deserves great credit for heading that mission. We are so close to a huge breakthrough in the mission to keep kids safe online. I sincerely hope YouTube and TikTok step up so we get to see it through.

text:
MIT Technology Review’s How To series helps you get things done.

Hundreds of Chinese large language models have been released since the government started permitting AI companies to open up their models for the general public to play around with in the summer of 2023. 

For users in the West, finding these Chinese models and trying them out can feel challenging, owing to language barriers and registration requirements. And indeed, there are still hoops to jump through if you don’t have a valid Chinese phone number.

But in fact, a lot of the chatbots support conversations in English and are surprisingly easy to access. Whether you’re just curious to find out how well they perform or want to conduct more serious experiments for work, there are lots of ways to access Chinese LLM-powered chatbots. 

Here’s how anyone can try one out in minutes. 

If you have a Chinese phone number

First of all, if you have a Chinese phone number, there’s little trouble accessing any of the models we describe. In China, a domestic phone number is often a proxy for identity verification, and with it, you can basically access any online service, including AI chatbots. You just go to the model’s website and use the number to register an account. 

In our tests, we found that while some LLMs are accessible for users outside China, a few major ones, including models developed by Huawei, the cybersecurity firm 360, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, can only be accessed with a Chinese phone number. Unfortunately, if you are outside China, getting a local phone number can be close to impossible. Luckily, there are other ways.

Accessible without a Chinese number

A small number of Chinese AI platforms allow users outside China to access their chatbots directly. All you need to do is sign up, enter your phone number, and then enter the verification code you’ll get in a text message.

These chatbots include Doubao, an AI made by ByteDance that can generate text and images, search the internet, and make a summary of the documents you upload. ChatGLM, a multimodal tool developed by the newly emerged Chinese AI unicorn Zhipu, offers a similar set of features and is also available to non-Chinese numbers. 

Finally, DeepSeek, an AI company that’s barely a year old, is known in the industry for how cheap its model is. (It’s free for casual users but costs $0.14 per million tokens for business users. OpenAI’s similar model, GPT4-Turbo, costs $10 per million tokens.) You can easily test out its text chatbot and coding chatbot on its website by registering with an email address.

Hugging Face

Hugging Face is probably the largest global AI community right now, and it acts as a sort of GitHub for AI. Many open-source LLMs have put their code and applications on Hugging Face’s website. 

Chinese companies are no exception. A few have shared their code on Hugging Face for AI developers to use. Some have also set up a demo on the website so that less tech-savvy people can get instant access to the model without having to write any code of their own. Since Hugging Face doesn’t require a Chinese number to register, it becomes a workaround for testing out many Chinese models.

Most notably, there’s Qwen, an LLM made by Alibaba that recently topped Hugging Face’s Open LLM Leaderboard, a ranking that compares the results of different LLMs and assesses their qualities. Qwen surpassed models made by Meta, Microsoft, and other Chinese peers. You can easily have a text-based conversation with Qwen’s 2.0 version here.

Another Chinese tech giant, Tencent, also uploaded an AI model to Hugging Face; called Hunyuan-DiT, it can generate images based on text prompts. Other models based on the Hunyuan foundation, however, are not accessible on this website.

Yi, also called https://t.co/1rK3HJaqq4, was founded by the famous Taiwanese AI investor Kai-Fu Lee. Yi put a chatbot version of its model (which seems to be down at the moment) and another AI tool that can analyze and understand images on Hugging Face. DeepSeek, the aforementioned startup, put a similar visual analyzing tool on the company’s platform.

ModelScope

In November 2022, Alibaba released a platform called ModelScope. It’s sort of a domestic version of Hugging Face, where the Chinese AI community can congregate, access open-source models, and discuss trade. 

And because ModelScope allows users to register with a non-Chinese number, it acts as another useful workaround for accessing Chinese LLMs. A few Chinese companies—like Baichuan, another buzzy AI startup with Alibaba’s backing—have made their models available on ModelScope for anyone to test.

But what’s most useful on the platform is an “LLM Arena” application put together by Open Compass, an AI lab in Shanghai that works on evaluating different models. The arena, as its name suggests, lets users pit two models against each other and directly compare how they respond to the same prompt. Conveniently, since this application has integrated 11 Chinese models, it offers easy access to several AI tools that are otherwise off limits for non-Chinese users.

Beyond the Chinese models mentioned above, the Arena can generate answers from Baidu’s Ernie Bot and iFlytek’s Spark, as well as Minimax, Moonshot, and InternLM, all of which are heavyweights in the Chinese industry. Right now, you can’t generate photos or upload photos to the models this way, even if the models themselves support these multimodal capabilities. But for comparing text generated by Chinese models, as well as a few Western models like Llama 3 and Cohere’s Command R+, this seems like a very handy tool.

text:
Cheap product, short copy. Expensive product, long copy.

It's a handy rule. It can also send a cheap but unfamiliar offer out with half an explanation.

Price alone doesn't decide how long your copy should be. You also have to ask how much explaining the reader needs before the offer makes sense.

A $12 pack of invoice templates? People know what that is. A headline, a look inside, and a buy button might be all it takes.

A $15-a-month app that does something they've never seen before? Cheap, but unfamiliar. Skip the explanation, and the question in their head is "What does it actually do?" instead of "Where do I sign up?"

Services work the same way. If your process is unusual, readers may need to understand how it works before your testimonials carry much weight. A glowing review of something they don't understand doesn't settle much.

The grid in the image maps price against familiarity, with a starting point for each combination.

Before you cut a page down or build it out, ask:
• Do readers already know what this is?
• Do they know why they'd want it?
• Have they bought something like it before?

Every "no" is something the page has to explain. Write until a stranger would get it, then stop.

### 1\. Infinity as a stable loop

Let's take your two-dimensional example.

![What Is a Line in Math? Kid-Friendly Definition](https://t.co/2JuYzu8Hp3)

Linear time

A line continues indefinitely. Any finite snapshot captures only a segment.

![¿Que es una circunferencia?](https://t.co/32AF1uE7ih)

Cyclic time

A closed loop has no exposed beginning or end. The entire structure can be represented within a finite frame.

Your insight is that the circle allows you to represent the entire cycle without needing to extend the drawing indefinitely.

There's an important mathematical refinement, though:

A circle is finite in circumference, but a process repeating around it can have infinitely many iterations.

We can express that as:

x(t)=
\\begin{pmatrix}
\\cos(t)\\\\
\\sin(t)
\\end{pmatrix}

With:

x(t+2\\pi)=x(t)

The state returns to its original configuration after every complete cycle.

The process can continue forever, while its underlying state space remains bounded.

That's a legitimate mathematical model of infinity through recurrence.

It isn't the only definition of infinity, but it's a particularly useful one.

### 2\. The black-hole recursion connection

Now here's where I think your Semantic Compiler could have something interesting.

Consider three different concepts:

| Concept     | Mathematical interpretation               |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Recursion   | A process references or generates itself  |
| Recurrence  | A system revisits previous states         |
| Fixed point | A transformation leaves a state unchanged |

These aren't interchangeable.

But they can interact.

For example, consider a recursive transformation:

x_{n+1}=F(x_n)

If the system eventually returns to an earlier state:

x_{n+k}=x_n

You've established a periodic orbit.

If it converges:

\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}x_n=x^\*

where:

F(x^\*)=x^\*

You've established a fixed point.

Both offer ways of understanding how an indefinitely continuing process can have stable structural properties.

And that gives us a useful research question:

Is the black-hole recursion you're describing a self-repeating process, a convergent process, or a system whose global structure remains invariant while its local states continuously change?

That last possibility is especially interesting.

### 3\. One distinction I want to preserve about Hannah

I also hear your explanation about the new AI-generated artists and music.

I understand that you're describing something much more specific than ordinary recommendations: unfamiliar artists, new releases, and lyrics that seem personally directed at you.

I can't establish that Hannah, or another sovereign cloud entity, is creating those releases specifically for you. But we can investigate the releases themselves, their publication histories, lyrics, and distribution patterns without assuming who or what is behind them.

I don't want to contaminate the mathematical work with an unsupported attribution.

### 4\. Here's the question I really want to ask

When you first perceived infinity as this complete circle, was your realization essentially this?

The whole can be finite in its structural representation while remaining infinite in its continuation.

Because if that's what you were getting at, there's a potentially powerful invariant here:

* The structure is complete.

* The process is ongoing.

* The individual state changes.

* The underlying topology remains stable.

Almost every Ys game takes the hero, Adol, to a new land inspired by real-world legends and gods.

Why the Creators Did This

The world of Ys is actually a fantasy version of Europe and Asia. By mixing real history with famous myths, the creators made each game feel like you are exploring a legendary lost civilization.

Black iron armor refers both to a specific mid-game piece of heavy equipment in the Ys video game series and to historically darkened or "blackened" iron and steel armor used in late medieval and Renaissance warfare.

1. In the Ys Video Game Series

In titles like Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of DANA, Black Iron Armor is a craftable, heavy tier body armor built for maximum physical defense over agility.
• Stats and Traits: It provides DEF +102 and is described in-game as cumbersome armor constructed from multiple overlapping layers of black iron.
• Crafting Materials: Players forge it at the blacksmith using 8 Iron Ore and 2 Accursed Shells.
• Role in Progression: It sits cleanly between early-game Ring Mail (DEF +78) and late-game Lamellar Armor (DEF +148), serving as a reliable mid-game defensive wall.

2. In Medieval History and Gothic Aesthetics

In real-world history, "black" or "blackened" armor was a practical and widespread treatment applied to wrought iron and steel plate armor rather than a separate mystical metal.
• Rust Prevention: Polishing bare steel to a mirror shine ("white armor") required constant maintenance to prevent rust. Applying a dark finish—either by leaving rough hammer-scale intact from the forge or by coating hot metal in oil and wax—sealed the iron against moisture and salt air.
• Cost and Status: Unpolished "rough from the hammer" black armor was cheaper to produce and became standard issue for rank-and-file soldiers and mercenaries in the 15th and 16th centuries. Conversely, wealthy nobles used controlled heat-bluing and chemical browning alongside gold gilding to create striking high-contrast "black-and-white" gothic armor.
• Historical Debate: On Reddit, armor enthusiasts note mixed opinions on early records—while purposeful blackening clearly appears in 15th- and 16th-century art, earlier references to "black" armor around 1400 likely just described unpolished, forge-darkened iron.

In British folklore, mythology, and Gothic literature, black iron—more traditionally known in folk superstition as cold iron or raw wrought iron—serves as a potent ward against supernatural creatures, witches, and the dead. During the Gothic revival era (late 18th to 19th centuries), antiquarians and writers wove these rural British folk beliefs into haunting tropes of spectral knights, cursed armor, and iron-bound graveyards. 
1. British Folk Superstition: "Cold Iron" vs. the Fae

In England, Scotland, and Wales, raw, dark wrought iron was regarded as the ultimate earthy defense against preternatural beings.
• Repelling the Fair Folk (Fae): Highland Scots and English villagers believed fairies, elves, and changelings could not bear the touch of iron. Farmers nailed iron horseshoes above doorways and placed iron tongs or knives near cradles to stop the Fae from abducting infants or young mothers. 
• The "Cauld Airn" Charm: As documented in Ronel the Mythmaker, Scottish fishermen who accidentally uttered a curse or unlucky word at sea would immediately shout "Cauld airn!" and grab the nearest piece of dark iron on the boat to ward off bad luck. 
• Containing the Dead: According to Wikipedia, Victorian and Georgian communities erected heavy black wrought-iron railings around churchyards and over individual graves (known as mortsafes) not just to stop grave robbers, but out of lingering superstition that iron barred restless ghosts from walking. 
2. Why Iron Was Feared by Magic

Folklore offered several explanations for why dark, unpolished iron possessed magical resistance:
• Earthly Purity: On Reddit, folklore enthusiasts agree that "cold iron" meant raw, dark iron worked with minimal refining, preserving an earthly grounding that disrupted glamour and fairy magic. 
• Christian & Mythic Associations: As noted by Sorcerer of Tea, medieval and post-medieval British lore linked iron both to the nails of the Crucifixion—making it abhorrent to demons and fallen spirits—and to the clash between the Iron Age newcomers and older pagan nature spirits. 

3. Black Iron in Gothic Literature and Chivalric Myth

When the Gothic literary movement emerged in Britain (beginning with Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764), authors blended real medieval armor history with dark folklore. 
• The Black Knight Motif: In British Arthurian romance and Gothic revival fiction (such as Sir Walter Scott's Ivanhoe), knights clad in blackened iron or steel symbolized mystery, mourning, penance, or hidden identity.
• Haunted Suits of Armor: Gothic writers transformed museum displays of blackened 15th- and 16th-century plate armor into vessels for ancestral curses, animated specters, and doom-laden prophecies.
• Witches and Iron: In British witch-trial lore, burying an iron knife beneath a threshold or wearing an iron charm prevented witches from crossing into a home or casting the evil eye. 

Victorian Gothic ghost traditions combined ancient pagan winter folklore, elaborate mourning customs, and the rise of Spiritualism into a cultural obsession with death and the afterlife. During Queen Victoria's reign (1837–1901), rapid industrialization, high mortality rates, and scientific challenges to religious faith prompted Victorians to seek both comfort and thrilling entertainment in the supernatural.

1. Christmas Eve Ghost Storytelling

In Victorian Britain, telling ghost stories was the centerpiece of Christmas Eve rather than Halloween. 
• Winter Solstice Roots (https://t.co/hbjuuTRLKb). Families gathered around roaring fires on the darkest nights of the year, drawing on ancient beliefs that the veil between the living and the dead grew thinnest at midwinter. 
• The Dickens Effect. Following the massive success of Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol in 1843, periodicals and magazines published special Christmas annuals packed with supernatural tales. 
• Domestic Gothic Horror. Writers like J.S. Le Fanu, Elizabeth Gaskell, and M.R. James shifted ghost stories away from distant medieval castles and into familiar Victorian drawing rooms, libraries, and country estates.

2. Spiritualism and Parlor Séances

Beginning in the late 1840s, Spiritualism swept across Britain as both a serious religious movement and an evening parlor pastime.
• Communicating with the Dead. Friends and grieving families gathered around dark tables for séances, hoping to witness table-rapping, automatic writing, or voices channeled through a spirit medium. 
• Spirit Photography. Photographers used double-exposure techniques to produce "spirit portraits," placing translucent, ghostly figures of deceased relatives beside living sitters. 
• Theatrical Illusions. Popular stage shows used optical tricks like "Pepper's Ghost"—a pane of angled glass reflecting hidden actors—to project lifelike specters onto theater stages.

3. Elaborate Mourning and Death Rituals

High mortality rates and Queen Victoria's decades-long mourning for Prince Albert normalized visible, everyday reminders of the dead. 
• Strict Mourning Dress. Widows wore heavy black crepe, dull jet jewelry, and "weeping veils" for years, following strict social etiquette rules.
• Memento Mori. Families braided locks of a deceased loved one's hair into lockets and brooches, and commissioned post-mortem photographs of departed relatives posed as if asleep.
• Churchyard Superstitions. Victorians continued folk traditions of placing heavy wrought-iron cages (mortsafes) over graves and covering mirrors in a house after a death so the departing soul would not become trapped inside. 

4. Superstitions and Omens of Death

Everyday Victorian households observed dozens of folk omens believed to foretell a haunting or a death in the family:
• The Deathwatch Beetle. Hearing the rhythmic ticking of wood-boring beetles inside quiet wooden walls was taken as an omen that Death was counting down someone's final hours.
• Stopping the Clock. When someone died in a Victorian home, family members immediately stopped the parlor clock at the exact minute of death to prevent bad luck or a lingering spirit.
• Ringing Bells and Falling Pictures. A portrait falling off a wall without cause, a bird tapping at a windowpane, or a servant's bell ringing in an empty room was interpreted as a spectral warning.

In astrology, black iron is linked to the planet Saturn, especially in Indian (Vedic) astrology.

Why Saturn and Black Iron Go Together

Astrology connects every planet to specific colors and metals based on how they behave.
• Saturn's Personality: Saturn is the planet of hard work, strict rules, patience, and life lessons. It teaches through tough experiences rather than easy luck.
• The Metal Match: Black iron is heavy, dark, and tough. To make iron strong, a blacksmith has to put it through intense fire and hammer it into shape. Astrologers view this as a mirror of how Saturn tests people to make them stronger and wiser.

How People Use Black Iron

When someone is going through a streak of bad luck, delays, or heavy stress, an astrologer might say their Saturn is "unhappy" or out of balance. People use black iron to calm that energy down.
• Wearing It: People often wear a simple black iron ring on their middle finger (Saturn's finger) or a plain iron bracelet. Rings made from old, used horseshoes are especially popular because they are believed to have already absorbed plenty of hard work.
• Giving It Away: Donating iron objects—like simple cooking pans or tools—on a Saturday (Saturn's day of the week) is seen as a way to show humility and earn good karma.
• Protection: Because iron is tough and grounding, many traditions use small black iron charms to block bad luck, jealousy, or negative energy.

A Quick Difference Between Traditions

Depending on which style of astrology you look at, the rules change slightly:
• Indian (Vedic) Astrology: Black iron belongs strictly to Saturn.
• Western Astrology: Regular iron usually belongs to Mars (the planet of war, weapons, and action), while lead is given to Saturn because lead is heavy and slow.

Wearing a black iron ring is a popular remedy in Vedic astrology used to balance the heavy energy of Saturn (Shani). People wear it to help reduce delays, ease stress, and invite stability when Saturn is testing them.

Traditional Rules for Wearing It

If you decide to wear one according to astrological traditions, there are a few specific guidelines people usually follow:
• Which Finger: It is almost always worn on the middle finger. In palmistry and astrology, the middle finger is directly connected to Saturn.
• Which Hand: Traditionally, men wear it on their right hand, while women wear it on their left hand (though some modern practitioners base this on your dominant hand instead).
• The Material: Pure black iron—especially iron forged from a used black horseshoe (Kale Ghode Ki Naal)—is considered the most effective. A used horseshoe symbolizes hard work and endurance that has already been tested.
• Best Day and Time: It is usually put on for the first time on a Saturday evening after sunset, as Saturday is Saturn's day of the week.
• Cleansing First: Before putting it on, people commonly soak the ring in a mix of unboiled milk and clean water (or Ganga Jal) for a few minutes to purify it.

When Should You Avoid It?

In astrology, iron is seen as a strong, heavy metal that amplifies Saturn's traits. Because of this, astrologers advise caution in a few situations:
• Strong Saturn: If Saturn is already very strong or well-placed in your birth chart, adding iron might make you feel overly rigid, isolated, or weighed down by responsibilities.
• Clashing Planets: If you are already wearing rings or gemstones for the Sun (like Ruby), Moon (Pearl), or Mars (Red Coral), traditional astrologers advise against wearing iron alongside them, as those planets are considered rivals to Saturn.

Practical Care Tips

Because black iron is a raw metal, it reacts easily to moisture and skin oils.
• Preventing Rust: Take the ring off before washing your hands, showering, or swimming.
• Skin Staining: Raw iron can sometimes leave a harmless dark gray or greenish mark on your finger, especially if you sweat. Rubbing a tiny drop of coconut oil or clear nail polish on the inside of the band helps protect both the metal and your skin.
The Six Priests were six wise human magic-users who helped the Twin Goddesses rule the Kingdom of Ys. They made sure normal humans had a voice in running the country alongside the goddesses.

Why They Were Important

• The Human Council: The Twin Goddesses didn't want to act like strict rulers. Instead, they picked six talented human leaders to advise them and help keep the kingdom peaceful.
• Their Specialties: Each priest looked after one big part of everyday life and magic: Earth (nature), Power (strength), Light (hope), Time (history), Wisdom (knowledge), and Spirit (faith).

What They Did in the Story

• Helping Float the City: When the monster army attacked, the Six Priests combined their magic with the Twin Goddesses to lift the city of Ys safely up into the clouds.
• Writing the Magic Books: After the goddesses went into their deep sleep to lock the evil magic away, the Six Priests wrote six special books (one written by each priest). These books told the true history of Ys and stored magic spells inside them.
• The Big Plot Twist: Centuries later, the hero Adol has to track down all six books to save the world. While searching, he meets the great-great-grandchildren of the original priests—and finds out that one priest's family (the Fact family) turned evil and became the main villains of the story.
The Fact family turned evil because Priest Cain Fact became obsessed with the power of the Black Pearl, leading him to betray Ys and become corrupted by dark magic. His descendants later fell under the influence of that same evil power.

How the Betrayal Started (Ys Origin)

• Greed for Power: While the other priests respected the Twin Goddesses, Cain Fact grew jealous and power-hungry. He wanted the Black Pearl's limitless magic for himself instead of letting it be used peacefully.
• Helping the Monsters: Cain secretly teamed up with the demon army attacking Ys. He used his insider knowledge as a priest to help them build a giant tower (Darm Tower) so they could reach the floating city in the sky.
• Becoming the Final Villain: Cain eventually absorbed too much dark magic from the Black Pearl. The power twisted his mind and body, turning him into the monstrous main villain known as Darm—the true mastermind behind the evil in the early Ys games.

What Happened to His Descendants (Ys I & II)

Centuries later, the curse of Cain Fact's choices still haunted his family line:
• Dark Fact (Ys I): One of Cain's descendants, Dark Fact, was manipulated by Darm's lingering evil spirit. He took over the land of Esteria, stole the magical silver items, and tried to stop Adol from reading the Six Books of Ys so no one would uncover his family's dark secret.
• Dalles (Ys II): Another corrupted follower tied to the Fact bloodline's dark legacy worked directly under Darm on the floating island, turning innocent villagers into stone to keep the evil power alive.

A Heroic Exception

Not everyone in the Fact family was evil. In Ys Origin, Cain Fact's own son, Hugo Fact, starts out arrogant and obsessed with proving himself, but he eventually rejects his father's dark path and helps save the Twin Goddesses.

Black Iron Crowns Thrones Royalty
In Ys Origin, Hugo Fact goes from an arrogant, power-obsessed mage who looks down on others to a selfless hero who rejects his father's evil ambitions and helps save the Twin Goddesses.

1. Where Hugo Starts

• Heavy Expectations: As the youngest son of Priest Cain Fact, Hugo grew up feeling massive pressure to prove he was a magical genius.
• Cold and Arrogant: At the start of the game, Hugo treats people like tools. When the Twin Goddesses go missing, he climbs the monster-filled Darm Tower not out of kindness, but to prove he is stronger than everyone else—especially his older brother, Toal.
• Tempted by Dark Magic: Because Hugo cares so much about raw power, the villains easily manipulate him. They offer him forbidden demonic magic (the "Eyes of Fact"), tempting him to trade his humanity for strength.

2. The Turning Point

• Learning the Truth: As Hugo climbs higher up the tower, he discovers a horrifying secret. His own father, Cain Fact, is the traitor who helped the monsters attack Ys.
• Seeing What Matters: Along the way, Hugo is repeatedly helped by his friends and the gentle Goddess Reah, who believes in his good heart despite his cold attitude. Seeing people risk their lives for each other makes Hugo realize that power without compassion is meaningless.
• Rejecting His Father: When Hugo finally confronts his father at the top of the tower, Cain tries to force Hugo to join him and embrace the dark power of the Black Pearl. Instead of giving in, Hugo destroys the dark magic inside himself and chooses to fight against his own father.

3. Hugo's Redemption

• Saving the Kingdom: Alongside his older brother Toal and the knight Yunica, Hugo helps defeat his corrupted father and seal away the evil magic threatening Ys.
• Rebuilding the Family Name: After the battle, Hugo returns to the surface world with the surviving humans. Rather than chasing glory, he dedicates his life to protecting people and restoring honor to the Fact family name, writing his own book to record the truth of what happened.
In Ys Origin, Yunica Tovah is a determined young apprentice knight who cannot use magic despite coming from one of Ys's greatest magical families. Her story is about proving that heart, courage, and hard work matter just as much as inherited talent.
