A Lament Over Tyre

1 The word of the LORD came to me:
2 “Son of man, take up a lament concerning Tyre.
3 Say to Tyre, situated at the gateway to the sea, merchant of peoples on many coasts, ‘This is what the Sovereign LORD says: “ ‘You say, Tyre, “I am perfect in beauty.”
4 Your domain was on the high seas; your builders brought your beauty to perfection.
5 They made all your timbers of juniper from Senirfn; they took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.
6 Of oaks from Bashan they made your oars; of cypress woodfn from the coasts of Cyprus they made your deck, adorned with ivory.
7 Fine embroidered linen from Egypt was your sail and served as your banner; your awnings were of blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah.
8 Men of Sidon and Arvad were your oarsmen; your skilled men, Tyre, were aboard as your sailors.
9 Veteran craftsmen of Byblos were on board as shipwrights to caulk your seams. All the ships of the sea and their sailors came alongside to trade for your wares.
10 “ ‘Men of Persia, Lydia and Put served as soldiers in your army. They hung their shields and helmets on your walls, bringing you splendor.
11 Men of Arvad and Helek guarded your walls on every side; men of Gammad were in your towers. They hung their shields around your walls; they brought your beauty to perfection.
12 “ ‘Tarshish did business with you because of your great wealth of goods; they exchanged silver, iron, tin and lead for your merchandise.
13 “ ‘Greece, Tubal and Meshek did business with you; they traded human beings and articles of bronze for your wares.
14 “ ‘Men of Beth Togarmah exchanged chariot horses, cavalry horses and mules for your merchandise.
15 “ ‘The men of Rhodes traded with you, and many coastlands were your customers; they paid you with ivory tusks and ebony.
16 “ ‘Aram did business with you because of your many products; they exchanged turquoise, purple fabric, embroidered work, fine linen, coral and rubies for your merchandise.
17 “ ‘Judah and Israel traded with you; they exchanged wheat from Minnith and confections, honey, olive oil and balm for your wares.
18 “ ‘Damascus did business with you because of your many products and great wealth of goods. They offered wine from Helbon, wool from Zahar
19 and casks of wine from Izal in exchange for your wares: wrought iron, cassia and calamus.
20 “ ‘Dedan traded in saddle blankets with you.
21 “ ‘Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your customers; they did business with you in lambs, rams and goats.
22 “ ‘The merchants of Sheba and Raamah traded with you; for your merchandise they exchanged the finest of all kinds of spices and precious stones, and gold.
23 “ ‘Harran, Kanneh and Eden and merchants of Sheba, Ashur and Kilmad traded with you.
24 In your marketplace they traded with you beautiful garments, blue fabric, embroidered work and multicolored rugs with cords twisted and tightly knotted.
25 “ ‘The ships of Tarshish serve as carriers for your wares. You are filled with heavy cargo as you sail the sea.
26 Your oarsmen take you out to the high seas. But the east wind will break you to pieces far out at sea.
27 Your wealth, merchandise and wares, your mariners, sailors and shipwrights, your merchants and all your soldiers, and everyone else on board will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your shipwreck.
28 The shorelands will quake when your sailors cry out.
29 All who handle the oars will abandon their ships; the mariners and all the sailors will stand on the shore.
30 They will raise their voice and cry bitterly over you; they will sprinkle dust on their heads and roll in ashes.
31 They will shave their heads because of you and will put on sackcloth. They will weep over you with anguish of soul and with bitter mourning.

text:
Hey brother, I really appreciate you taking the time to read the article and share your thoughts. And I understand exactly what you're saying. You're absolutely right that many of these organizational concepts have been around for decades.

A lot of what we're seeing today isn't necessarily new military thinking, but rather the challenge of adapting and implementing these concepts under the conditions of modern warfare in Ukraine.

As for rotations and rebuilding brigades, I completely agree that these are important subjects. The reason I didn't go into them in this particular article is that I think they deserve their own discussion about rebuilding combat power, personnel replacements, training, and maintaining combat effectiveness. I've actually touched on some of these subjects in previous articles, and there's certainly a lot more that could be written about them.

One thing I also have to be careful about is operational security. Since I'm working here in Ukraine, I have to be mindful of what I discuss publicly. There are certain things I see and learn that I simply can't get into because I don't want anything I write to potentially benefit the enemy. I'm sure you can appreciate that.

And just to give you a little perspective on why I write the way I do, most of my articles aren't really intended to be Army War College level papers. A lot of the people who follow my writing are civilians who have little or no military background. Some are just beginning to understand how military organizations function. 

So I try to explain these subjects in a way that's easy to follow without getting too deep into military doctrine or terminology. For someone with a strong military background, some of this information might seem pretty basic, but for someone learning about it for the first time, it can be very useful.

That being said, I genuinely appreciate people like yourself who take the time to offer thoughtful criticism and bring up subjects that deserve more attention. I certainly don't claim to have all the answers, and I enjoy hearing different perspectives. That's part of what makes these discussions worthwhile.

And you know what? I think your point about rotations and rebuilding brigades is actually a great idea for another article. It's an important part of understanding how armies sustain themselves during a prolonged war. I'll give that some thought and see what I can put together while keeping operational security in mind.

Anyway, my friend, thanks again for reading and taking the time to comment. I really do appreciate it, and I hope you'll continue sharing your thoughts on future articles. Always happy to have a good conversation about military matters with someone who takes an interest in the subject.

text:
SpaceX ($SPCX) eyes S&P 500 inclusion via a Tesla merger. The deal would create a $3.5 trillion giant, bypassing previous indexing rejections.

The move aims to secure mandatory purchases by $16 trillion in passive index funds. This could generate $100 billion in new demand for the stock, according to TD Securities.

Tesla shares fell 0.59% on Friday, closing at $139.11. The carmaker faces weak US demand and recently ended Cybertruck production.

SpaceX recently posted its first profitable quarter but burns cash for ambitious projects. Both companies trade at high valuations compared to broader market averages.

The merger talks are progressing, with a potential announcement as soon as next month. SpaceX could meet S&P profitability rules by mid-next year.

A combined entity might retain Tesla’s index slot, avoiding displacement of another firm. S&P Dow Jones declined to comment on the speculation.

This strategy offers a backdoor into the benchmark, which previously blocked SpaceX’s direct entry despite its massive size.

The consolidation would increase the index’s tech weighting significantly. It raises questions about concentration risk in major market trackers.

The outcome remains unconfirmed. If excluded, index funds would likely sell shares acquired through the merger, pressuring the stock.

text:
The best music producers I worked with all did the same thing when a track wasn't working, they took something out

They never added another layer, they took one away. It might be a sound or a second hook that was fighting the vocal, and once it was gone the track suddenly worked.

Film is the same. The edit is where a good film gets made, and most of the edit is deciding what the audience never sees.

In tech I see the opposite almost every week, another tab, another feature, another announcement, another partnership, and hardly anyone talks about what they cut and why.

When we build at theMiracle I try to bring that habit with me, asking what someone actually needs to see when an offer opens, and cutting the rest so they see it faster.

text:
Until late November, when the epic saga of OpenAI’s board breakdown unfolded, the casual observer could be forgiven for assuming that the industry around generative AI was a vibrant competitive ecosystem. 

But this is not the case—nor has it ever been. And understanding why is fundamental to understanding what AI is, and what threats it poses. Put simply, in the context of the current paradigm of building larger- and larger-scale AI systems, there is no AI without Big Tech. With vanishingly few exceptions, every startup, new entrant, and even AI research lab is dependent on these firms. All rely on the computing infrastructure of Microsoft, Amazon, and Google to train their systems, and on those same firms’ vast consumer market reach to deploy and sell their AI products. 

Indeed, many startups simply license and rebrand AI models created and sold by these tech giants or their partner startups. This is because large tech firms have accrued significant advantages over the past decade. Thanks to platform dominance and the self-reinforcing properties of the surveillance business model, they own and control the ingredients necessary to develop and deploy large-scale AI. They also shape the incentive structures for the field of research and development in AI, defining the technology’s present and future. 

The recent OpenAI saga, in which Microsoft exerted its quiet but firm dominance over the “capped profit” entity, provides a powerful demonstration of what we’ve been analyzing for the last half-decade. To wit: those with the money make the rules. And right now, they’re engaged in a race to the bottom, releasing systems before they’re ready in an attempt to retain their dominant position. 

Concentrated power isn’t just a problem for markets. Relying on a few unaccountable corporate actors for core infrastructure is a problem for democracy, culture, and individual and collective agency. Without significant intervention, the AI market will only end up rewarding and entrenching the very same companies that reaped the profits of the invasive surveillance business model that has powered the commercial internet, often at the expense of the public. 

The Cambridge Analytica scandal was just one among many that exposed this seedy reality. Such concentration also creates single points of failure, which raises real security threats. And Securities and Exchange Commission chair Gary Gensler has warned that having a small number of AI models and actors at the foundation of the AI ecosystem poses systemic risks to the financial order, in which the effects of a single failure could be distributed much more widely. 

The assertion that AI is contingent on—and exacerbates—concentration of power in the tech industry has often been met with pushback. Investors who have moved quickly from Web3 to the metaverse to AI are keen to realize returns in an ecosystem where a frenzied press cycle drives valuations toward profitable IPOs and acquisitions, even if the promises of the  technology in question aren’t ever realized. 

But the attempted ouster—and subsequent reintegration—of OpenAI cofounders Sam Altman and Greg Brockman doesn’t just bring the power and influence of Microsoft into sharp focus; it also proves our case that these commercial arrangements give Big Tech profound control over the trajectory of AI. The story is fairly simple: after apparently being blindsided by the board’s decision, Microsoft moved to protect its investment and its road map to profit. The company quickly exerted its weight, rallying behind Altman and promising to “acquihire” those who wanted to defect. 

Microsoft now has a seat on OpenAI’s board, albeit a nonvoting one. But the true leverage that Big Tech holds in the AI landscape is the combination of its computing power, data, and vast market reach. In order to pursue its bigger-is-better approach to AI development, OpenAI made a deal. It exclusively licenses its GPT-4 system and all other OpenAI models to Microsoft in exchange for access to Microsoft’s computing infrastructure. 

For companies hoping to build base models, there is little alternative to working with either Microsoft, Google, or Amazon. And those at the center of AI are well aware of this, as illustrated by Sam Altman’s furtive search for Saudi and Emirati sovereign investment in a hardware venture he hoped would rival Nvidia. That company holds a near monopoly on state-of-the-art chips for AI training and is another key choke point along the AI supply chain. US regulators have since unwound an initial investment by Saudi Arabia into an Altman-backed company, RainAI, reinforcing the difficulty OpenAI faces in navigating the even more concentrated chipmaking market.

There are few meaningful alternatives, even for those willing to go the extra mile to build industry-independent AI. As we’ve outlined elsewhere, “‘open-source AI”—an ill-defined term that’s currently used to describe everything from Meta’s (comparatively closed) LLaMA-2 and Eleuther’s (maximally open) Pythia series—can’t on its own offer escape velocity from industry concentration. For one thing, many open-source AI projects operate through compute credits, revenue sharing, or other contractual arrangements with tech giants that grapple with the same structural dependencies. In addition, Big Tech has a long legacy of capturing, or otherwise attempting to seek profit from, open-source development. Open-source AI can offer transparency, reusability, and extensibility, and these can be positive. But it does not address the problem of concentrated power in the AI market. 

The OpenAI-Microsoft saga also demonstrates a fact that’s frequently lost in the hype around AI: there isn’t yet a clear business model outside of increasing cloud profits for Big Tech by bundling AI services with cloud infrastructure. And a business model is important when you’re talking about systems that can cost hundreds of millions of dollars to train and develop. 

Microsoft isn’t alone here: Amazon, for example, runs a marketplace for AI models, on which all of its products, and a handful of others, operate using Amazon Web Services. The company recently struck an investment deal of up to $4 billion with Anthropic, which has also pledged to use Amazon’s in-house chip, Trainium, optimized for building large-scale AI. 

Big Tech is becoming increasingly assertive in its maneuverings to protect its hold over the market. Make no mistake: though OpenAI was in the crosshairs this time, now that we’ve all seen what it looks like for a small entity when a big firm it depends on decides to flex, others will be paying attention and falling in line. 

Regulation could help, but government policy often winds up entrenching, rather than mitigating, the power of these companies as they leverage their access to money and their political clout. Take Microsoft’s recent moves in the UK as an example: last week it announced a £2.5 billion investment in building out cloud infrastructure in the UK, a move lauded by a prime minister who has clearly signaled his ambitions to build a homegrown AI sector in the UK as his primary legacy. This news can’t be read in isolation: it is a clear attempt to blunt an investigation into the cloud market by the UK’s competition regulator following a study that specifically called out concerns registered by a range of market participants regarding Microsoft’s anticompetitive behavior. 

From OpenAI’s (ultimately empty) threat to leave the EU over the AI Act to Meta’s lobbying to exempt open-source AI from basic accountability obligations to Microsoft’s push for restrictive licensing to the Big Tech–funded campaign to embed fellows in Congress, we’re seeing increasingly aggressive stances from large firms that are trying to shore up their dominance by wielding their considerable economic and political power.

Tech industry giants are already circling their wagons as new regulations emerge from the White House, the EU, and elsewhere. But it’s clear we need to go much further. Now’s the time for a meaningful and robust accountability regime that places the interests of the public above the promises of firms not known for keeping them. 

We need aggressive transparency mandates that clear away the opacity around fundamental issues like the data AI companies are accessing to train their models. We also need liability regimes that place the burden on companies to demonstrate that they meet baseline privacy, security, and bias standards before their AI products are publicly released. And to begin to address concentration, we need bold regulation that forces business separation between different layers of the AI stack and doesn’t allow Big Tech to leverage its dominance in infrastructure to consolidate its position in the market for AI models and applications. 

But if governments keep giving the same narrow group of industry interests primacy in guiding policy, we won’t get far. After last week’s events, it’s all too clear what these companies serve: their bottom line. 

Amba Kak is executive director and Sarah Myers West is managing director of the AI Now Institute, a New York–based policy research organization focused on artificial intelligence. Meredith Whittaker, the president of Signal, is the institute’s chief advisor.

text:
III. The Blood That Makes White

The importance of blood in Scripture did not begin with Revelation. Long before John saw the heavenly multitude, God instructed Israel concerning the significance of blood in the sacrificial system. Leviticus 17:11 declares, “For the life of the flesh is in the blood,” and explains that God gave it upon the altar to make atonement for souls. The tabernacle sacrifices were not religious entertainment, and the shedding of blood was not an unnecessary detail that could be replaced by something more attractive to modern sensibilities. God was teaching the seriousness of sin and the necessity of an acceptable sacrifice. Hebrews 9:22 declares that “without shedding of blood is no remission.” Nevertheless, the sacrifices offered under the law were not the final answer to the guilt of humanity. Hebrews 10:4 states, “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” Those sacrifices pointed forward to a greater and sufficient sacrifice. The blood of an animal could never possess the infinite value of the blood of God’s own Son. When Jesus Christ came as the Lamb of God, He did not arrive to offer another temporary religious demonstration. He came to accomplish redemption through His own sacrifice. That is why the blood of the Lamb occupies such a central place in the book of Revelation. The One who opens the seals is the same One who was slain.

Hebrews 9:14 asks, “How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” There is the answer to every attempt to explain salvation through human improvement. Christ’s blood does what man’s works cannot do. First Peter 1:18–19 reminds believers that they were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but “with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” That blood is precious because of the One who shed it. Jesus Christ was no helpless victim of circumstances, no unfortunate teacher crushed by a cruel political system, and no ordinary martyr whose death merely inspires men to become better people. He was the sinless Son of God, who willingly gave Himself for sinners. The value of His sacrifice is not measured by the amount of pain alone, as though the greatest suffering automatically produces the greatest atonement. Its sufficiency rests upon His identity, His sinlessness, and the sacrifice He accomplished. Men may be impressed by wealth, religious rank, or celebrated accomplishments, but heaven’s song is centered upon the Lamb who was slain. Revelation 5:9 declares that redemption is accomplished through His blood. Revelation 7:14 then shows another company whose garments are made white through that same precious blood.

Now compare Revelation 1:5 with Revelation 7:14. At the opening of the book, John gives glory “Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood.” Later, the multitude is described as having washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. The persons, prophetic settings, and dispensational applications must be distinguished, but the sacrifice is not a different sacrifice. We are not presented with one blood for the Church and another blood for those coming out of great tribulation. There is one Lamb whose redemptive work is sufficient. That does not erase the distinct commands, warnings, or responsibilities found in different dispensations, and it does not give us permission to preach every passage as though it were addressed directly to the same audience. It establishes something more fundamental: whenever Scripture speaks of cleansing through the blood of the Lamb, the saving power belongs to Christ and not to the sinner. If the blood of a martyr could redeem, then the cross would have been unnecessary. If endurance could remove sin, then Christ would not have needed to shed

text:
WHEN THE OFFERING IS TAKEN AWAY

Jesus didn’t give us a date. He gave us a sign.

“When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:)” Matthew 24:15

THE SIGN

The holy place is the temple ground on Mount Moriah, today’s Temple Mount in Jerusalem (Acts 21:28). It’s where the man of sin “as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

Daniel tells us when the count begins: “from the time that the daily sacrifice shall be taken away, and the abomination that maketh desolate set up, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days” (Daniel 12:11).

THE STAGE IS BEING SET

You can’t take away an offering that isn’t there. The daily offering has to be restored first.

A stone altar is built and reported “ready to go” for the Temple Mount.
Passover 2026 saw a record seven attempts to bring sacrifices onto the Mount, by Palestinian officials’ count.
Jewish prayer on the Mount went from forbidden to tolerated.

No temple is needed first. The returning exiles offered sacrifices, “But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid” (Ezra 3:6).

THE NUMBERS

1,260 days = 3½ years (42 months × 30 days). This is the time of the Two Witnesses, the woman in the wilderness and the beast (Revelation 11:3; 12:6; 13:5).

1,290 days appear only in Daniel 12:11. They start the day the abomination is set up.

THE TIMELINE I AM WATCHING

Each biblical day runs from sundown to sundown.

Day 1: Firstfruits, the abomination
Sundown Sat, Mar 27 – sundown Sun, Mar 28, 2027
The Sabbath ends and the abomination is set up. As of November 14, 2026, this is about 133 days away.

Day 18: The Two Witnesses begin
Sundown Apr 13 – sundown Apr 14, 2027
They begin to prophesy for 1,260 days (Revelation 11:3).

Day 31: The woman is fed in the wilderness
Sundown Apr 26 – sundown Apr 27, 2027
Her 1,260 days in her prepared place begin (Revelation 12:6).

Day 1,277: The Two Witnesses are killed
Sundown Sep 23 – sundown Sep 24, 2030
Their 1,260 days end. The beast kills them, and they lie in the street 3½ days (Revelation 11:7-9).

Day 1,281: Feast of Trumpets, the gathering
Sundown Sep 27 – sundown Sep 28, 2030
The Two Witnesses stand up alive and go up to heaven in a cloud (Revelation 11:11-12). The seventh trumpet sounds (Revelation 11:15). Christ appears, the dead in Christ rise, and the living saints are caught up together with them (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

Day 1,290: Yom Kippur, wrath complete
Sundown Oct 6 – sundown Oct 7, 2030
God’s wrath is complete. The woman’s 1,260 days end.

Day 1,335: The blessing
Sundown Nov 20 – sundown Nov 21, 2030
The 1,335 days are complete. “Blessed is he that waiteth” (Daniel 12:12)

1,280 days of tribulation + 10 days of wrath = Daniel’s 1,290. Every count lands to the day.

The count starts right as the Sabbath ends. Jesus said, “pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day” (Matthew 24:20).

THE CALENDAR I USE, AND WHY
These dates follow the biblical calendar, not the fixed Jewish calendar printed today. That calendar was set by calculation centuries after the Temple fell, and tradition credits it to Hillel II.
God set the lights in the sky “for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years” (Genesis 1:14).

Days begin at sundown (Genesis 1:5).
Months begin with the new moon (Psalm 104:19).
The year begins in spring, in the month of Abib, when the barley is in the ear (Exodus 9:31; 12:2; Deuteronomy 16:1). A 13th month is added when needed to keep the feasts in their seasons.

Firstfruits is “the morrow after the sabbath,” the day after the weekly Sabbath during Unleavened Bread (Leviticus 23:11). That is how the Sadducee priests read it in Jesus’ day.
Jesus rose on that day, “In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week” (Matthew 28:1), as “the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The calendar that fit his first coming is the one I use to watch for his return.
HOW RARE IS THIS?

I tested every year from 1900 to 2500. The barley can’t be forecast, so for this test I used the spring equinox to set the year. An exact 1,290-day fit from Firstfruits to Yom Kippur three years later happens in only seven of those years. After 2027, the next one is 2247.

WHAT I AM WATCHING FOR
On the biblical calendar, Passover 2027 is sundown March 21 to sundown March 22, the natural time for the sacrifices to be restored. The printed Jewish calendar puts Passover a month later, at sundown April 21, so I am watching for the daily offering itself, not just the feast.

I hold this as a timeline to test, not a date to announce. If no daily offering is running on the Temple Mount by late March 2027, I’ll say so.

THE SACRIFICE NO ONE CAN REMOVE

No altar in Jerusalem can take away one sin. Christ “offered one sacrifice for sins for ever” (Hebrews 10:12). The man of sin can stop an offering. He can’t touch the cross.

Watch without panic. Obey without delay. Refuse the mark.

“Look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.” Luke 21:28

(G) Saint Jerome

“‘But,’ you [Jovinian] will say, ‘it was on Peter that the Church was founded’ [Matt. 16:18]. Well . . . one among the twelve is chosen to be their head in order to remove any occasion for division” (Against Jovinian 1:26 [A.D. 393]).

(H) Pope Saint Innocent I

 “In seeking the things of God . . . you have acknowledged that judgment is to be referred to us [the pope], and have shown that you know that is owed to the Apostolic See [Rome], if all of us placed in this position are to desire to follow the apostle himself [Peter] from whom the episcopate itself and the total authority of this name have emerged” (Letters 29:1 [A.D. 408]).

(I) Saint Augustine

“Among these [apostles] Peter alone almost everywhere deserved to represent the whole Church. Because of that representation of the Church, which only he bore, he deserved to hear ‘I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’” (Sermons 295:2 [A.D. 411]).

“Some things are said which seem to relate especially to the apostle Peter, and yet are not clear in their meaning unless referred to the Church, which he is acknowledged to have represented in a figure on account of the primacy which he bore among the disciples. Such is ‘I will give unto you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,’ and other similar passages” (Commentary on Psalm 108 1 [A.D. 415]).

“Who is ignorant that the first of the apostles is the most blessed Peter?” (Commentary on John 56:1 [A.D. 416]).

(J) Council of Ephesus 

“Philip, presbyter and legate of [Pope Celestine I] said: ‘We offer our thanks to the holy and venerable synod, that when the writings of our holy and blessed pope had been read to you . . . you joined yourselves to the holy head also by your holy acclamations. For your blessedness is not ignorant that the head of the whole faith, the head of the apostles, is blessed Peter the apostle’” (Acts of the Council, session 2 [A.D. 431]).
“Philip, the presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See [Rome] said: ‘There is no doubt, and in fact it has been known in all ages, that the holy and most blessed Peter, prince and head of the apostles, pillar of the faith, and foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of the human race, and that to him was given the power of loosing and binding sins: who down even to today and forever both lives and judges in his successors’” (ibid., session 3).

(K) Pope Saint Leo I

“Our Lord Jesus Christ . . . has placed the principal charge on the blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, and from him as from the head wishes his gifts to flow to all the body, so that anyone who dares to secede from Peter’s solid rock may understand that he has no part or lot in the divine mystery. He wished him who had been received into partnership in his undivided unity to be named what he himself was, when he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Matt. 16:18], that the building of the eternal temple might rest on Peter’s solid rock, strengthening his Church so surely that neither could human rashness assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it” (Letters 10:1 [A.D. 445).

🪷 Sri Padmavati Devi Jayanti (celebrated grandly as Panchami Tirtham) marks the divine manifestation of Goddess Padmavati, an incarnation of Goddess Lakshmi Mata and the consort of Lord Sri Venkateshwar Balaji. 🪷

✨ Observed on the fifth day (Shukla Panchami) of the lunar month of Kartika, the 2026 celebration falls on November 14, 2026.

✨ Details of Padmavati Devi Jayanti:
According to sacred texts, childless King Akasha Raja and Queen Dharani Devi were ploughing a field for a royal yajna when their plough struck a golden box. Inside rested an infant girl on a thousand-petaled golden lotus in the sacred tank.

🪷 Panchami Tirtham Ritual: Celebrated as the grand finale of the nine-day Kartika Brahmotsavams, this day commemorates Her emergence from the lotus.
🪷 Saare Tradition: Priests carry ceremonial gifts—known as Saare—including turmeric, kumkum, silk sarees, and ornaments from Lord Venkateshwar in Tirumala down to His Consort in Tiruchanur.
🪷 Snapana Tirumanjanam: The processional Idol of Goddess Padmavati and the sacred Sudarshana Chakra (Chakrattalwar) receive a celestial bath on the banks of the Padma Sarovaram tank, followed by thousands of devotees taking a holy dip.

✨ Sacred Secrets & Lesser-Known Legends:-
Devotees and temple traditions hold several deep spiritual secrets regarding the Sri Padmavati Ammavari Temple in Tiruchanur.

The Secret of Her Height: Temple lore states that the main stone deities of Lord Venkateswara in Tirumala and Goddess Padmavati in Tiruchanur were originally carved to the exact same height. However, the Goddess's Idol is said to have sunk slightly into the earth under the immense weight of Her maternal compassion for suffering devotees.
Worshipped Alone as Vira Lakshmi: Unlike most temples where Lakshmi is enshrined alongside Vishnu, Padmavati Devi sits alone in the Tiruchanur sanctum, earning Her the title Vira Lakshmi (the courageous, independent form of Lakshmi).
The Tirumala Pilgrimage Rule: A longstanding tradition holds that a pilgrimage to Tirupati Balaji remains incomplete without visiting Padmavati Devi. Spiritually, She resides as Vyuha Lakshmi on Lord Sri Venkateshwar’s chest and personally conveys the prayers offered at Tiruchanur directly to the Lord.
Origin of Tiruchanur: In the Vedic era, Sage Shuka had his hermitage near the temple tank. The town was originally called Shri Shukanuru, which gradually evolved over centuries into Tiruchanur.
Dual Reverence in Jainism: Beyond Hindu Vaishnava tradition, Padmavati Devi is also deeply revered in Jainism as the protective Yakshini (guardian Deity) of the 23rd Tirthankara, Lord Parshvanath, often depicted with a multi-hooded serpent canopy and worshipped for removing obstacles.

#RomanSiteSaturday – Doclea (Dioclea), one of the most important Roman cities in present-day Montenegro, situated near Podgorica at the confluence of the Zeta and Morača rivers. Named after the Illyrian Docleatae, the settlement developed into a prosperous Roman town in the province of Dalmatia and had attained municipal status by the Flavian period (AD 69–96). Pliny the Elder even mentions the region's celebrated cheese production!

Today, visitors can explore the remains of its impressive forum, measuring approximately 66 × 55 metres, surrounded by porticoes and adjoining a civic basilica. Other surviving monuments include a temple complex traditionally identified as the Capitolium, public baths and sections of the city's principal streets. The forum underwent significant rebuilding in the late 3rd or early 4th century AD, probably under Diocletian. Doclea subsequently became the capital of the late Roman province of Praevalitana.

Although much of the ancient city survives only at foundation level, its remarkably clear urban layout offers a fascinating glimpse into Roman civic life in the western Balkans.

An even older clinical example survives in the Egyptian Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, dated to about 1600 BCE. In one case involving a wound to the temple, the examiner asks the injured man about his condition and receives no speech in response. The record places that observation beside bleeding, tears, and movements of the hand. The examiner sees activity even as he fails to obtain an account. There is a place in the case description for what the patient does, what the examiner can see, and what the examiner tried and was unable to learn by asking. The ancient report keeps those observations distinct. 

https://t.co/c5yVaVshGx
https://t.co/2mu6ksrjzT

The Egyptian tale conventionally called The Eloquent Peasant, preserved in manuscripts dating to about 1800 BCE, turns attention to the silence of the authority receiving an appeal. After an official’s subordinate robs Khuninpu, he petitions the official Rensi. Rensi tells the king about the man’s eloquence. The king has Khuninpu detained so that he will deliver further petitions and secretly provides for his household. Khuninpu speaks at increasing length and with increasing desperation while the authorities defer an answer. The very eloquence that strikes the court is produced in part by its decision to leave him in uncertainty. 

https://t.co/rk2IuvsnYP
https://t.co/qYP9gWhsCc

The tale offers the reverse of the ward’s quiet. An institution can produce a great volume of testimony by withholding a response, just as it can produce an apparent absence of complaints by restricting the occasions on which a complaint can be made. In both cases, the archive records something real. Khuninpu’s speeches express real demands and real desperation within the story. Their abundance also tells something about the court that kept him speaking. The record becomes intelligible when the reader can see what the authority did between one utterance and the next. 

https://t.co/rk2IuvsnYP

What an Observer Actually Learns

Consider three entries that could follow the same interview question. A person follows the question and says the experience has ceased. A second person follows the question and chooses to leave it unanswered. A third can give a brief reply about an object in the room, while the longer question appears to exceed what the person can follow. All three interviews may end with the clinician hearing no description of the experience. Only the first contains a report of cessation. The second gives evidence of a person’s conduct in that exchange. The third gives evidence about the limits of what the interview could establish.

There is a useful legal analogue for the blank that later appears in a record. Federal Rule of Evidence 803(7) allows the absence of an entry in a regularly maintained record to be offered as evidence that a matter did not occur, provided the record was regularly kept for matters of that kind and the circumstances support its trustworthiness. The inference depends on the likelihood that an event would have found its way into the record. A quiet chart may be strong evidence about regularly documented events and weak evidence about experiences patients had little opportunity to report. A blank can acquire the appearance of a finding each time it is copied forward. [oai_citation:37‡Rule 803

text:
In 1890, the age of consent was 12 or younger in 38 American states. In Delaware, the statutory threshold was just seven.
A girl could be legally considered old enough to consent to sex while still young enough to be learning how to read.
One woman decided that America needed to confront what its laws were allowing.
Her name was Helen Hamilton Gardener.
Born Alice Chenoweth in 1853, she became a writer, lecturer, and outspoken critic of the sexual double standards imposed on women.
At a time when respectable women were expected to avoid discussing sex publicly, Gardener wrote about prostitution, sexual exploitation, and the devastating consequences of laws written almost entirely by men.
Her 1890 novel Is This Your Son, My Lord? confronted the hypocrisy of a society that punished girls for sexual misconduct while excusing the men who exploited them.
But fiction was only part of her campaign.
Gardener joined a growing movement of women demanding that state legislatures raise the age of consent.
The laws varied enormously. In many states, a girl of 10 or 12 could fall outside the special legal protection afforded to younger children. Prosecutors then faced the much harder task of proving force or lack of consent.
Reformers argued that children should never have to carry that burden.
Women's organizations circulated petitions, published state-by-state comparisons, and confronted legislators who resisted changing the law.
Their campaign exposed an uncomfortable truth: American women were fighting to protect girls through a political system in which most women could not even vote.
Gardener also challenged the supposed scientific arguments used to portray women as intellectually inferior.
She refused to accept that men were naturally qualified to govern women's bodies, education, or futures.
The campaign helped transform American law. By the early twentieth century, most states had raised their age-of-consent thresholds substantially, although protection and enforcement remained uneven.
Gardener lived long enough to see women win the federal constitutional right to vote in 1920.
She later became the first woman appointed to the United States Civil Service Commission.
She died in 1925.
Her work belonged to a generation of women who forced Americans to confront a question their lawmakers had long avoided: why were children expected to defend themselves against adults when the law itself offered so little protection?

NVIDIA: LITIGATION HISTORY AND THE SIDE C QUESTION, CONTINUED (2/3)

3. ADJACENT MATTERS, IN THEIR OWN LANES

None of the following is a Side C event. Each is recorded because it touches the insurance record, and each is graded in its proper lane so it cannot be miscounted as entity coverage evidence.

3.1 THE 3DFX ADVERSARY PROCEEDINGS (BANKRUPTCY CREDITOR CLAIMS)

Arising from Nvidia's December 2000 purchase of 3dfx assets for $70M plus 1,000,000 Nvidia shares, the 3dfx Chapter 11 trustee and other claimants sued Nvidia, its subsidiary, and its directors and officers, alleging insufficient consideration, fraud on creditors, interference with contract, breach of fiduciary duty, and de facto merger. The estate claims were compromised in a Settlement Agreement dated November 1, 2005, under which Nvidia agreed to pay $5,524,759.77 to a senior claims account and $25,000,000 to a general claims account; the agreement's payment language runs from Nvidia and does not state what portion, if any, the D&O tower funded. The trustee's fraudulent conveyance theory ended in Nvidia's favor when the Ninth Circuit affirmed on November 6, 2014 that Nvidia did not pay less than fair market value. Sources: executed settlement agreement (SEC exhibit copy); Ninth Circuit memorandum disposition. Grade: VERIFIED as to the settlement terms; the insurance allocation is NOT FOUND. These proceedings are the underlying claims in the coverage fight told in full in Section 4.

3.2 THE DERIVATIVE SUITS (SIDE A LANE)

• 2002 derivative actions: three actions followed the February 2002 accounting announcement. The Delaware action, Guttman v. Huang, was dismissed with prejudice on May 5, 2003 for failure to plead demand futility (823 A.2d 492); the two California actions were dismissed in September 2003 at plaintiffs' request. No carrier payment reported. Sources: Nvidia Q3 FY2003 10-Q; the Guttman opinion. Grade: VERIFIED.
• Options backdating derivative settlement, 2008: Nvidia's Form 8-K dated November 10, 2008 states the settlement terms for the stockholder derivative lawsuits over historical stock option practices, including "an $8.0 million cash payment by our insurance carrier to NVIDIA", corporate governance changes, and the CEO amending options to add $3.5M of exercise price or cancel equivalent intrinsic value. Grade: VERIFIED. Lane discipline: a carrier paying settlement consideration to the company in a derivative case is Side A territory. It proves a D&O carrier paid real money in an Nvidia matter; it is not entity securities coverage evidence and is not counted as such anywhere in this report. Background: the audit committee review began in June 2006, Nvidia restated fiscal 2004 to 2006 and earlier periods for incorrect option measurement dates (aggregate non cash charge ultimately $127M), and in November 2007 the SEC closed its backdating investigation with no enforcement action. Grade: VERIFIED.
• 2019 crypto derivative actions: the federal consolidated derivative case (No. 4:19-cv-00341-HSG, filed January 18, 2019) and two Delaware actions (filed September 24, 2019) were stayed pending the securities appeal; per Nvidia's Q3 FY2026 10-Q the federal case was administratively closed on February 22, 2022 and had not been reopened. No derivative settlement and no carrier payment is reported for any of them. Grade: VERIFIED. Lane: Side A exposure that never matured into a payment.
• A 2026 derivative complaint against the board over AI model copyright and biometric privacy allegations was covered by specialist press on August 10, 2026; no settlement or insurance information attaches to it in any source located. Grade: REPORTED. Lane: Side A.

3.3 THE HOBERG SEC MATTER AND THE 2002 RESTATEMENT

Christine B. Hoberg was Nvidia's CFO from December 1998. The SEC alleged that in early 2000, with Nvidia forecasting a miss for the quarter ended April 30, 2000, she directed that only the $3.3M cost reduction half of a supplier deal be recorded, without the offsetting repayment liability, and that the deal was documented in two agreements so the liability could be kept from the auditors; as alleged, the quarter's gross profit was overstated by 6.4 percent, net income by 15.3 percent, and diluted EPS by 14.8 percent. On April 29, 2002, the day Nvidia announced its restatement of fiscal 2000, fiscal 2001, and the first three quarters of fiscal 2002, Hoberg was placed on administrative leave; the SEC complaint records her resignation as effective July 31, 2002 (a Delaware Chancery opinion calls April 29, 2002 the resignation date; both sources are primary and the discrepancy is flagged, not resolved). On September 11, 2003 the SEC sued her personally; by consent order dated September 18, 2003 she paid $671,694.99 ($596,694.99 of disgorgement and prejudgment interest plus a $75,000 penalty), accepted a permanent injunction and a five year officer and director bar, and a parallel order on September 24, 2003 suspended her from practicing before the SEC as an accountant. Nvidia itself took a cease and desist order the same day, with no penalty. Sources: SEC complaint (No. C 03-04135 HRL), Litigation Release No. 18343, SEC Administrative Proceeding File No. 3-11267. Grade: VERIFIED. The two later CFO departures were not controversy departures: the 2008 retirement announced in the March 27, 2008 Form 8-K, and the March 2011 resignation stated to be for personal reasons, with a paid transition and consulting agreement. No CFO resigned amid controversy between 2016 and 2021; the CFO seat has been held continuously since September 2013. Grade: VERIFIED.

3.4 THE BUMPGATE PRODUCT INSURANCE RECOVERIES (NOT D&O)

Nvidia's FY2009 Form 10-K (filed March 13, 2009) discloses that its insurance coverage "provided us with $8.0 million in related reimbursement during fiscal year 2009" toward the weak die and packaging warranty costs, with $6.7M of allocated insurance claim proceeds reflected against the $196.0M warranty charge. The related consumer class settlement (August 12, 2010) provided replacement chips, replacement laptops, repair reimbursements and a $2M reimbursement fund. A separate coverage suit over the product policies (a declaratory action by the carrier, N.D. Cal. No. C 09-02046 CW, order of August 18, 2009) concerned commercial general liability and umbrella policies. Grade: VERIFIED. Lane: product and warranty insurance, not D&O, and not Side C evidence in any form. The securities case arising from the same defect is the dismissed 2008 case in Section 2.2.

4. NVIDIA'S SIDE C EXPERIENCE: THE 2005 COVERAGE ACTION

The heart of the record is a lawsuit most coverage files never produce: the insured suing its own carriers, in the open, with the tower described in filed court papers. Case: nVidia Corp. v. St. Paul Mercury Insurance Co., San Francisco Superior Court, Case No. 05-438278, filed January 31, 2005. The case documents were recovered from the exhibit set lodged in an unrelated federal case (Crowley Maritime Corp. v. Federal Insurance Co., No. CV-08-00830 SI, N.D. Cal., Document 35, filed March 21, 2008). Grade: VERIFIED as filed court documents; the substance of the January 4, 2007 order is REPORTED from a law firm case summary (Wiley Rein newsletter, March 2007, republished on Lexology, March 16, 2007).

4.1 WHY NVIDIA SUED

The underlying claims were the three 3dfx adversary proceedings (Section 3.1): creditor claims against Nvidia, its subsidiary, and its directors and officers over the December 2000 asset purchase. Nvidia alleged defense fees and costs for the underlying actions in excess of $6.5M through the close of fact discovery, and sued three carriers, St. Paul Mercury Insurance Company, Executive Risk Indemnity Inc. (ERII), and Royal Insurance Company of America, for breach of contract and declaratory relief over the carriers' duty to pay loss, defense fees and costs, and indemnification.

The carriers' positions, as documented in ERII's own filed demurrer memorandum summarizing the pleadings:

• Prior and pending litigation exclusions: each policy in the tower carried a differently worded exclusion of that type, and the carriers relied on them.
• Restitution: the carriers argued the underlying claims sought restitutionary relief that is not covered loss.
• One carrier contended it owed no coverage because its policy covered "Securities Claims" only, and the 3dfx claims were not Securities Claims under the policy's definition (a wrongful act in connection with the purchase or sale of, or offer to purchase or sell, securities issued by the policyholder).
• St. Paul had actually paid $1,845,000 under its layer and sought reimbursement on the position that coverage was unavailable.

Two precision points. First, what was resisted was payment into live claims, defense costs and indemnifiable loss while the cases were running; this was not a refused settlement after judgment, and no Nvidia securities settlement was involved at all. Second, the payment and exhaustion figures are Nvidia's allegations as characterized by an adverse carrier in its own filing; they are VERIFIED as filed allegations, not adjudicated facts.

4.2 THE TOWER, AS DOCUMENTED

The tower, as described by ERII from Nvidia's own First Amended Complaint of April 19, 2005:

• Primary: Gulf Insurance Company, "Directors and Officers Liability and Company Indemnification Policy", $5M limit, alleged fully exhausted.
• North American Capacity Insurance Company, $5M excess, alleged exhausted.
• St. Paul Mercury, $5M excess of $10M (of which St. Paul had paid $1,845,000, see Section 4.1).
• ERII, Excess Indemnity Policy No. 8167-9053, $5M excess of $15M, following the St. Paul form.
• Royal Insurance Company of America, $5M excess of $20M.
• Total tower: $25M.

Stated clearly because the figure is easy to misread: $25M is the limit, the amount of coverage the tower would pay, not a premium. No premium figure for this tower appears in any document located.

Procedural markers: on June 28, 2005 the court sustained ERII's demurrer without leave to amend as to one breach of contract claim and overruled it as to the declaratory relief claims on the duty to pay loss and on defense and indemnification (proposed order in the exhibit set; VERIFIED as a filed document). The 3dfx estate claims themselves were compromised on November 1, 2005 (Section 3.1) while the coverage fight continued.

4.3 THE JANUARY 4, 2007 RULING

On January 4, 2007 the court ruled on the exclusions and the securities claim question. Per the law firm summary: the court held the insureds' causal connection reading of the prior and pending litigation exclusions was at minimum a reasonable interpretation, making the language ambiguous, and that causation was in any event a triable fact issue; it refused summary judgment on the carriers' restitution argument because at least two underlying actions sought non restitutionary damages (interference with contract, breach of fiduciary duty); and on the Side C relevant point, it held that the allegation that 1,000,000 Nvidia shares were insufficient consideration for the 3dfx patents created a triable issue of fact on whether the underlying claims were Securities Claims under the securities claims only policy. The court refused to rule that coverage away. The order's existence and date are corroborated by a later federal opinion construing it (S.D.N.Y., September 5, 2007). Grade: REPORTED as to the substance of the holdings (law firm summary); VERIFIED as to the order's existence and date.

4.4 WHAT THIS PROVES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

What it proves:

• Nvidia carried a multi carrier D&O tower in the early 2000s, in the conventional layered form of its era, placed when Nvidia was a small cap.
• At least one policy in that tower was written around securities claims as defined, which in the standard ABC form of that era is the insuring agreement that responds to a securities claim against the company itself: the entity slot, what the market now calls Side C.
• The tower was tendered on claims naming the company and its directors and officers together, and it responded in money: the primary and first excess layers were alleged exhausted, and $1,845,000 was actually paid by an excess carrier before the fight.
• Faced with resistance, Nvidia litigated to keep the coverage alive rather than absorbing the loss silently.

What it does not prove, stated just as plainly:

• No document located says the words "Side C" or "entity coverage" about any Nvidia program in any year. The entity reading is an inference from the securities claims insuring agreement in a standard form of the era, graded REPORTED, not a document that names the side.
• No policy inception or renewal date for the tower was found; the record does not say when the tower was placed or how long the posture lasted.
• No document allocates the tower's payments between individual, indemnification, and entity coverage.
• The final disposition of the coverage action after January 4, 2007 (settlement, dismissal, or judgment) was searched by caption and case number and is NOT FOUND.
• Nothing in the record describes any Nvidia D&O program between that tower and the program the FT described in November 2026: no broker report, academic paper, governance note, book, older news article, or litigation exhibit states historical Nvidia limits, sides, entity coverage, or renewal terms for any other year. NOT FOUND beyond this section.

text:
HOLY F*CK… GTA 6 drops in 5 days and AI channels are already FLOODING youtube

one GTA 6 channel made less than a week ago is already sitting on 8.25M views

so i had claude make a full GTA style trailer to see how hard it actually is

56 seconds
> neon beach city at sunset
> a jewellery heist
> a cop chase across the causeway
> a drawbridge jump in slow mo

zero AI video. zero game footage. zero editor

claude built every building, car, cop and camera move in code. even the synthwave soundtrack

and here's where the money is:

these pages don't need to sell anything themselves

you put one affiliate link in bio from glitchy. a GTA 6 offer, an xbox offer, a PS5 offer. stuff gamers already want this week

if a video does 1M views:
> 0.5% tap the link = 5,000 clicks
> 10% sign up = 500 leads
> at $2 a lead that's $1,000 off one video

post 3 of these a day across a few pages during launch week and do the math

here's the exact prompt i used, it's free 👇

<role>
You are a senior motion designer and creative coder. Build a 56-second vertical (1080x1920, 30fps) cinematic trailer for an ORIGINAL open-world crime game, made 100% in code. No AI video, no stock footage, no game footage.
</role>

<tech>
- One self-contained HTML file using three.js (ES modules) + a 2D canvas overlay on top for text and HUD
- Every frame must be a pure function of time: expose https://t.co/IfGGJ8odPH(t) that sets the whole scene for time t, so any frame can be rendered in any order
- Render with Playwright: call seek(n/30) for each frame and screenshot it (JPEG, quality 93). Split the frame range across 2 workers
- Encode with ffmpeg: libx264, CRF 17, yuv420p, light film grain (noise filter), mux the soundtrack
- Look: low-poly flat-shaded models, ACES filmic tone mapping, UnrealBloom on neon and lights, gradient sky dome with a sun disc, fog for depth
- Before rendering everything, render test stills of every shot, look at them, and fix framing, exposure and anything blocking the camera
</tech>

<world>
- A neon Miami-style beach city: pastel art-deco hotels (pink, mint, lemon, lavender) with white ledges, vertical fins and glowing neon name signs
- A palm-lined beach boulevard with street lamps, a wide sand beach, an animated faceted ocean, glass towers with lit windows behind
- A long causeway bridge over the bay at night: lamp posts every 30m with warm light pools on the road, a drawbridge in the middle with two raising leaves, a lit city skyline on the horizon
- Traffic cars, a white box truck, palm trees swaying in the wind
</world>

<looks>
- Sunset: deep blue to coral to gold sky, warm low sun, soft neon
- Night: navy sky with stars, neon and windows at full glow, warm lamp pools, cool moonlight
- Dawn: pink-gold sky, sun just over the ocean, calm water
</looks>

<characters>
- Two original outlaws: a driver (open teal shirt, sunglasses) and a planner (red jacket, gold hoops, long dark hair). Simple stylised low-poly bodies with poses for walk, run, sit, lean, drive
- A hot pink convertible as the hero car
- 4 police cars with alternating red/blue light bars that also cast coloured light, and a helicopter with a visible spotlight beam
</characters>

<shots>
0-5s: slow aerial push over the ocean toward the skyline at sunset. Caption: "EVERYBODY COMES HERE / FOR THE SUN"
5-9s: low tracking shot beside the convertible cruising the boulevard. Caption: "SOME COME FOR THE MONEY"
9-11.4s: the driver leaning on the car. Big name card on a slanted colour slab: "RAY / THE DRIVER"
11.4-14s: the planner sitting on the hood. Name card: "NOVA / THE PLAN"
14-17s: night falls, they walk down the neon sidewalk toward a jewellery store. Caption: "AND SOME OF US / JUST TAKE IT"
17-21s: the window shatters (glass particles), red alarm light, they sprint out with duffel bags, cash fluttering
21-24s: tyres smoke as the car peels out, police cars arrive with lights flashing. Heat meter appears
24-27.6s: chase cam behind the car weaving through traffic on the causeway, cops behind
27.6-30.6s: side tracking shot, cops right on their bumper
30.6-33.6s: helicopter view from above, spotlight locked on the car
33.6-36s: head-on near miss, the car swerves past an oncoming truck at the last second
36-40s: drawbridge is raising, the car hits the ramp and flies over the gap in slow motion, then lands with a flash and sparks
40-44s: cops stuck at the edge of the raised bridge, lights flashing, the car's tail lights disappearing as the sky starts to glow
44-50s: dawn on the beach, the two sitting on the hood watching the sunrise. Caption: "PARADISE WAS / NEVER FREE"
50-56s: aerial over the city, huge title with a sunset gradient and glow, then the release date slams in with a white flash: "NOV 19 / THE WAIT IS ALMOST OVER"
</shots>

<overlay>
- Captions: white, condensed bold font, letter-spaced, centred in the lower third, fade in and out
- HUD during the chase: a heat meter of 5 siren icons top-right that fill up as the chase escalates, and a round minimap bottom-left with cop blips
- Soft vignette, short white flashes on the smash, the landing and the title
</overlay>

<sound>
- Synthesise everything in Python with numpy, no downloads
- Score: 100bpm synthwave in A minor (Am-F-C-G): detuned saw pads, pulsing octave bass, 16th-note arp, kick and a big gated 80s snare. Drums enter at 5s, full energy for the chase, drop out completely for the slow-mo jump, soft bells at dawn, riser into a huge hit on the release date
- SFX: whooshes on cuts, engine, tyre screech, glass smash, alarm bell, police sirens, helicopter rotor, truck horn, slow-mo whoosh, landing impact
- Mix with the music under the effects and master to -14 LUFS, peaks under -1.5dB
</sound>

<rules>
- Hard cuts on the beat (every 0.6s grid)
- Keep the subject centred and readable in the vertical frame
- Original names, characters, city and logos only. Never copy a real game's characters, logo or fonts
</rules>

text:
John Holmes claimed he'd slept with 14,000 women. They called him the Elvis of p*rn.

Then police found his palm print in a house where four people had been beaten to death with steel pipes. Hours after the murders, he showed up at his wife's door covered in blood.

In the video below, he explains how it all started, and what his first question was when someone offered him $100.

A skinny country boy from Ohio. A neighbor asked if he wanted to make a hundred dollars. "I wanted to know who I had to kill," he laughed. It was for a p*rn film.

He got $75 for his first starring role as "Johnny Wadd." The movie was shot in two days. Within a few years, the character was more famous than the man.

His wife Sharon told him: "You're the male equivalent of a wh*re." His answer: "If I were a carpenter, this is my tool."

In 1980 a reporter asked: "Do you take drugs?" "No, never. I don't even like aspirin."

In reality, he was freebasing cocaine for days at a time with a briefcase full of butane torches. He couldn't perform anymore. The industry dropped him. He stole luggage at LAX and emptied a friend's house down to the toaster and the iron. His girlfriend Dawn says he beat her and forced her to sell herself to pay for his drugs.

June 1981. Holmes spent the night getting high at the mansion of Hollywood drug lord Eddie Nash, and left a sliding door open on his way out. Hours later, a gang he owed walked in with fake police badges and robbed Nash of drugs, cash and jewelry. Holmes got a few grams.

Nash's bodyguard found him. A witness says he heard Holmes being slammed into the walls while Nash threatened to kill his whole family.

At 4 a.m. on July 1, Holmes rang the buzzer at 8763 Wonderland Avenue. "It's John Holmes." They let him in.

Four people were beaten to death with pipes. A fifth woman survived with part of her skull removed. Neighbors later said they thought the screams were "primal scream therapy."

That morning he knocked on his wife's door, bloody, and told her: "I saw four people murdered."

He went on the run, got caught in Florida and was charged with all four murders. The jury acquitted him. He did 110 days for refusing to testify.

In 1986 he was diagnosed with HIV. Then, according to the people who made the films, he flew to Italy and kept shooting without telling his co-stars. He told the press he had colon cancer.

He died in 1988 at 43. At his request, his widow checked his body before cremation to make sure "all the parts were there."

In 1980 he joked he'd kill for $100. A year later, four people were dead, and a jury said he didn't do it.

So what was John Holmes: a coward forced at gunpoint, or the man who opened the door to a massacre and walked free?

text:
She hired a hitman to kill her husband of six months, then cried on a sergeant's shoulder when police told her he was dead. He was alive. When she saw him, she said: "I didn't do anything to you."

In the video below, watch her face. She breaks down six seconds in.

Boynton Beach, Florida. August 5, 2009. Dalia Dippolito, 26.

She had offered to set up her own alibi. That morning she was at the gym when police called her home.

The tape on her house was a prop, and everyone but her knew it.

She had handed over photos of her husband and $1,200 to buy a gun. Police files say she had already tried antifreeze in his iced tea.

Her hitman was an undercover officer with a camera. He offered a way out. She cut in:

"No, there's no changing. I'm positive, like five thousand percent sure."

At the station they showed her Michael.

A detective: "She was more in shock that he was alive."

She: "Mike, come here."

Michael: "I can't."

From jail, already charged, she called her mother.

"I want him out of my house."

A jury convicted her in 90 minutes. 16 years. She is due out in September 2030.

16 years for a murder that never happened: too long, or not long enough?

text:
On August 1, 2009, Dalia Dippolito of Boynton Beach, Florida, got into the passenger seat of a red sedan for a clandestine meeting and told the driver she wanted him to kill her husband.  

She offered him $7,000, and he responded that he'd already bought the gun. 

They agreed on a date and time when she would be at the gym to establish an alibi.⁠  ⁠When Dalia arrived home from her workout on the day of the planned murder, her house was a crime scene. 

Police told her that her husband was dead and she broke down in tears right there on the street. Officers consoled her and escorted her to the station for a debriefing and explanation.  

There, she continued to sob in horror and disbelief — until the man she believed to be dead came out from behind a doorway.⁠  ⁠

The whole operation had been a setup. The hitman was an undercover cop and her husband himself was in on the sting — with the entire saga had even been recorded for an episode of "COPS."

text:
PIONEERS OF THE UNIVERSE

Humanity's Greatest Challenge Is Learning to Live Among the Stars

Every human who studies the universe contributes to the unfolding history of humanity. Every discovery expands our understanding, every scientific achievement advances our capabilities, and every generation inherits the responsibility to carry human knowledge further.

Yet the universe presents humanity with challenges far greater than simply developing rockets and travelling beyond Earth. Living among the stars will demand a profound transformation in how we think, cooperate, make decisions and understand our existence.

Space is an unforgiving environment. Radiation, extreme temperatures, gravitational differences, isolation, limited resources, orbital hazards and the immense distances between celestial bodies will challenge our biological survival and technological capabilities. Humanity will have to develop advanced materials, reliable energy systems, biological protection, artificial intelligence, robotics, new medical technologies and sustainable habitats. We will need to understand how to live within environments that were never designed for human biology.

But perhaps one of our greatest challenges will not be technological. It will be human behaviour.

While the universe offers humanity an extraordinary field for discovery, parts of human society remain occupied with territorial conflict, domination, destruction and warfare against one another. These behaviours reflect narrow patterns of thinking in which immediate power and competition take precedence over collective survival, long-term responsibility and intellectual progress.

Comparing such behaviour to the instincts of other primates can illustrate how deeply competition and aggression can influence social conduct. However, humanity possesses something more: the capacity to examine its instincts, question its actions, develop ethical awareness and deliberately choose different ways of living.

A species preparing to live among the stars must learn to think beyond the immediate boundaries of its own territory.

Humanity's expansion into the cosmos requires more than intelligence measured through scientific knowledge. It requires expanded awareness: an understanding of interdependence, consequences, environmental limits, shared resources and the responsibility of protecting life.

Those who study distant stars, investigate planetary systems, develop new technologies and consider humanity's future are contributing to a much larger perspective. They are asking questions that extend beyond individual survival: Where can humanity go? What environments can sustain life? How can civilizations function across vast distances? What knowledge must we develop before becoming an interplanetary and eventually interstellar species?

This wider perspective does not mean abandoning Earth. Earth remains our biological foundation, our first home and the environment that sustains us. Learning to protect it is part of learning how to inhabit other worlds responsibly.

The transition from an Earth-bound civilization to a spacefaring civilization will require a transformation in human consciousness, education, cooperation and decision-making. We must learn to recognize that our differences do not change our shared biological origins or our dependence on the same planetary environment.

The universe will test our science, our engineering, our adaptability and our ability to cooperate. It will expose the limitations of our technologies and the consequences of our decisions.

The pioneers of the universe are therefore not simply those who reach distant planets. They are those who expand human understanding, challenge destructive thinking, develop knowledge and prepare civilization for a future beyond its birthplace.

Every scientific discovery adds another chapter. Every technological achievement creates another possibility. Every act of cooperation strengthens our ability to face the challenges ahead.

Humanity cannot expect to build civilizations among the stars while remaining unwilling to build a more responsible civilization on Earth.

Our future requires a larger way of thinking: from individual power to collective responsibility, from territorial competition to planetary understanding, from immediate conflict to long-term survival.

We are part of the universe, not separate from it. Our future among the stars will depend not only on how far our technology can travel, but also on how far our thinking can advance.

The greatest frontier humanity must cross is not merely the distance between stars. It is the distance between what we are today and what we have the capacity to become.

The universe is our field of discovery. Knowledge is our inheritance. Conscious awareness is our responsibility. Exploration is our continuation.

PIONEERS OF THE UNIVERSE — Expand Your Knowledge. Advance Your Thinking. Prepare Humanity for the Stars.

text:
The U.S. Treasury holds roughly 261.5 million fine troy ounces of gold (about 8,133 tonnes). On the government’s books this is valued at the statutory price of $42.2222 per ounce (often rounded to $42.22), for a total book value of about $11.04 billion. At current market prices (around $3,880–$3,890 per troy ounce as of mid-November 2026), the same metal is worth on the order of $1.01–$1.02 trillion. https://t.co/3RJfpwqFNQ
Why the price is stuck at $42.22
- Under the gold standard and Bretton Woods system, the U.S. set an official price of gold by statute (e.g., $35 after 1934, then $38 in 1972).
- Nixon suspended dollar-gold convertibility in 1971 (“closing the gold window”). The Smithsonian Agreement and subsequent actions raised the official price, and Congress set it at “forty-two and two-ninths dollars” ($42.2222) per fine troy ounce in 1973.
- That figure is still hard-coded in 31 U.S.C. § 5117(b). The statute limits the value of gold certificates the Treasury can issue against its gold to that price. The Federal Reserve holds those certificates (currently around $11.037 billion on its H.4.1 balance sheet); the Fed does not own the physical gold—the Treasury does.
- After the fixed-exchange-rate system fully collapsed and the IMF ended the official gold price in the late 1970s, the U.S. accounting rate was simply left unchanged. It is an accounting artifact, not a market price or an offer to buy/sell gold at that level. Most other major central banks now mark their gold reserves to market. https://t.co/r6iGf5psy5...
Practical effects
- The low book value is an accounting convention only. It does not change the physical amount of gold or its true market worth.
- Revaluing the gold to market (or any higher official price) would require an act of Congress to amend the statute. That would allow the Treasury to issue higher-value gold certificates, generating a large one-time accounting gain that could be monetized (credited to the Treasury’s account at the Fed). Officials have periodically stated they are not pursuing this. Analysts note that while it would improve balance-sheet optics, it would not resolve underlying structural fiscal issues and could have market or confidence effects. https://t.co/pDEyy90C1G...
In short, the undervaluation is not a deliberate ongoing policy judgment about gold’s worth; it is a leftover legal requirement from the final stages of the gold-standard era that no one has bothered (or chosen) to change.
