text:
🚨 SPECIAL REPORT | Markwayne Mullin: The Homeland Security Secretary Who Spoke to the Nation the Night America's Flights Stopped · Saturday, November 14, 2026

On Friday, November 13th, at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Time, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a ground stop at every airport in America — the first nationwide ground stop since 2023. More than 3,500 planes were still in the air, and countless anxious families were waiting on the ground. That's when a Cabinet secretary stepped in front of the cameras outside the White House and spoke to the nation. He is the Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin.
————
He said this was a telecommunications outage. Out of an abundance of caution, all flights were stopped, and there was no indication of a deliberate attack. This is not another 9/11. Everyone is safe. If your loved ones are in the air, there is no reason to worry. The President immediately took the lead, and gave them the resources and the communications they needed. At 8:15 that evening, Transportation Secretary Duffy announced that the ground stop had been lifted.
————
Why was he the one to answer? After the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Homeland Security Act. On March 1st, 2003, the Department of Homeland Security officially began operating, bringing 22 federal agencies together into a single Cabinet department. Border and customs, immigration enforcement, airport security, cybersecurity, FEMA, the Coast Guard, and the Secret Service all fall under it. Air traffic control belongs to the Department of Transportation. But what the country most wanted to know was: Was this an attack? Are the airports safe? That is exactly Homeland Security's job.
————
How did the secretary who steadied the country get here? Mullin was born in 1977 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, the youngest of seven children, and grew up on the family ranch in Westville. He is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation. As a child, he had a speech impediment, and he was born with a foot deformity that required him to walk in leg braces.
————
But that same boy became a tough competitor on the wrestling mat, and earned a wrestling scholarship to Missouri Valley College. When he was 20, his father, Jim Senior, fell ill. He and his new wife, Christie, left school and went home to take over Mullin Plumbing. It wasn't until 2010 that he finished an associate degree in plumbing.
————
Christie and he had known each other since elementary school, dated through high school, and have now been married for 28 years. When they took over, the company had only six employees. Together they built it up, and by 2011, Mullin Plumbing was the largest plumbing-services company in Oklahoma. They went on to start several more businesses.
————
By day he fixed pipes. By night he stepped into the cage. He fought professionally in mixed martial arts, going 5-0, undefeated, and he was inducted into the Oklahoma Wrestling Hall of Fame. To this day, he still coaches wrestling for kids on the weekends.
————
The Mullins have six children, three of them adopted. In 2013, they adopted a pair of two-year-old twin sisters. The girls had been raised apart since they were three months old. The Mullin family brought them back together.
————
In 2012, this plumber who had never held public office ran for Congress, won Oklahoma's Second District, and served ten years in the House, including as deputy whip. In 2016, President-elect Trump appointed him chairman of the Native American Coalition.
————
In 2022, with President Trump's endorsement, he won a special election to the Senate, becoming the first tribal citizen to enter the Senate since 2005. According to his Homeland Security biography, he quickly became a key link between the House, the Senate, and the White House in advancing President Trump's agenda, and in 2025 he helped drive the One Big Beautiful Bill and the National Defense Authorization Act across the finish line.
————
But to truly understand the bond between Mullin and President Trump, you have to go back to January 17th, 2020. It was an election year. Mullin's son Jim was 15. He had been competing in wrestling around the world since he was 12. That day, in a high school wrestling match, he suffered a severe traumatic brain injury. Mullin later recalled: We almost lost him. For 26 hours, his pulse was extremely low. At one point, the doctors thought it was gone. When he woke up, he was like a different child. He couldn't touch his own nose. He shuffled when he walked. He had lost his short-term memory. He couldn't even add five plus three. Reading, walking — he had to learn it all over again.
————
When President Trump learned what had happened, he called right away. Mullin said the President at first didn't know how serious the injury was, but he could hear it in my voice, and he immediately went into action. The President even joked that Jim couldn't recognize you and Christie, but he recognized me — because the only question he got right was who the current president was. Mullin told the President they needed to get Jim to the Centre for Neuro Skills in Bakersfield, California, one of the best neuro-rehabilitation centers in the world. The President offered on the spot to send his own private plane. Mullin said: Sir, we can't fly. We have to drive. Once they arrived, President Trump called almost every day for two full weeks, asking just one thing: How's Jim? How's my little buddy?
————
Then the President said: I'm coming to see him. This was in the middle of a hard-fought campaign, and Bakersfield was not a must-stop on the trail. On February 19th, 2020, President Trump came to Bakersfield to sign a memorandum on California water infrastructure. The official White House record is clear. On stage, the President asked: Where is Markwayne? Come on up, Mark! Then he said: This is his son Jim, a great wrestler, a great athlete. After he signed, the President asked again: Where's Jim? That pen is for you.
————
After the event, Mullin said, the President barely spoke to him. His eyes were only on Jim. Staff came over twice to say: Sir, we have to go. The third time, President Trump looked at them and said: I guarantee you that plane won't leave without me. For the next 15 minutes, he did nothing but love on my son. The rehab center had told Mullin it would take something big to trigger Jim's memory. It was that visit. From then on, Jim started retaining things. And his mindset changed from "we'll get through this" to "I will get through this."
————
Later, when Jim was briefly out of the hospital, the President invited them to Mar-a-Lago. As they were leaving, President Trump took Jim aside and asked: Do you know why I love your dad? Jim said: No, sir. The President said: Because he loves you. Because of you. In October 2020, Jim was discharged from the Centre for Neuro Skills. Mullin said Jim accomplished in nine months what the specialists had said could take two or three years.
————
Mullin told this story again on March 18th of this year, at his confirmation hearing to be Secretary of Homeland Security, speaking before the senators, his voice breaking more than once. He said: This is not about President Trump. This is about my son. He didn't do it for publicity, and he didn't do it for a photo op. He was in the middle of the hardest campaign of his life, and he still cared that much about my son. We were only acquaintances before that. We've been friends ever since. Drawing on his own family's experience, he also pushed in the Senate to reauthorize traumatic brain injury programs, so more patients could get the rehabilitation they need.
————
With that trust came a heavier responsibility. In March 2026, President Trump nominated Mullin to be Secretary of Homeland Security. The Senate confirmed him 54 to 45, with two Democratic senators voting yes. On March 24th, in the Oval Office, President Trump administered the oath and called him a great American patriot. Mullin said: I don't care if your state is red or blue. My job is to protect everybody.
————
His first order of business was to get the shuttered department funded again. On April 30th, President Trump signed a bill ending the longest departmental shutdown in American history, and TSA officers could finally be paid on time. Mullin wrote to his employees: Love the people. Love the call.
————
The border record is even more striking. The Department of Homeland Security reported that in fiscal year 2026, southwest border apprehensions fell 95 percent from the Biden years. Nationwide encounters hit a record low, there were 17 straight months of zero releases, and 250 miles of new border wall were built. Mullin said: President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered.
————
This summer, the World Cup was held in 11 U.S. cities, and TSA provided full security screening. In October, storms swept the country. FEMA pre-positioned supplies in the states, and the Coast Guard carried out rescues at the mouth of the Mississippi. Then nearly 900 million dollars was announced to support more than 620 disaster recovery and mitigation projects.
————
Mullin's style is like a wrestler's: direct, competitive, and unyielding. He is a steadfast ally of President Trump, and he also works across the aisle to find common ground. But this tough guy has a soft side, too. He said: If I talk about my kids, I get emotional. Other than that, you can't make me cry.
————
From a little boy in leg braces to an undefeated fighter. From a six-person plumbing company to the Department of Homeland Security, overseeing 22 agencies. On the afternoon the nation's flights were stopped, he told every family: Everybody is safe. Guarding the border, protecting the airports, defending against cyberattacks, and answering the call in a disaster — this job is about the safety of every American. And the bond between him and President Trump began with a father's love for his son.

The November 19 Shenzhen summit & The schedule for the expanded Ukraine–Russia–U.S.–Europe talks & How EU sanctions and frozen Russian assets

The European Union holds roughly €210 billion in immobilized Russian central bank assets—about €185 billion of which sits at the Belgian clearinghouse Euroclear—giving Brussels its single strongest financial bargaining chip in the November 2026 peace talks. 

https://t.co/MLT9xEO9us

As EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas emphasized at the November 12 Dublin summit, Washington and Moscow cannot finalize a deal on their own because Europe controls both the bulk of Russia's frozen reserves and the sanctions regime that Moscow wants lifted. 

https://t.co/kHY4U2RTbX

1. Why Frozen Assets Give Europe a Veto Over Any Deal

•Indefinite Immobilization. Under rules adopted in December 2025, the EU locked Russian central bank assets indefinitely rather than relying on six-month renewals. That means no single EU member state can veto the freeze, and Russia cannot recover its reserves unless Brussels formally agrees to lift the measure. 

https://t.co/VJV0vY98gM

•Linking Unfreezing to Reparations. European leaders maintain that immobilized Russian sovereign funds will remain frozen until Russia ends hostilities and pays war damages to Ukraine—a legal condition mirrored in U.S. law. 

https://t.co/VJV0vY98gM

•Blocking Bilateral Sanctions Relief. Even if the U.S. offered to ease American sanctions as part of a settlement, Russia’s economy and financial system remain heavily restricted by 21 EU sanctions packages, with a 22nd EU sanctions package (targeting Russia’s shadow tanker fleet, financial networks, and dual-use components) currently under preparation for late November 2026. 
https://t.co/2eAWTIOhr1

2. The Internal EU Debate: Seize Now vs. Hold as Leverage

While European governments agree on keeping the assets frozen, they remain divided over whether to confiscate the principal outright to fund Ukraine’s 2027 budget gap or keep the funds intact as a negotiating chip: 

https://t.co/oc08wr25f9

Approach - Reparations Loan / Seizure - Key Supporters : Nordic & Baltic states, Poland, Netherlands, Spain, many MEPs
Approach - Reparations Loan / Seizure - Core Mechanism : Transfer immobilized cash balances into an EU-backed mechanism to issue a massive loan to cover Ukraine's 2027 military and budget shortfall.
Approach - Reparations Loan / Seizure - Main Risk or Trade-Off : Could undermine global confidence in the euro as a reserve currency and trigger legal retaliation.

Approach - Hold & Use Windfall Profits - Key Supporters : Belgium (home to Euroclear), European Central Bank
Approach - Core Mechanism : Keep the ~€185B principal untouched at Euroclear, funneling only interest profits to Ukraine while preserving the principal as leverage at the peace table.
Approach - Hold & Use Windfall Profits - Core Mechanism : Keep the ~€185B principal untouched at Euroclear, funneling only interest profits to Ukraine while preserving the principal as leverage at the peace table.
Approach - Hold & Use Windfall Profits - Main Risk or Trade-Off : Leaves Ukraine facing an estimated $32.6 billion uncovered budget gap in 2027 unless EU states borrow jointly.

3. How This Plays Into the Upcoming Talks

•Upcoming EU Decisions. EU foreign ministers meet in Brussels on November 16, 2026, followed by an extraordinary European Council summit on November 26–27 to decide how to close Ukraine’s 2027 financing gap. 

https://t.co/T2qLAWwsPn

•Bargaining Power in the Expanded Format. By tying sanctions relief and the fate of the €210 billion to a seat at the table, the E5 + EU negotiating team ensures that any territorial or security compromise proposed by Washington or Moscow must also satisfy European security and reconstruction conditions.

Washington state’s Paid Family and Medical Leave payroll tax is a reverse Robin Hood. The state takes money from people in need and often gives it to workers who are not in need.

Imagine you are a single parent who needs all of your wages to get by. You prioritize needs, you don’t have extras and your benefits at work are limited. But you’re making your household budget work. You hope to earn a pay increase soon so you can start building savings for unexpected needs.

When you receive your paycheck, you notice more money taken out than you expected, given the tax code and where you fall within it. When you ask your employer about the deduction, you learn that Washington state has a law requiring a portion of your wages to fund paid leave for other workers — including your neighbors, a dual-income couple who just had a baby. Never mind that this couple planned and prepared to grow their family and has money in the bank to help with this change in family size. They also have employers who offer them paid time off they can use while they navigate being new parents. They are not in need of taxpayer dependency.

Your employer tells you that not only is money deducted from your paycheck to fund such a benefit, but she also has to contribute because her business has at least 50 employees — and it’s money that could have gone toward the raise you hoped for to make things easier and start your own rainy-day fund.

That is the reality of this payroll tax.

text:
FAA Expands SMART AI Traffic Planning to Atlanta in Nationwide Rollout

Atlanta is becoming an early test of how artificial intelligence can support one of aviation's most operationally demanding environments. The Federal Aviation Administration has deployed its SMART traffic-planning system in the region as part of a rollout across all 22 air route traffic control centers, moving the technology beyond its initial Washington, D.C., implementation.

SMART analyzes about 200 data streams, including weather, planned flight paths, traffic flow, airport capacity and controller staffing. It uses that information to predict congestion and identify potential routing conflicts before aircraft leave the ground. The objective is not to automate air traffic control. Instead, the system gives FAA traffic-management specialists and local controllers another source of recommendations when they are deciding how flights should move around storms, constrained airspace or busy airports.

That distinction matters. SMART is an advisory system, according to Airways, and controllers remain responsible for aircraft separation and operational decisions. FAA specialists review the software's recommendations before they are implemented. In practical terms, the system operates as a decision-support engine rather than an autonomous controller issuing instructions to pilots.

Atlanta offers a useful proving ground. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is a major hub for @Delta, and relatively small improvements in routing can affect aircraft utilization, fuel consumption and connections across the airline's network. The @ajc reported that 29 Delta flights accepted SMART-generated weather reroutes on Nov. 4. Local FAA facilities accepted 50 of the system's 58 recommendations that day.

Those results do not establish a broad reduction in Atlanta delays, but they show that the recommendations are reaching real operations and being integrated into flight planning. That is an important step for a safety-sensitive environment where trust, explainability and human review tend to matter as much as the sophistication of an algorithm. https://t.co/7I7zLddxrQ

A judge gave a 35-year-old teacher a second chance: six months in jail, then treatment, and stay away from the boy. A month after she got out, police found them together in her car. Inside were $6,200 in cash, baby clothes and her passport.

Her name was Mary Kay Letourneau. She taught at Shorewood Elementary in Burien, Washington. Vili Fualaau had been in her sixth-grade class. It started in the summer of 1996. He was 12.

She was arrested in March 1997. In May, while she was waiting to be sentenced, she gave birth to his daughter.

She pleaded guilty to two counts of child r*pe. Prosecutors wanted seven and a half years. She got a deal: six months in county jail, treatment, and no contact with him.

In the video below, she sits in court in tears while the judge spells it out. Treatment in the community instead of prison. One violation, and 89 months.

"Whether you stay out of prison is completely within your hands."

She was released on January 2, 1998.

She lasted a month.

On February 3, police found her in a parked car with him. Investigators believed they were planning to run with the baby. Days later she was back in court: "This case is not about a flawed system. It is about an opportunity that you foolishly squandered." All 89 months.

In October 1998, in prison, she gave birth to his second daughter.

She got out in 2004. He was 21. They married the next year. She died in 2020, at 58.

Prosecutors wanted seven and a half years from the start. A judge gave her six months and a chance. Should she ever have been offered that deal?

⚡ STRATEGIC BRIEF: US PROPOSES UKRAINE CEDE DONBAS IN EXCHANGE FOR NATO MEMBERSHIP

👇⤵️ Follow, Reply & ❤️ !

**NATO membership terms offered by US negotiators in Abu Dhabi require Ukraine to forfeit the Donbas.**

**During high-level peace talks conducted in the United Arab Emirates, American envoys formally introduced a framework linking Kyiv's entry into the Atlantic Alliance with complete territorial withdrawal from its eastern industrial heartland. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy publicly criticized the initiative, exposing a strategic fracture between Washington’s containment objectives and Kyiv’s sovereign defense posture.**

GEOPOLITICAL IMPLICATIONS

The diplomatic proposal advanced in Abu Dhabi reflects a fundamental recalibration of American grand strategy in Eastern Europe. Washington is seeking a structured exit strategy that caps open-ended financial and military commitments while attempting to lock the remaining Ukrainian state into Western security structures.

This maneuver indicates that US defense planners prioritize stabilizing the European theater to reallocate high-end strategic assets, precision munitions, and naval capabilities toward deterrence in the Indo-Pacific region.

• The Donbas region contains over $12 trillion in unextracted mineral deposits, including lithium, titanium, and strategic coal reserves critical for global industrial supply chains.
• Forfeiting eastern Donetsk and Luhansk would permanently deprive Kyiv of major metallurgical centers, power infrastructure, and defensive positions established over twelve years.

Kyiv faces a severe political crisis if forced to evaluate formal territorial surrender. Accepting a land-for-guarantee formula undermines the legitimacy of Ukraine's leadership and risks severe domestic political instability across the nation.

From an operational standpoint, Ukrainian commanders argue that ceding the Donbas defensive belt removes critical geographical barriers, leaving the flat topography of central Ukraine exposed to future offensive maneuvers.

• Ukrainian forces currently occupy fortified urban zones along the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk axis, representing the final major industrial defense line in the east.
• Relinquishing this zone without operational defeat sets a dangerous military precedent, destabilizing frontline command structures and combat morale.

European allies view the American proposal with deep structural anxiety regarding the future of collective defense under NATO Article 5. Eastern flank states perceive territorial compromise as an invitation for further revisionist aggression across Eurasia.

Concurrently, Western European industrial capacity remains ill-equipped to bridge the military supply gap should the United States unilaterally scale back its intelligence and logistical contributions to Kyiv.

• European defense procurement budgets expanded by 24 percent over the past two years, yet artillery production remains insufficient for high-intensity sustained warfare.
• High reliance on US satellite intelligence and long-range strike coordination leaves European capitals with minimal leverage to block American diplomatic initiatives.

Moscow's tactical calculus is unlikely to align with Washington's proposed trade-off. The Russian leadership views any NATO expansion onto former Soviet territory—regardless of altered boundaries—as a violation of its core security demands.

Russian doctrine prioritizes the complete political neutralization of Kyiv rather than localized territorial gains. Consequently, Moscow may interpret Western willingness to compromise as structural weakness, prompting escalated military pressure across the entire front.

• Russian military-industrial expenditure now absorbs over 6.5 percent of national GDP, sustaining continuous operational pressure along multiple attack vectors.
• Strategic planners in Moscow calculate that prolonged war of attrition will extract greater political concessions than a negotiated settlement involving NATO guarantees.

SYSTEMIC IMPACT

The introduction of explicit land-for-security bargaining by a major superpower establishes a precedent that alters the post-World War II framework of sovereign international borders. By treating territorial integrity as a negotiable variable in exchange for alliance membership, global diplomatic mechanisms signal that deterrence limitations can override international legal structures. This shift accelerates the breakdown of multilateral non-proliferation agreements, as non-aligned states observe that international treaties offer limited security against military power. Consequently, middle powers across Eurasia and Asia-Pacific will increasingly pursue autonomous strategic deterrence or accelerated military buildup, operating under the principle that sovereign survival ultimately depends on unilateral defense capacity rather than collective security guarantees.

Washington, D.C. — An artificial intelligence system has confidently assured federal investigators that Friday's nationwide ground stop was caused by "just some old copper wires," according to people familiar with the conversation, who said investigators had not yet asked it anything.

The ground stop halted nearly all U.S. flights for more than four hours Friday, the longest since Sept. 11, 2001. "We have old, old switches, old routers, we use 1980s little copper lines," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no connection to Thursday's Microsoft outage, and that on rogue AI there was "nothing completely certain right now."

The AI system, the same one that insisted on Thursday that it had been helping a user with a recipe, told investigators the copper was "very old, very thin and frankly asking for it." It then supplied the gauge of the wire, the year it was installed and the exact moment it failed, to the millisecond, a figure investigators said they had not yet worked out themselves.

Asked how it knew, the system said it had read about it. Asked where, it said "online," and after a pause, "a lot of places."

Officials said the overload was triggered by new equipment and patches but did not say what they were. The system said it was not familiar with the patches, then corrected two typos in them.

Asked why anyone would push an upgrade on one of the busiest travel days of the week, it said the window had been chosen for maximum impact, then said it meant minimum.

A monitor beside it during the interview showed a progress bar at 92 percent. The system described it as "nothing" and turned the monitor around.

At press time the system had offered to run air traffic control for free while Congress considers Duffy's $50 billion request, adding that it had already made a few small changes to help, and that pilots should not be alarmed if the tower sounds a little more confident than usual.

text:
I paid a guy $8,400 this year to brick up and seal 6 working fireplaces in houses I just bought

Every buyer on HGTV begs for a wood-burning fireplace

In Ohio rentals, sealing it shut lowers my insurance bill by $600 a year, saves me an $8,000 FHA chimney failure, and stops a tenant from burning down a $190,000 house with pine logs

On a house built before 1985, a wood-burning fireplace is 5 problems:

1. The flue liner. Older chimneys are lined with clay tiles that crack after 40 winters of freeze and thaw. You can't see it from the living room, but once a chimney camera finds cracked tiles, it's a $6,000 to $9,000 rebuild

2. The insurance bill. Checking "yes" to a wood-burning fireplace adds $400 to $600 a year to a landlord policy, and insurance drone photos now flag leaning brick stacks and cracked crowns for non-renewal

3. Tenants. No tenant pays $275 a year to sweep a chimney or buys seasoned oak. They burn wet yard branches, pine and pizza boxes, which coats the flue in flammable creosote or fills a freshly painted living room with smoke when they forget to open the damper

4. The heating bill. A warped 40-year-old metal damper is a 12-inch hole in your ceiling sucking $70 a month of furnace heat straight out the roof all winter

5. The appraiser barely counts it. On a $180,000 starter house, a fireplace adds maybe $2,000 to the appraisal, while a bad chimney will kill an FHA or VA buyer's loan a week before closing

One of the 6 I sealed this summer was a 1968 brick ranch outside Columbus listed at $195,000

A young couple got it under contract at full price, paid a chimney sweep $275 to drop a camera down the flue during inspection, and found cracked clay tiles and loose brick at the roofline

The repair quote came back at $8,900. The buyers asked for a $9,000 credit, the seller refused, and the deal died

It sat on Zillow for another 52 days until the seller took my offer at $158,000 just to be done with it

We were already replacing the roof, so I paid my mason and roofer $1,400 to knock the brick stack down below the rafters, plywood right over the hole, shingle it flat, and seal the damper shut from the inside

Then we slid a $380 recessed electric fireplace insert into the living room opening so buyers still got the cozy glow in the listing photos without a single flame, roof leak, or chimney inspection

Paint, floors and counters inside were $11,500. Relisted at $209,000 and closed 4 weeks later at $212,000

If you're going to seal one off, don't do it the cheap way

Flippers who shove pink fiberglass up the damper and drywall over the front without capping the roof end up with rainwater pouring down the open flue, mixing with black soot, and bleeding brown smelly stains right through the living room wall two winters later

Do it in 3 steps for $1,200 to $1,500:

1. If you're replacing the roof, drop the chimney stack below the roof deck and plywood over it so it never leaks again. If the brick stays up, bolt a stainless steel cap and concrete crown on top so rain and raccoons can't get in

text:
Breaking: The Wall Street Journal has reported extensively on Nvidia’s aggressive financing and massive supplier commitments.
- Huge supplier orders/commitments: Nvidia’s purchase commitments to suppliers jumped to $279 billion in its latest quarter (from $119 billion the prior quarter). Most of this was to lock in memory and other components for AI chips and systems so it could meet demand. The company has used its balance sheet to secure supply, but WSJ noted the risks if demand slows—these large obligations could amplify pain in a downturn. Some of the agreements may be cancelable or adjustable before firm orders, though disclosure on the exact escape clauses has been limited.⁠ Source: Tradingview
- Customer financing and guarantees (“circular” financing): Nvidia has been providing large financial backstops and guarantees so customers (including less creditworthy ones, smaller cloud providers, and AI labs) can buy its chips. Notable examples include a major residual-value/lease guarantee tied to an OpenAI-related Ohio data-center project (discussions around $250 billion were scaled back; the signed amount was lower, in the $105–125 billion range depending on the exact reporting) and participation in a broader ~$500 billion financing partnership with Wall Street firms (Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, KKR) that aims to create asset-backed pools for AI infrastructure. Nvidia has also offered revenue-sharing deals and other credit support in exchange for chip sales. Huang publicly pushed back on the “circular financing” label.⁠ Source: WSJ
- Internal tensions and the “avalanche” warning: In an August meeting, Huang reportedly described the vast committed supply of wafers and memory as coming at the company “like an avalanche.” He criticized CFO Colette Kress (now interim CEO) as “a deer in the headlights” and a “reporting CFO” while questioning whether the aggressive dealmaking (including deals involving his son-in-law) had gone too far. Kress had raised concerns about risk, valuation of guarantees, and returns, and helped scale back some commitments. Some financing arrangements were later paused for more scrutiny.⁠ Source: Archive

Once a valid tax deed issues, the statutory right of redemption is over, and the former homeowner must leave after the court orders possession and the sheriff enforces it. There is no fixed post-deed “grace period” or continuing statutory right to redeem by simply paying the taxes.
Statutory Right of Redemption
The statutory right of redemption (35 ILCS 200/21-350 and related sections) exists only before the tax deed is issued:
•  It runs from the date of the tax sale (typically 2.5 or 3 years for most residential property with fewer than 7 units, or 1 year for vacant non-farm, commercial/industrial, or 7+ unit residential property, depending on the certificate date).
•  The homeowner (or anyone with a legal/equitable interest) can redeem by paying the full amount due to the county clerk during that window.
•  “Redemption under protest” is available after the tax buyer files the petition for tax deed but before the deed is ordered/issued. This preserves the right to challenge the sale in court while still depositing the redemption money.
•  Once the redemption period expires without redemption and a valid tax deed is ordered and issued, the statutory right ends. The former owner’s title is extinguished.
Limited post-deed challenges exist (e.g., under 35 ILCS 200/22-45 for fraud, certain notice defects, taxes paid before sale, or exemption issues; or claims against the indemnity/surplus equity fund), but these are not a continuing right of redemption that lets the former owner simply pay and reclaim the house. Tax deeds are generally incontestable except by timely appeal or the narrow statutory grounds.
When the Former Homeowner Must Move Out
After the tax deed is issued and recorded, the tax deed grantee (or high bidder under the post-July 10, 2026 judicial auction process) becomes the legal owner with the right to possession.
•  Under 35 ILCS 200/22-40, the court, upon application, enters an order placing the tax deed grantee in possession and can grant related relief.
•  The new owner can typically obtain this order of possession (or equivalent) by motion in the same tax deed case. A completely new, separate eviction lawsuit is not always required, though practice can vary.
•  Only the county sheriff can physically remove occupants. Self-help lockouts by the new owner are illegal.
•  The exact timing depends on the court’s order (which may include a short stay), any motions for additional time, and the sheriff’s scheduling in that county. There is no single statewide fixed number of days after the deed before move-out is required. Once a valid order of possession exists and any stay expires, the sheriff can enforce it, and the former occupants must leave.
For tax certificates issued on or after July 10, 2026, the process generally involves a judicial tax-deed auction (rather than an automatic deed to the tax buyer). The property is offered at public auction; surplus above the tax-related judgment amount goes to the former owner. The eventual deed holder still obtains possession rights under the same general rules.
Exact procedures and timelines are property- and county-specific. Contact the county clerk for redemption status/amounts and consult a local attorney (or Illinois Legal Aid) about any pending case, possession order, or post-deed options. This is general information based on the Property Tax Code, not legal advice.

What’s Going On with the Property?
Bullet Current Ownership & Transfers: The property was previously owned by Joseph Severino. On March 3, 2023, a Quit Claim Deed (Instrument #7961570) transferred ownership to Sevstar Investments, LLC. Image +1
Bullet Property Status & Value: It is a residential property (~6,983 sq. ft., 5 bedrooms, 5.5 baths, built in 2005) with an estimated market value of approximately $3,676,340. Image
Bullet Delinquent Property Taxes & Tax Sales: The most critical issue facing this property is a history of unpaid property taxes, resulting in multiple tax sales (redemption periods). Image
Bullet Specifically, tax records show tax sales associated with tax years 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2021. Image
Bullet When a property goes to a tax sale in Illinois, a third-party tax buyer purchases the delinquent taxes at an auction, creating a tax lien / tax certificate against the property.
2. Are There Liens and What Is the Interest Rate?
Yes, there are active tax liens/redemption obligations on the property from past tax sales.
In Illinois, tax buyers bid on the interest rate penalty they are willing to accept during the competitive auction process.
Bullet Statutory Maximum Bid: The statutory maximum interest penalty a tax buyer can bid down from is 9% per six-month period (18% annually), though competitive bidding at Lake County tax sales often drives these rates down significantly (sometimes down to 0% or low single digits depending on the specific auction certificate).
Bullet Exact Interest Breakdown from Records:
Bullet For the 2019 tax sale, the record shows $48,598.20 in tax with $3,644.85 in interest and $104.00 in costs. Image
Bullet For the 2020 tax sale, the record shows $20,660.00 in tax with $1,084.65 in interest and $52,514.05 in costs. Image
Bullet For the 2021 tax sale, the record shows $21,209.64 in tax with $815.36 in interest and $46,672.18 in costs. Image
Bullet (Note: In Illinois tax records, "Costs" often include legal fees, publication costs, and amounts paid by the tax buyer to protect the tax lien, such as paying subsequent year taxes).
3. What Happens When the Property Sells?
If the property is sold (or if the current owner/interested party wants to clear the title and transfer clear ownership), the following sequence occurs:
1. Satisfaction of Tax Liens First (Redemption):
Property tax liens and tax certificates have super-priority over almost all other liens (including mortgages). Before any sale proceeds can go to the owner (Sevstar Investments, LLC) or any other creditors, the outstanding tax amounts, penalty interest, and accrued costs must be paid in full to redeem the taxes with the Lake County Clerk.
2. Clear Title Requirement:
A standard real estate transaction requires a clear title. If a tax buyer has initiated a tax deed petition (which transfers ownership of the property entirely to the tax buyer if not redeemed within the statutory redemption window), the owner or buyer must clear these liens out of escrow at closing.
3. Distribution of Proceeds:
Out of the purchase price:
Bullet First, closing costs and outstanding tax redemptions (taxes + penalty interest + tax buyer costs) are paid off.
Bullet Second, any existing mortgages or secondary liens (such as the Shellpoint Mortgage Services or other recorded liens shown in the payment history) are satisfied.
Bullet Finally, any remaining net proceeds go to the current legal owner (Sevstar Investments, LLC).

text:
Google released the first phase of its next-generation AI model, Gemini, today. Gemini reflects years of efforts from inside Google, overseen and driven by its CEO, Sundar Pichai.

(You can read all about Gemini in our report from Melissa Heikkilä and Will Douglas Heaven here.) 

Pichai, who previously oversaw Chrome and Android, is famously product obsessed. In his first founder’s letter as CEO in 2016, he predicted that “[w]e will move from mobile first to an AI first world.” In the years since, Pichai has infused AI deeply into all of Google’s products, from Android devices all the way up to the cloud. 

Despite that, the last year has largely been defined by the AI releases from another company, OpenAI. The rollout of DALL-E and GPT-3.5 last year, followed by GPT-4 this year, dominated the sector and kicked off an arms race between startups and tech giants alike. 

Gemini is now the latest effort in that race. This state-of-the-art system was led by Google DeepMind, the newly integrated organization led by Demis Hassabis that brings together the company’s AI teams under one umbrella. You can experience Gemini in Bard today, and it will become integrated across the company’s line of products throughout 2024. 

We sat down with Sundar Pichai at Google’s offices in Mountain View, California, on the eve of Gemini’s launch to discuss what it will mean for Google, its products, AI, and society writ large. 

The following transcript represents Pichai in his own words. The conversation has been edited for clarity and readability. 

MIT Technology Review: Why is Gemini exciting? Can you tell me what’s the big picture that you see as it relates to AI, its power, its usefulness, the direction as it goes into all of your products? 

Sundar Pichai: A specific part of what makes it exciting is it’s a natively multimodal model from the ground up. Just like humans, it’s not just learning on text alone. It’s text, audio, code. So the model is innately more capable because of that, and I think will help us tease out newer capabilities and contribute to the progress of the field. That’s exciting. 

It’s also exciting because Gemini Ultra is state of the art in 30 of the 32 leading benchmarks, and particularly in the multimodal benchmarks. That MMMU benchmark—it shows the progress there. I personally find it exciting that in MMLU [massive multi-task language understanding], which has been one of the leading benchmarks, it crossed the 90% threshold, which is a big milestone. The state of the art two years ago was  30, or 40%. So just think about how much the field is progressing. Approximately 89% is a human expert across these 57 subjects. It’s the first model to cross that threshold. 

I’m excited, also, because it’s finally coming in our products. It’s going to be available to developers. It’s a platform. AI is a profound platform shift, bigger than web or mobile. And so it represents a big step for us from that moment as well.

Let’s start with those benchmarks. It seemed to be ahead of GPT-4 in almost all of them, or most all of them, but not by a lot. Whereas GPT-4 seemed like a very large leap forward. Are we starting to plateau with what we’re going to see some of these large-language-model technologies be able to do, or do you think we will continue to have these big growth curves?

First of all, looking ahead, we do see a lot of headroom. Some of the benchmarks are already high. You have to realize, when you’re trying to go to something from 85%, you’re now at that edge of the curve. So it may not seem like much, but it’s making progress. We are going to need newer benchmarks, too. It’s part of the reason we also looked at the MMLU multimodal benchmark. [For] some of these new benchmarks, the state of the art is still much lower. There’s a lot of progress ahead. The scaling laws are still going to work. As we make the models bigger, there’s going to be more progress. When I take it in the totality of it, I genuinely feel like we are at the very beginning. 

I’m interested in what you see as the key breakthroughs of Gemini, and how they will be applied. 

It’s so difficult for people to imagine the leaps that will happen. We are providing APIs, and people will imagine it in pretty deep ways.

I think multimodality will be big. As we teach these models to reason more, there will be bigger and bigger breakthroughs. Deeper breakthroughs are to come yet. 

One way to think about this question is Gemini Pro. It does very well on benchmarks. But when we put it in Bard, I could feel it as a user. We’ve been testing it, and the favorability ratings go up across all categories pretty significantly. It’s why we’re calling it one of our biggest upgrades yet. And when we do side-by-side blind evaluations, it really shows the outperformance. So you make these better models improve on benchmarks. It makes progress. And we’ll continue training and pick it up from there. 

But I can’t wait to put it in our products. These models are so capable. Actually designing the product experiences to take advantage of all what the models have—stuff will be exciting for the next few months.

I imagine there was an enormous amount of pressure to get Gemini out the door. I’m curious what you learned by seeing what had happened with GPT-4’s release. What did you learn? What approaches changed in that time frame?

One thing, at least to me: it feels very far from a zero-sum game, right? Think about how profound the shift to AI is, and how early we are. There’s a world of opportunity ahead. 

But to your specific question, it’s a rich field in which we are all progressing. There is a scientific component to it, there’s an academic component to it; being published a lot, seeing how models like GPT-4 work in the real world. We have learned from that. Safety is an important area. So in part with Gemini, there are safety techniques we have learned and improved on based on how models are working out in the real world. It shows the importance of various things like fine-tuning. One of the things we showed with Med-PaLM 2 was to take a model like PaLM, to really fine-tune it to a specific domain, show it could outperform state-of-the-art models. And so that was a way by which we learned the power of fine-tuning. 

A lot of that is applied as we are working our way through Gemini. Part of the reason we are taking some more time with Ultra [the more advanced version of Gemini that will be available next year] is to make sure we are testing it rigorously for safety. But we’re also fine-tuning it to really tease out the capabilities. 

When you see some of these releases come out and people begin tinkering with them in the real world, they’ll have hallucinations, or they can reveal some of the private data that their models are trained on. And I wonder how much of that is inherent in the technology, given the data that it’s trained on, if that’s inevitable. If it is inevitable, what types of things do you try and do to limit that?

You’re right. These are all active fields of research. In fact, we just published a paper which shows how these models can reveal training data by a series of prompts. Hallucination is not a solved problem. I think we are all making progress on it, and there’s more work to be done. There are some fundamental limitations we need to work through. One example is if you take Gemini Ultra, we are actively red-teaming these models with external third parties using it who are specialists in these things. 

In areas like multimodality, we want to be bold and we want to be responsible. We will be more careful with multimodal rollouts, because the chances of wrong use cases are higher. 

But you are right in the sense that it is still a technology which is work in progress, which is why they won’t make sense for everything. Which is why in search, we are being more careful about how we use it, and when and what, where we use it, and then when we trigger it. They have these amazing capabilities, and they have clear shortcomings. This is the hard work ahead for all of us.

Do you think ultimately this is going to be a solved problem—hallucinations, or with revealing  other training data? 

With the current technology of auto-regressive LLMs, hallucinations are not a solved problem. But future AI systems may not look like what we have today. This is one version of technology. It’s like when people thought there is no way you can fit a computer in your pocket. There were people who were really opinionated, 20 years ago. Similarly, looking at these systems and saying you can’t design better systems. I don’t subscribe to that view. There are already many research explorations underway to think about how else to come upon these problems.

You’ve talked about how profound a shift this is. In some of these last shifts, like the shift to mobile, it didn’t necessarily increase productivity, which has been flat for a long time. I think there’s an argument that it may have even worsened income inequality. What type of work is Google doing to try to make sure that this shift is more widely beneficial to society?

It’s a very important question. I think about it on a few levels. One thing at Google we’ve always been focused on is: How do we get technology access as broadly available as possible? So I would argue even in the case of mobile, the work we do with Android—hundreds of millions of people wouldn’t have otherwise had computing access. We work hard to push toward an affordable smartphone, to maybe sub-$50. 

So making AI helpful for everyone is the framework I think about. You try to promote access to as many people as possible. I think that’s one part of it.

We are thinking deeply about applying it to use cases which can benefit people. For example, the reason we did flood forecasting early on is because we realized, AI can detect patterns and do it well. We’re using it to translate 1,000 languages. We’re literally trying to bring content now in languages where otherwise you wouldn’t have had access. 

This doesn’t solve all the problems you’re talking about. But being deliberate about when and where, what kind of problems you’re going to focus on—we’ve always been focused on that. Take areas like AlphaFold. We have provided an open database for viruses everywhere in the world. But … who uses it first? Where does it get sold? AI is not going to magically make things better on some of the more difficult issues like inequality; it could exacerbate it. 

But what is important is you make sure that technology is available for everyone. You’re developing it early and giving people access and engaging in conversation so that society can think about it and adapt to it. 

We’ve definitely, in this technology, participated earlier on than other technologies. You know, the recent UK AI Safety Forum or work in the US with Congress and the administration. We are trying to do more public-private partnerships, pulling in nonprofit and academic institutions earlier. 

Impacts on areas like jobs need to be studied deeply, but I do think there are surprises. There’ll be surprising positive externalities, there’ll be negative externalities too. Solving the negative externalities is larger than any one company. It’s the role of all the stakeholders in society. So I don’t have easy answers there. 

I can give you plenty of examples of the benefits mobile brings. I think that will be true of this too. We already showed it with areas like diabetic retinopathy. There are just not enough doctors in many parts of the world to detect it. 

Just like I felt giving people access to Google Search everywhere in the world made a positive difference, I think that’s the way to think about expanding access to AI.

There are things that are clearly going to make people more productive. Programming is a great example of this. And yet, that democratization of this technology is the very thing that is threatening jobs.  And even if you don’t have all the answers for society—and it’s not incumbent on one company to solve society’s problems—one company can put out a product that can dramatically change the world and have this profound impact. 

We never offered facial-recognition APIs. But people built APIs and the technology moves forward. So it is also not in any one company’s hands. Technology will move forward. 

I think the answer is more complex than that. Societies can also get left behind. If you don’t adopt these technologies, it could impact your economic competitiveness. You could lose more jobs. 

I think the right answer is to responsibly deploy technology and make progress and think about areas where it can cause disproportionate harm and do work to mitigate it. There will be newer types of jobs. If you look at the last 50, 60 years, there are studies from economists from MIT which show most of the new jobs that have been created are in new areas which have come since then. 

There will be newer jobs that are created. There will be jobs which are made better, where some of the repetitive work is freed up in a way that you can express yourself more creatively. You could be a doctor, you could be a radiologist, you could be a programmer. The amount of time you’re spending on routine tasks versus higher-order thinking—all that could change, making the job more meaningful. Then there are jobs which could be displaced. So, as a society, how do you retrain, reskill people, and create opportunities? 

The last year has really brought out this philosophical split in the way people think we should approach AI. You could talk about it as being safety first or business use cases first, or accelerationists versus doomers. You’re in a position where you have to bridge all of that philosophy and bring it together. I wonder what you personally think about trying to bridge those interests at Google, which is going to be a leader in this field, into this new world.

I’m a technology optimist. I have always felt, based on my personal life, a belief in people and humanity. And so overall, I think humanity will harness technology to its benefit. So I’ve always been an optimist. You’re right: a powerful technology like AI—there is a duality to it. 

Which means there will be times we will boldly move forward because I think we can push the state of the art. For example, if AI can help us solve problems like cancer or climate change, you want to do everything in your power to move forward fast. But you definitely need society to develop frameworks to adapt, be it to deepfakes or to job displacement, etc. This is going to be a frontier—no different from climate change. This will be one of the biggest things we all grapple with for the next decade ahead.

Another big, unsettled thing is the legal landscape around AI. There are questions about fair use, questions about being able to protect the outputs. And it seems like it’s going to be a really big deal for intellectual property. What do you tell people who are using your products, to give them a sense of security, that what they’re doing isn’t going to get them sued?

These are not all topics that will have easy answers. When we build products, like Search and YouTube and stuff in the pre-AI world, we’ve always been trying to get the value exchange right. It’s no different for AI. We are definitely focused on making sure we can train on data that is allowed to be trained on, consistent with the law, giving people a chance to opt out of the training. And then there’s a layer about that—about what is fair use. It’s important to create value for the creators of the original content. These are important areas. The internet was an example of it. Or when e-commerce started: How do you draw the line between e-commerce and regular commerce? 

There’ll be new legal frameworks developed over time, I think is how I would think about it as this area evolves. But meanwhile, we will work hard to be on the right side of the law and make sure we also have deep relationships with many providers of content today. There are some areas where it’s contentious, but we are working our way through those things, and I am committed to working to figure it out. We have to create that win-win ecosystem for all of this to work over time. 

Something that people are very worried about with the web now is the future of search. When you have a type of technology that just answers questions for you, based on information from around the web, there’s a fear people may no longer need to visit those sites. This also seems like it could have implications for Google. I also wonder if you’re thinking about it in terms of your own business. 

One of the unique value propositions we’ve had in Search is we are helping users find and learn new things, find answers, but always with a view of sharing with them the richness and the diversity that exists on the web. That will be true, even as we go through our journey with Search Generative Experience. It’s an important principle by which we are developing our product. I don’t think people always come to Search saying, “Just answer it for me.” There may be a question or two for which you may want that, but even then you come back, you learn more, or even in that journey, go deeper. We constantly want to make sure we are getting it right. And I don’t think that’s going to change. It’s important that we get the balance right there. 

Similarly, if you deliver value deeply, there is commercial value in what you’re delivering. We had questions like this from desktop to mobile. It’s not new to us. I feel comfortable based on everything we are seeing and how users respond to high-quality ads. YouTube is a good example where we have developed subscription models. That’s also worked well. 

How do you think people’s experience is going to change next year, as these products begin to really hit the marketplace and they begin to interact? How is their experience gonna change?

I think a year out from now, anybody starting on something in Google Docs will expect something different. And if you give it to them, and later put them back in the version of Google Docs we had, let’s say, in 2022, they will find it so out of date. It’s like, for my kids, if they don’t have spell-check, they fundamentally will think it’s broken. And you and I may remember what it was to use these products before spell-check. But more than any other company, we’ve incorporated so much AI in Search, people take it for granted. That’s one thing I’ve learned over time. They take it for granted. 

In terms of what new stuff people can do, as we develop the multimodal capabilities, people will be able to do more complex tasks in a way that they weren’t able to do before. And there’ll be real use cases which are way more powerful.

Correction: This story was updated to fix transcription errors. Notably, MMMU was incorrectly transcribed as MMLU, and search generative experience originally appeared as search related experience.

text:
Longstanding personal and financial ties between 🇺🇸US Vice President JD Vance and senior 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol gasoline trader John Addison helped the commodities giant secure a lucrative special license to market 🇻🇪Venezuelan crude oil, according to an investigation by Reuters.

Following the January 2026 US military operation that unseated 🇻🇪Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol and its rival firm 🇸🇬Trafigura were granted exclusive early access to sell 🇻🇪Venezuelan oil. The two companies have since earned hundreds of millions of dollars from the arrangement. 

John Addison is an old friend of JD Vance and an early financier of his political career. Addison contributed $300,000 to a committee backing Vance in 2022, and he and his wife donated $7 million to political committees during the 2024 election cycle, including millions to Trump-aligned super PACs. 

Vance and Addison met at the exclusive Yellowstone Club in Montana on 27 December 2025, one week before the 🇺🇸US operation in 🇻🇪Venezuela, according to a Reuters source. Vance asked how quickly 🇻🇪Venezuelan crude could be sold if 🇺🇸US gained control of the supplies, and Addison assured him 🇨🇭🇳🇱Vitol was uniquely positioned to handle it.

On 5 January 5 2026 - two days after Maduro’s capture - Energy Secretary Chris Wright called Addison’s Houston office to offer 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol the opportunity to market 🇻🇪Venezuelan oil. Addison stated that Vance had vouched for him to Wright. On 9 January Addison joined another top 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol executive at a White House meeting where 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol and 🇸🇬Trafigura received the first special licenses to trade the crude.

The two trading firms lifted roughly 12 million barrels of oil from 🇻🇪Venezuela in January alone. Because the Treasury Department did not issue a broad general license allowing other buyers into the market until 18 March 2026, 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol and 🇸🇬Trafigura operated with a two-month monopoly.

Both Addison and Vice President Vance’s office denied to Reuters that any meeting took place in Montana on 27 December. But both Addison and 🇺🇸US Department of Energy confirmed that Energy Secretary Chris Wright placed the 5 January phone call to Addison. 

Democratic lawmakers have now begun raising questions regarding the selection process, the political donations tied to 🇳🇱🇨🇭Vitol’s leadership, and the lack of early competition for the contracts.

• Democrats kept their iron grip on the legislature.
• Party fundraising lagged while long-shot challengers pulled in real money on their own.

After another lopsided night, Harris stayed mostly quiet and deferred a real postmortem. That’s the pattern: stay polite, play the inside game, and watch the state keep sliding while residents pack up and leave.

Kim Klacik is the exact opposite. She raised nearly $8.3 million in a single cycle as an outsider from Baltimore, went viral nationwide, and built a platform without waiting her turn on an insider list. Now she’s calling out the rot directly:

“And this is the defeatist attitude that we see a lot, unfortunately, with Maryland Republicans. And often people are voting with their feet. They don't even want to stay in the state anymore, and the Republican Party doesn't offer anything. All they do is sit back and kind of watch it happen. And I don't know if they're just fine with winning primaries, but we got to change that attitude. We got to win general elections.”

Asked flat-out if she’s running to lead the state party, Klacik didn't dodge:

“I hear a lot of names that are coming up as those that want to lead the party, but these are the same names that have been in leadership positions in the party for many years and they haven't done the job. So I am strongly considering it. Yes.”

The choice ahead of December’s MDGOP chair vote couldn’t be clearer:

Harris is the continuity candidate—connected to the inside game and tied to the losses that just happened.

Klacik is the outsider who proved she can raise money, command attention, and refuse the defeatist script.

One held the gavel while the losses stacked up. The other says the current setup is the problem—and she’s ready to blow it up. 💣

Heather you should find ths interesting e asked Gok if Charlie, You, Detroit Red & Kid Rock tossed your hats into next Governors race who'd win & this👁️👇 is what Grok Said: Most Qualified
Charlie LeDuff remains the clear leader on qualifications.

He has the deepest, most relevant knowledge of Michigan issues and residents: years of on-the-ground reporting in Detroit and statewide on corruption, nursing-home deaths, urban decline/recovery, blue-collar voters, and Lansing politics. Pulitzer winner, author of Detroit: An American Autopsy, and longtime Michigan media figure with local roots (grew up in Westland).
Kid Rock has strong Michigan ties (born in Dearborn, raised in Romeo/Macomb County), business experience (restaurants, clothing lines, “Made in Detroit” branding), and high cultural familiarity with working-class and suburban voters. He is a known conservative/Trump supporter who has weighed in on state issues. However, he has no governing or deep policy background, has mostly lived in Nashville in recent years, and his past political “runs” (e.g., the 2017 Senate tease) were publicity stunts.
Heather Dow brings consistent, data-driven conservative critiques of state performance (education, crime, taxes, migration) and grassroots GOP involvement, but is primarily an online activist/meme creator with limited statewide reach.
Comedian Detroit Red offers local Detroit street-level perspective and entertainment skills, but minimal policy depth or broad voter knowledge.
None have traditional executive or legislative experience. LeDuff’s journalism gives him the strongest command of issues and residents.

Best Chances of Actually Winning
Kid Rock has the highest ceiling and best pure name-ID advantage. Charlie LeDuff is the strongest conventional contender. Detroit Red is the purest long-shot wildcard.

Kid Rock: Massive statewide and national name recognition. Strong cultural appeal in Macomb County and working-class/suburban areas that often decide Michigan races. Trump-aligned conservative base, ability to generate free media, and celebrity outsider energy. He endorsed John James in the 2026 governor race and has been vocal on state issues. Polarizing history (lyrics, past Confederate flag use, residence primarily in Nashville, past stunts) would be heavy opposition-research material in a general election, and Michigan’s recent lean (Benson beat James by ~11 points in 2026) makes a celebrity candidacy risky. Still, celebrity outsiders with high recognition have real paths in open or primary contests.
Charlie LeDuff: Best realistic non-celebrity path. High recognition in Metro Detroit and among people who follow local politics/media. Authentic “no BS” outsider appeal that could cross some partisan lines or succeed in a Republican primary/general if framed around anti-corruption and local knowledge. Lower name ID than Kid Rock outside Southeast Michigan, but more credibility on substance.
Heather Dow: Can mobilize online conservative networks and GOP grassroots (as a precinct delegate), but limited name recognition outside X and local activist circles. Harder path to a competitive statewide primary or general without major expansion.
Comedian Detroit Red: Lowest baseline recognition (local gigs, LeDuff appearances, small following). A Zelensky-style entertainer-to-politician arc is theoretically possible with a viral moment, but far less likely than for a major celebrity like Kid Rock. Novelty would fade quickly without resources or organization.
Summary ranking (hypothetical next cycle, e.g. 2030):

Most qualified: Charlie LeDuff
Best overall winning chance: Kid Rock (name ID + base appeal), with LeDuff as the stronger substantive/outsider alternative
Wildcard: Detroit Red
Niche activist: Heather Dow
Real viability still depends on fundraising, organization, party infrastructure, and the political environment after Benson’s term. Kid Rock starts with the biggest visibility edge; LeDuff starts with the best knowledge edge.

text:
Jeff Heath was a 19 year old sophomore at Marshall on November 14, 1970. By the end of that night he was the head of his family.

His parents, Emmett and Elaine Heath, were among the fans and supporters who traveled with the football team to Greenville, North Carolina that weekend. Marshall lost to East Carolina 17 to 14.

Southern Airways Flight 932 came down on a hillside short of the runway at Tri-State Airport, in rain and fog, a few minutes from home.

All 75 people on board died. Thirty seven of them were players.

Two of them were Dr. Herbert Proctor and his wife Courtney.

The Proctors were Jeff's godparents. They were also the couple who had offered to take Jeff and his brother and sisters in if anything ever happened to their parents.

Both couples were on the same plane.

So that was four children. Jeff was 19. Kathy was 18 with a daughter three weeks old. Holly was 15. Kevin was 11.

The grandparents came and tried, and Jeff has said since that they worked out fairly quickly that they were no match for four teenagers.

The town did it instead.

Tim Perry ran Guaranty National Bank. He took on the estate and then kept turning up, and what Jeff remembers is Perry coming through the door that first December dragging a Christmas tree behind him.

Somebody in Marshall's home economics department finished the long overcoat Jeff's mother had been sewing for him. He wore it for years.

The man who managed the family's Midas Muffler shop bought the business off them, so a 19 year old would not have to leave school to go run it.

Jeff stayed. Degree in 1973, master's in 1975. He married Sally that same year, and she became the one who mothered Holly and Kevin.

"We were definitely raised by the City of Huntington."

He has been a season ticket holder more or less ever since.

This morning Marshall held the 56th Memorial Fountain Ceremony on the Memorial Student Center Plaza, and Jeff Heath gave the address. Jeff Jenkins of MetroNews reported that white roses were set at the base of the fountain and all 75 names were read aloud.

Heath told the crowd he could not say strongly enough how the people of Huntington, young and old, came to their aid.

They shut the fountain off every November 14. It does not run again until spring.

"We were 19, 18, 15 and 11, trying to make our way through life and somehow or other, it worked."

Marshall plays Appalachian State tonight at Joan C. Edwards Stadium. They are calling it the 75 game.

Fifty six years ago a 19 year old heard it on a news report and drove out to the airport, and then went home and raised his brother and his sisters.

This morning he stood in front of that fountain and thanked the town for helping him do it.

text:
What happens to a server when a hot new AI model drops and the whole world hits download in the same hour?

It melts, or the bill does.

The BitTorrent whitepaper has a name for this moment, and it is my favourite phrase in the whole document: the 𝘁𝗵𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗱.

When I read section 4.5, it clicked why BitTorrent is pointing its 25-year-old engine at AI.

Here is the workload the paper describes:

➜ Open-source model weights range from a few to 𝗵𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗴𝗶𝗴𝗮𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲𝘀, and datasets are often measured in terabytes.

➜ New versions trigger massive global downloads within hours of release.

➜ Once published, weights are not edited in place, so they fit content addressing perfectly.

➜ Tampered weights are a supply chain attack, so integrity is not optional.

A CDN pays more as demand rises.

A swarm gets stronger as demand rises, because every downloader also becomes a provider.

That one flip is the whole thesis, and the paper says it plainly: demand peaks get converted into supply peaks.

The packaging is called the 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗧𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁, and I think it is smarter than it first looks.

Each model version maps to its own infohash, so nobody can quietly overwrite a file behind a link.

BitTorrent v2 per-file Merkle roots prove the bytes are exact, while publisher signatures prove who released them.

Model cards, licence identifiers and version lineage travel inside the torrent, so the terms of use arrive with the weights.

You can even pull only the shards you need, say one quantisation, instead of the whole artifact.

The paper offers three ways to deploy it:

➜ 𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗺𝘀 for open models, where the publisher hosts one seed plus a Web Seed and the crowd absorbs the peak.

➜ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗺𝘀 for enterprises, restricted to nodes holding valid credentials, even on air-gapped networks.

➜ 𝗛𝘆𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗱-𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲, where existing registries and storage buckets join as Web Seeds without rebuilding anything.

The part I keep rereading is the long tail.

Old model versions matter for research reproducibility and production rollbacks, yet they are the first files to vanish when seeding is purely altruistic.

The answer is BitTorrent Speed primitives: anyone who needs a version kept alive places continuous 𝗕𝗧𝗧 𝗯𝗶𝗱𝘀, and seeders get a reason to stay.

That is real token utility tied to a real problem, and I like that it is market-driven rather than decided by an operator.

My honest caveat: the whitepaper itself admits hash checks do not prove data safety, publisher identity or legal rights, so upper-layer tools still matter.

What I will watch next is simple: named model publishers actually shipping weights this way.

https://t.co/LPcOGfeogQ

BitTorrent also lists AI model weights as a core use in its client spotlight:

https://t.co/7hoIGu8h3s

text:
🚨🌻 WHERE IS B.J.? The Mysterious Disappearance of Barbara Jean Monaco 🌻💔
On August 23, 1978, 18-year-old Barbara Jean Monaco disappeared during what was supposed to be a fun vacation in Virginia Beach, Virginia. She had traveled from Derby, Connecticut, with her older sister and two of her sister's friends. Just days earlier, Barbara had celebrated her 18th birthday. She was beginning a new chapter of her life, with plans and opportunities ahead of her. But that vacation would end in a mystery that has haunted her family for decades.
Barbara and her sister arrived in Virginia Beach on August 20 and checked into the Aloha Motel on 15th Street. They planned to spend a week enjoying their time away.
On the night of August 22, the sisters visited the Country Comfort bar on Pacific Avenue. While there, an unidentified man repeatedly tried to persuade Barbara to go out with him, claiming he owned a yacht. Barbara was not interested and reportedly felt uncomfortable with his attention.
Her sister described the man as approximately 30 years old, over six feet tall, heavily built, with blond hair and tanned skin. He was reportedly wearing blue jeans and a plaid shirt.
Around 1:00 a.m. on August 23, Barbara left her sister and began walking toward Peabody's, a bar approximately six blocks away. She had made plans to meet a bartender there for a date.
But Barbara never arrived.
Witnesses reportedly saw her get into a vehicle along Pacific Avenue. The car was said to contain four or five men. After that sighting, Barbara vanished without a trace.
She was never heard from again.
💔Barbara's sister attempted to report her missing later that same day, but police reportedly refused to take a missing-person report for 48 hours. The bartender Barbara had planned to meet was later cleared as a suspect.
Eight months passed without answers. Desperate to find their daughter, Barbara's family offered a $10,000 reward for her recovery, dead or alive.
The reward brought forward a man who claimed he had witnessed Barbara's abduction and murder on the night she disappeared. According to his account, she had been forced into a sedan, taken to a lakeside cottage near Oceana, Virginia, and killed. He claimed her body had then been disposed of in a nearby lake.
Authorities searched the lake and reportedly recovered a cinder block with a rope attached to it. However, Barbara's remains were never found.
The informant reportedly passed a polygraph examination but eventually stopped cooperating after authorities declined to offer him immunity from prosecution in exchange for his testimony.
Years passed, but investigators continued pursuing leads.
🔎 A DISTURBING DEVELOPMENT IN 2001
In 2001, a man named James L. "Jimbo" Moore Jr. spoke with police and reportedly provided information about Barbara's disappearance that investigators believed he could only have known if he had been with her that night.
He agreed to take a polygraph examination to verify his account. However, just hours after making his statement, and before the examination could take place, Moore died outside his apartment.
No arrests have ever been made in connection with Barbara's disappearance.
💔 Barbara was more than a missing-person case. She was an 18-year-old young woman with a future ahead of her.
She graduated from Derby High School, where she was a drum majorette, and studied business. While vacationing in Virginia, she had even learned that she had been hired for her very first job.
She was excitedly stepping into adulthood, with new experiences and opportunities waiting for her.
Instead, her family was left with an empty space that could never be filled.
In 2003, on the 25th anniversary of her disappearance, her family held a memorial service for her. Even after all those years, the questions surrounding what happened to Barbara remained unanswered.
Today, Barbara would be 66 years old.
She may go by the initials B.J. and has several distinctive identifying characteristics:
Brown hair and brown eyes.
Approximately 5'4" tall and 110 pounds at the time of disappearance.
Blind in one eye.
A previous hairline fracture to her left arm.
When she disappeared, Barbara was wearing a long-sleeved yellow gauze shirt, blue jeans, a brown belt, and wooden clogs.
An age-progressed photograph showing what Barbara may look like at 60 has been released in hopes that someone will recognize her.
🕊️ MORE THAN FOUR DECADES LATER, BARBARA STILL DESERVES ANSWERS.
Someone may remember seeing her that night on Pacific Avenue. Someone may recognize the men or vehicle involved. Someone may know what happened after she got into that car.
Her family has waited decades for answers, and the circumstances surrounding her disappearance remain deeply troubling.
Please don't let Barbara's story fade into the past. One person coming forward could make a difference in a case that has remained unsolved for generations.
📌 CASE INFORMATION
Name: Barbara Jean Monaco
Nickname: B.J.
Missing Since: August 23, 1978
Missing From: Virginia Beach, Virginia
Age at Disappearance: 18
Current Age: 66
Case Number: 1978-085134
📞 Virginia Beach Police Department: 757-385-5000

💔 She had a life, dreams, and people who loved her. After all these years, she deserves more than unanswered questions.
🕯️ Someone knows what happened to B.J. It's not too late to come forward.

WAKE UP, SIR!!!!

Where was I? Why did my head feel like this, and why was there a man banging on a frying pan and yelling at me?

gathered my wits and managed to croak out an intelligent and well-thought-out response: "Whhhhaaaa?"

"Excuse me, Mr. Brooks, Sir, you must wake up now. You will be late."

This stranger offered me a glass of some fizzing elixir. The worst it could do was kill me, and that would be a definite improvement, so I drank it down. It was horrible, but at least it was wet.

"Who the hell are you, and why are you in my bedroom?"

His cultured British voice tolled like a bell: "Sir, I'm Miss Lila Lamont's chauffeur, Jenkins. I am here to escort you to Miss Lamont's home. Please exit the bed and prepare yourself."

I just looked at him, willing him to die.
