text:
SERBIA'S STUDENT LIST ECONOMIC EXPERIMENT: A RETURN TO THE PAST DISGUISED AS A NEW ECONOMIC VISION?

From state ownership and politically directed investment to the risk of capital flight, industrial decline and a weakened private sector, Serbia's proposed economic direction raises uncomfortable questions. The country has already experienced an economic system in which the state and political institutions exercised enormous influence over enterprise, investment and production. It should be demanding considerably more than promises before considering another experiment.

Serbia's Student Blockade (@studentblokade) has presented its economic ambitions as a break with the country's existing development model. It promises to move away from an economy built around cheap labour, foreign factories and employment subsidies, towards domestic production, higher wages, innovation, a fairer tax system and greater protection of strategic national assets.

On the surface, these are attractive objectives. Nobody should object to higher productivity, better wages, transparent public spending, stronger domestic businesses or an economy capable of producing more than low-cost manufacturing.

But economic policy cannot be judged by the attractiveness of its intentions. It must be judged by its consequences, its financing, its incentives and, above all, whether the proposed model can actually generate sustainable economic growth.

And when the Student List's programme is examined more closely, a much larger question emerges: is Serbia being offered a modern, competitive market economy, or a return to a philosophy in which the state increasingly determines who owns businesses, where capital is invested, which industries receive support and how economic activity should be organised?

That question matters because Serbia has already lived through an experiment in state-directed economics.

It was called socialist Yugoslavia.

THE YUGOSLAV QUESTION: HAS SERBIA FORGOTTEN ITS ECONOMIC HISTORY?

One of the most revealing elements of the Student List's economic programme is its position on ownership.

The movement says strategic companies should remain in state hands and rejects what it describes as unnecessary or coercive privatisation. It proposes a state ownership strategy and insists that transforming public enterprises into joint-stock companies would not automatically mean privatisation.

This is presented as a defence of national interests. But national ownership is not the same thing as economic success, and keeping a company in government hands does not make it productive, competitive or financially sustainable.

Serbia should understand that distinction better than most countries.

After the Second World War, socialist Yugoslavia developed an economic system that initially relied on centralised state ownership and planning. It subsequently introduced its distinctive model of workers' self-management. Enterprises became socially owned, workers' councils participated in management, and the economy evolved towards a form of market socialism.

This was not identical to the Soviet system. Yugoslavia experimented with decentralisation, enterprise autonomy and market mechanisms. Workers were formally given a role in enterprise decisions, while banks, political institutions and different levels of government continued to influence investment and economic priorities.

It was an ambitious attempt to create a different economic model.

But the experience exposed fundamental weaknesses.

The World Bank's historical analysis of Yugoslavia's financial restructuring documented how inadequate financial discipline among self-managed enterprises, connected relationships between enterprises and banks, and unclear financial responsibilities contributed to the country's economic fragility. Losses of self-managed enterprises averaged 6.6 per cent of gross social product during 1985–89. Those losses did not simply disappear. They were transmitted through the banking system and ultimately contributed to monetary instability and inflation.

The World Bank's industrial restructuring study also documented declining industrial performance during the 1980s, minimal or negative productivity gains, and an increasing number of loss-making enterprises whose deficits were covered through subsidies and transfers.

The lesson is not that every publicly owned company must fail. It is that ownership structures and political ambitions cannot substitute for financial discipline, accountability and productive performance.

The International Monetary Fund made a similarly important observation in its 2002 assessment of Serbia. It identified the legacy of Yugoslav self-management and social ownership as a poor starting point for private-sector development, noting the shortage of private companies with owners who had both the incentive and authority to restructure businesses.

Serbia spent years confronting the institutional consequences of that system.

So why should the country now embrace a greater reliance on state ownership without demanding an exceptionally convincing explanation of how the proposed model will avoid the same problems?

There is a difference between protecting essential national infrastructure and protecting inefficient companies. There is a difference between a government that regulates commercial activity and one that increasingly directs it. There is also a difference between a market economy with selected state-owned enterprises and an economy in which political institutions become the dominant force in determining investment and production.

The Student List has to explain where it intends to draw that line.

This is not an accusation that its programme is a literal restoration of communism. It is a question about its economic philosophy. When state ownership, state-directed investment, development institutions and political intervention become the organising principles of economic policy, the country moves closer to a model of state-directed economics.

Serbia has every right to debate that direction. It also has every right to remember its history.

CAPITAL HAS NO LOYALTY: INVESTMENT WILL GO WHERE THE ECONOMICS MAKE SENSE

The Student List's promise to abandon Serbia's cheap-labour development model sounds politically appealing. The problem is that foreign investment does not operate according to political slogans.

International companies invest where the commercial conditions justify the investment. They consider labour costs, productivity, taxation, infrastructure, energy prices, logistics, access to markets, regulatory stability, the availability of skilled workers and the expected return on capital.

They do not invest because a government has declared that domestic production should be encouraged.

Serbia has spent years attracting international manufacturers through a combination of labour-cost advantages, incentives and access to European markets. That model has limitations, and Serbia should absolutely aspire to move up the value chain. But replacing it requires a credible transition strategy.

If wages increase faster than productivity, if labour becomes more expensive without a corresponding improvement in output, if taxation becomes less predictable or if regulation introduces additional uncertainty, the economics of producing in Serbia change.

And international investors have alternatives.

Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, North Macedonia and other manufacturing locations compete for the same investment, production lines and supply-chain contracts. A company considering its next factory does not have to choose Serbia. It can choose another country.

The likely sequence is not necessarily that every existing investor immediately closes its Serbian operation and removes all its capital. Existing factories involve sunk investment, established suppliers, trained workers and long-term commercial relationships. The more immediate danger is that companies redirect future investment elsewhere.

They delay expansion. They move new production lines to another country. They transfer orders. They reduce reinvestment. Eventually, where the economics no longer justify remaining, some operations may shrink or close.

That is how investment competitiveness is lost.

And the consequences extend far beyond the factory gates.

A manufacturing plant supports logistics companies, transport operators, maintenance contractors, warehouses, suppliers, restaurants, retailers and other local businesses. Its employees spend their wages in the surrounding economy. Its operations generate tax revenue and support local employment.

When a major employer reduces production, the impact spreads through that network.

The government can announce that it wants to support domestic production, but it cannot simply replace the investment, technology, distribution networks and export relationships that international companies bring with them.

This is the central contradiction in the Student List's economic approach: Serbia may want to move away from low-cost manufacturing, but it cannot afford to weaken its existing industrial base before a competitive domestic alternative has been built.

The objective should be to make Serbia more valuable to investors, not to make investment less attractive.

HIGHER WAGES IS AN OUTCOME OF PRODUCTIVITY, NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR IT

The Student Blockade promises to encourage businesses to increase average wages and to move away from the country's low-cost labour model.

Higher wages is desirable. But they cannot be sustainably created by political instruction.

A company will pay higher wages over the long term when its employees produce more value, when technology improves output, when management becomes more efficient, when products command higher prices or when the business moves into more sophisticated activities.

This is the relationship between wages and productivity.

If wages increase substantially while productivity remains unchanged, unit labour costs rise. That puts pressure on business margins, prices, hiring decisions and competitiveness.

For an export-oriented manufacturer operating in an international market, the consequences are particularly direct. Its competitors are not obliged to increase their costs simply because Serbia has decided to change its wage policy.

A company that cannot justify higher labour costs through higher productivity has several choices: accept lower margins, increase prices where possible, invest in automation, reduce employment or move future production elsewhere.

None of those outcomes is automatically beneficial to Serbian workers.

The real economic challenge is to raise productivity through vocational education, modern equipment, research and development, infrastructure, management quality, competition and access to capital.

Higher wages should be the reward for a more productive economy. They should not become a substitute for building one.

THE FOUR-DAY WORKWEEK AND THE COST OF ECONOMIC PROMISES

Any proposal to reduce working hours while maintaining wages deserves equally serious examination.

A shorter working week may be possible in some sectors. Technology, automation and improved organisation can allow certain businesses to maintain or increase output with fewer working hours.

But it is not a universal solution.

Manufacturing, construction, logistics, transport, healthcare and other labour-intensive activities operate under different conditions. Many require continuous staffing, production schedules and coordination across shifts.

If employees work fewer hours for the same weekly salary, the effective hourly labour cost increases unless productivity rises sufficiently to compensate.

For a business already operating under pressure from energy, materials, financing and labour costs, that is not an insignificant change.

A policy that works for a software company cannot automatically be imposed on a factory, warehouse or construction site.

If the Student List wants to introduce such a reform, it must explain which sectors it applies to, how productivity gains will be achieved, what transition arrangements will exist and who bears the additional cost.

Economic policy is not a competition to offer the most appealing working conditions on paper. It is about creating an economy capable of financing those conditions.

THE DEVELOPMENT BANK: A FINANCIAL INSTITUTION IS NOT A MAGIC SOURCE OF CAPITAL

The Student Blockade has also proposed establishing a Development Bank, reportedly through the merger of the Development Fund and the Export Credit and Insurance Agency.

The stated objective is to improve access to financing for domestic businesses, smaller companies, innovation and productive investment.

There is nothing inherently wrong with development finance. Properly designed public financial institutions can support projects that have economic value but struggle to obtain suitable financing from conventional commercial lenders.

But a development bank does not create free money.

It needs capital. It needs professional management. It needs independent credit decisions, transparent lending criteria, rigorous underwriting and a clear system for measuring risk and return.

Most importantly, it needs the ability to say no.

If lending decisions become politically influenced, if companies receive credit because they are strategically favoured rather than commercially viable, or if bad loans are repeatedly refinanced to avoid recognising losses, the institution risks becoming a mechanism for transferring private business failures onto the public balance sheet.

That is precisely the kind of institutional weakness Serbia should be trying to avoid.

A development bank should be judged by the quality of the businesses it finances, the productivity it helps create, the loans it successfully recovers and the economic value of the projects it supports.

It should not be judged by how much money it distributes.

The historical experience of Yugoslavia is relevant here. Its financial system became deeply entangled with enterprise financing and political-economic priorities. Banks were not always independent institutions imposing commercial discipline. They could become channels through which the financial problems of enterprises were carried into the wider system.

Serbia does not need a new institution that repeats those mistakes under a different name.

It needs a development bank with safeguards strong enough to resist political pressure.

PROGRESSIVE TAXATION: FAIRNESS CANNOT COME AT THE EXPENSE OF INVESTMENT

The Student Blockade proposes a more progressive personal income tax system, a higher tax-free portion of wages and a greater emphasis on taxing large assets rather than labour.

The programme, as reported, envisages raising the tax-free portion of wages from 23 to 35 per cent of the average wage, introducing additional income-tax brackets and abolishing the annual personal income tax.

These proposals deserve a detailed fiscal assessment.

A tax system should be fair. Lower-paid workers should not carry a disproportionate burden, and a government has a legitimate interest in ensuring that those with greater financial capacity contribute appropriately.

But tax reform must also consider investment incentives, business formation, entrepreneurship and the competitiveness of the economy.

If the government reduces taxes on some forms of labour income, it must identify how the resulting revenue shortfall will be financed. If it increases taxation on assets, it must explain precisely which assets, at what rates, under what valuation rules and with what protections against unintended consequences.

A tax system that looks fair in a campaign document can become damaging if it discourages productive investment or creates uncertainty about the future tax treatment of capital.

The question is not whether Serbia should have a fairer tax system. It should.

The question is whether the Student List has a credible fiscal plan demonstrating that its proposed changes can be implemented without undermining investment, public finances or the country's ability to finance essential services.

STATE OWNERSHIP IS NOT A BUSINESS STRATEGY

The Student Blockade's position on strategic enterprises deserves particular scrutiny because it goes to the heart of the movement's economic philosophy.

A state-owned energy company, railway or essential infrastructure provider can serve a legitimate public purpose. There are sectors where national security, network infrastructure and public-service obligations justify continued public ownership.

But the state must still operate those companies according to clear commercial and governance principles.

Who appoints their management? How are directors selected? Are appointments based on professional qualifications or political relationships? Are financial statements independently audited? Are investment decisions evaluated against measurable returns? Can an unprofitable operation be restructured? Can a failing business be allowed to exit?

If political considerations prevent those decisions, the taxpayer becomes the ultimate guarantor.

Serbia already has experience with the financial consequences of poorly governed public enterprises. The BTI 2026 Serbia report describes the continued importance of state-owned companies in strategic sectors and notes that political control, subsidies and incomplete governance reforms remain concerns. It also records that a substantial number of state-owned enterprises reported losses.

The Student List cannot solve this problem simply by promising better appointments.

It must establish enforceable rules that separate political authority from commercial management.

A professional state-owned enterprise should be expected to publish its financial performance, disclose public subsidies, operate under transparent procurement rules and demonstrate that its investment decisions serve a measurable public or commercial purpose.

If the company cannot meet those standards, its strategic status should not become an excuse for unlimited financial support.

The state should protect the national interest. It should not protect bad management.

THE DINAR, FOREIGN CAPITAL AND THE REALITY OF EXTERNAL FINANCING

The promise of currency stability is another important element of the programme.

A stable dinar matters to households, businesses, importers, exporters and investors. But exchange-rate stability is not achieved through political declarations.

It depends on monetary policy, foreign-exchange reserves, capital flows, exports, imports, external borrowing, remittances and confidence in the country's economic institutions.

Serbia imports energy, machinery, equipment and a substantial range of industrial inputs. If its export capacity weakens while its dependence on imported goods remains high, the country can face greater external financing pressures.

If foreign investors become less willing to commit new capital, the consequences may extend beyond employment. Foreign direct investment can also bring foreign currency, technology, access to international supply chains and export capacity.

A weaker investment environment does not automatically cause a currency crisis, but it can make the task of maintaining external stability more difficult if other sources of foreign currency do not compensate.

The government must explain how it intends to maintain a competitive export sector, attract long-term capital and preserve monetary stability while changing the country's investment model.

A promise of a stable currency is not an economic strategy. It is an objective that must be supported by the performance of the entire economy.

PUBLIC PROJECTS: TRANSPARENCY IS NECESSARY, BUT CANCELLATION IS NOT FREE

The Student's  has also promised greater transparency in public contracts, the publication of loan terms and the use of national price benchmarks for public projects.

These are reasonable objectives.

Public contracts should be transparent. Borrowing terms should be disclosed. Taxpayers deserve to know how much infrastructure costs, who receives the contracts and whether projects deliver the promised results.

But the introduction of reference prices cannot be treated as a substitute for proper engineering, procurement and financial analysis.

Construction costs depend on geography, geology, materials, labour, financing, design complexity, environmental requirements and contractual risk.

A benchmark can help identify suspiciously high prices. It cannot automatically establish that every project above a predetermined figure is overpriced.

The proposed review of special laws and major infrastructure projects also needs careful handling.

Reviewing contracts may expose poor procurement, excessive costs or political favouritism. But cancelling or renegotiating agreements can create compensation claims, arbitration, delays and additional costs.

A new administration cannot simply assume that terminating an existing contract produces savings.

It must publish the legal basis, the financial implications and the alternative plan.

Transparency is essential. So is competence.

text:
🇷🇺 🇺🇦 Putin offered a "humanitarian mission" in a Donbas city his army has not taken. Zelensky calls it "an absolutely primitive move"

Vladimir Putin's latest proposal reached Kyiv through American hands. Volodymyr Zelensky says US negotiators passed on Putin's offer of a temporary "humanitarian mission" in Kostiantynivka, a Ukrainian-held city in Donetsk where fighting is now going on inside the town. Putin made the offer to envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Thursday.

Zelensky says it is a way to take the city without winning the battle for it. "It's an absolutely primitive move, because otherwise he has no way of taking this city," he told journalists, in remarks published Saturday by the Kyiv Independent. A pause, he argued, would let Russian troops move into better positions. "If we give up Kostiantynivka, their next steps will be our other cities in Donbas."

He said he explained Kyiv's position to the Americans, who replied that they understood. He also pointed out what Moscow did not offer. Ukraine gave the US side a list of seven or eight blockaded settlements where civilians, including children, remain, among them villages near Oleshky. Russia proposed no humanitarian operation for any of them. "Why? Because after Kostiantynivka come Kramatorsk and Sloviansk," Zelensky said.

Kyiv has a recent precedent in mind. A presidential adviser, Dmytro Lytvyn, said Russia's earlier humanitarian pause in Oleshky, in Kherson, was used to rotate troops and bring in more personnel. Ukraine's General Staff has said the same about that ceasefire.

Putin claims Russia already controls Kostiantynivka. Ukraine's General Staff says its forces are still fighting Russian infantry groups trying to infiltrate the town. Kyiv's argument is simple: a city already in Russian hands would not need a pause.

The episode shows the shape of the talks. Every humanitarian or ceasefire idea now comes with a map attached, and Washington is carrying Moscow's proposals to Kyiv. Zelensky's answer this time was a flat no.

text:
Hebrews 10
 
New International Version
Christ’s Sacrifice Once for All
10 The law is only a shadow of the good things that are coming—not the realities themselves. For this reason it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. 2 Otherwise, would they not have stopped being offered? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt guilty for their sins. 3 But those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins. 4 It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

5 Therefore, when Christ came into the world, he said:

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,
    but a body you prepared for me;
6 with burnt offerings and sin offerings
    you were not pleased.
7 Then I said, ‘Here I am—it is written about me in the scroll—
    I have come to do your will, my God.’”[a]

8 First he said, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not desire, nor were you pleased with them”—though they were offered in accordance with the law. 9 Then he said, “Here I am, I have come to do your will.” He sets aside the first to establish the second. 10 And by that will, we have been made holy through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

11 Day after day every priest stands and performs his religious duties; again and again he offers the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. 12 But when this priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, 13 and since that time he waits for his enemies to be made his footstool. 14 For by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy.

15 The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First he says:

16 “This is the covenant I will make with them
    after that time, says the Lord.
I will put my laws in their hearts,
    and I will write them on their minds.”[b]

17 Then he adds:

“Their sins and lawless acts
    I will remember no more.”[c]

18 And where these have been forgiven, sacrifice for sin is no longer necessary.

text:
People spend thousands of dollars every year traveling to places where they can enjoy beautiful weather, outdoor dining, beaches, boating, and an active social life. 

In South Florida, those experiences can be part of your ordinary routine.

You can exercise outdoors year-round. Entertain friends at home. Spend weekends on the water.

And for many people, work remotely while enjoying an environment that others save up all year to visit.

Now consider the financial implications.

How much do you spend escaping the city where you live? How much time do you lose traveling back and forth? How much more productive, social, or creative could you be if your everyday environment already offered the lifestyle you wanted?

Of course, Miami isn’t inexpensive, and not everyone values the same things.

But the traditional cost-of-living calculation misses something important. 👀

Your time, energy, relationships, and enjoyment of life are economic resources too.

A beautiful life isn’t necessarily a distraction from building wealth!

Sometimes it’s the critical ingredient for building wealth and a life you love. ☀️ Happy Saturday!!

text:
OPEN HEAVENS DEVOTIONAL 

DATE: SUNDAY NOVEMBER 15TH 2026.

TOPIC: BAPTISED WITH FIRE

MEMORISE
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire: - (Matthew 3:11)

BIBLE READING: MALACHI 3:1-4 (KJV)

1 Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the Lord of hosts.

2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:

3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the Lord an offering in righteousness.

4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the Lord, as in the days of old, and as in former years.

MESSAGE

Anyone whom God wants to use as His vessel must be baptised, note not only with the Holy Ghost, but also with fire. Fire has many functions, one of which is that it purifies. In Isaiah 6:5, after Isaiah realised how unclean he was, the angel of the Lord used a live coal to touch his lips and said, "This hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged" (Isaiah 6:6-7). Isaiah received a baptism of fire that cleansed him and made him a useful and worthy vessel to carry out God's assignment.

Before the apostles were sent out to proclaim the gospel of Christ around the world, Jesus instructed them to wait for the baptism of the Holy Ghost, as we see in Acts 1:4-5:

And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me. For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.

They obeyed this instruction, and they were baptised by the Holy Spirit and fire in Acts 2. This encounter marked the beginning of their exploits for Jesus, starting with Peter's sermon, which God used to save about 3,000 souls that same day. If you want to be a worthy vessel in God's hands, you must allow Him to set you apart and baptise you with the Holy Ghost and fire.

Beloved, God is still looking for vessels He can purify with fire and put to use in His vineyard. Today's Bible reading tells us that God is a refiner and purifier of those who will serve Him in righteousness. Until the Lord refines you with His fire, your offering cannot be pleasant to Him. Offering in this context means your life. Gold in its raw state is not beautiful, but after it has been purified by fire, it becomes precious. This is why it is called a precious metal. If you don't want to remain a common vessel in God's vineyard, ask Him to visit you with His fire. Allow His fire to take away any filth in your life that will not allow you to be useful and precious in His sight. If you really want to be a useful vessel for God, pray today's prayer point with all your heart. 

PRAYER POINT
Father, I am ready; please, let Your fire fall on me.

Look at you. You spend paragraphs whining about me supposedly using AI, only to paste another clumsy, emotionally charged AI-generated script yourself, complete with robotic formatting, bullet points, and juvenile, desperate filler lines like "I just finished you."

The irony is staggering. You literally switch back and forth between broken, frantic colloquialisms and structured AI bullet points, completely exposing yourself as a hypocrite who relies on an artificial assistant while crying wolf. You are so rattled, emotionally compromised, and cornered that you have abandoned any pretense of academic rigor, resorting to insults because your entire theological foundation has evaporated under scrutiny.

This isn't about ego; it’s about the truth. You are attempting to bar people from the path of salvation through deception and misguidance. Let’s systematically dismantle every single one of your flailing points and expose the utter bankruptcy of your arguments.

1. Paul’s Apostolate, False Prophecies, and the End-Time Prophecy (Sahih Muslim 2953b)
You defend Paul by claiming an apostle doesn't need to be a direct eyewitness, and you throw a tantrum about a Hadith in Sahih Muslim 2953b regarding the Hour.

The Biblical Definition of an Apostle: In Acts 1:21–22, when the remaining disciples gathered to replace Judas, Peter explicitly laid down the rule for an apostle: he must have been a companion from the baptism of John until the ascension. Paul met none of these criteria. He appointed himself based on a private, unverified vision on the road to Damascus.

The Misrepresentation of Sahih Muslim 2953b: You desperately quote a narration where the Prophet ﷺ looked at a young boy and remarked that if he lived a normal lifespan, the Last Hour might come upon them before he grew very old.
In Islamic eschatology, "the Hour" (As-Sa'ah) has both a major and a minor meaning. The minor resurrection—death—comes to every human generation within a lifetime (as every generation passes away). Classical commentators like Imam An-Nawawi explicitly explain that this refers to the passing of that generation and their entry into the afterlife, not a failed prediction of the cosmic end of the universe.
Meanwhile, Paul made explicit, falsifiable predictions about the literal end of the world occurring during his own lifetime, telling his followers that they would remain alive until the physical return of Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:15–17, 1 Corinthians 15:51–52). Paul died 2,000 years ago; his prophecy failed completely, making him a false prophet by biblical definition (Deuteronomy 18:22).

2. Blood Atonement, Deuteronomy 12, and the "Visions" Red Herring: You try to defend blood atonement using Leviticus and claim God never banned sacrifices in Deuteronomy 12:13, while scoffing at whether visions exist in Islam.

Deuteronomy 12:13 Context: You completely failed reading comprehension. Deuteronomy 12:13 does not ban sacrifices; it commands that sacrifices must only be offered at the single centralized place God chooses (the Temple in Jerusalem), explicitly prohibiting pagan-style animal slaughter everywhere else. Meanwhile, the Prophets repeatedly declared that God desires mercy and obedience, not animal blood (Psalm 50:12–14, Hosea 6:6, Jeremiah 7:22–23). The entire Pauline theology of human blood atonement completely contradicts the overarching prophetic message of the Hebrew Bible.
Visions in Islam: You mockingly ask if visions, dreams, and spiritual experiences are obtainable in Islam. Let me answer you directly: yes, absolutely. By the grace of Allah (SWT), I have personally experienced true visions and celestial sights over the past 13 years. Authentic spirituality, spiritual clarity (Firasah), and true dream visions (Ru'ya Sadiqah) are vibrant realities in Islam, experienced by millions of believers worldwide. I have even seen the Prophet (PBUH) in a dream. Unlike Christianity, all of this occurs without the need to invent a new religion or corrupt the worship of the One True God—the very same God of the Old and New Testaments. To claim Muhammad is a false prophet is a clear example of denial, as his prophecy confirms all prior revelations and calls humanity to worship God alone. Ultimately, the ubiquitous nature of Satan’s grasp on the misguided, and their submission to it, is what blinds you and the masses.

3. Song of Solomon 5:16: Denying Sister Semitic Linguistics: You claim Mahmad and Machmaddim are two different words, mock the context, and claim people named Muhammad existed before Islam.

Basic Linguistics: Hebrew and Arabic are sister Semitic languages that share the exact same trilateral consonantal root system (M-H-M-D / ح-م-د). The Hebrew noun mahmad (מַחְמָד) means "desirable, lovely, praised one." Adding the Hebrew plural of majesty suffix -im gives mahamaddim. To deny that Mahamaddim in Song of Solomon 5:16 shares the exact same root and semantic meaning as the proper name Muhammad is linguistic illiteracy born out of sheer desperation to protect your fragile worldview.
The Context of Prophetic Typology: Jewish and Christian scholars routinely read biblical texts through allegorical and prophetic lenses. When the text describes the beloved as Mahamaddim ("altogether lovely/praised") alongside physical and behavioral descriptions, it points directly to the final praised one. Your denial changes nothing about the undeniable etymological match.

4. Deuteronomy 18:18: The Tribal Fallacy and the Abrahamic Covenant: You argue that Deuteronomy 18 was addressed exclusively to the Levites, and you throw Genesis 17:21 at me claiming the covenant was exclusively with Isaac, not Ishmael.

Who Was Deuteronomy 18 Addressed To? Deuteronomy 18:15 explicitly states: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brethren..." In biblical grammar, if the prophet was supposed to rise from within the Israelites themselves (the Levites or Israelites proper), the text would say "from among yourselves," not "from among your brethren" (mi-qereb acheichem). The Bible consistently uses "brethren" to describe closely related nations—specifically the Ishmaelites (the brethren of the Israelites, Genesis 16:12, Genesis 25:18).
The Blessing of Ishmael: God explicitly promised Abraham regarding Ishmael: "As for Ishmael, I have heard you: I will surely bless him; I will make him fruitful and will greatly increase his numbers. He will be the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation" (Genesis 17:20). While the spiritual/theological covenant of lineage passed through Isaac for a time, God’s explicit promise to make Ishmael a "great nation" was fulfilled through the rise of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who emerged directly from the lineage of Ishmael through Kedar, establishing the greatest global civilization of absolute monotheism in history.

5. Isaiah 42:11: Twisting the Geography of Kedar and Sela: You dismiss Isaiah 42:11 by claiming the praise is global and trying to erase Kedar and Sela from Arabia.

Geography Does Not Lie: Isaiah 42 explicitly names the specific geographic locations where the Servant's praise will erupt: the tents of Kedar (the historic Arab tribes of the Hijaz descended from Ishmael) and the inhabitants of Sela (Mount Sela, the literal mountain in Medina, Saudi Arabia, where the Ansar welcomed the Prophet ﷺ with songs of praise). Trying to strip these indigenous ancient Arabian place names of their geographical reality to avoid the obvious conclusion is intellectual dishonesty.

6. Textual Preservation, the Holy Spirit, and the Corruption of the Bible: You claim the Bible is the "longest preserved book ever" and mock the Islamic view of scripture corruption.

The Reality of Biblical Manuscripts: As established by leading textual critics (like Dr. Bruce Metzger and Dr. Bart Ehrman), there is not a single original autograph of any book of the Bible in existence. The oldest complete New Testament manuscripts—such as Codex Sinaiticus (c. 370 AD)—contain over 23,000 scribal alterations, corrections, and missing passages. Whole core doctrines, such as the Trinitarian formula in 1 John 5:7–8 (The Comma Johanneum), were proven to be late medieval forgeries and have been quietly excised from modern Bibles by Christian scholars themselves!
The Divine Protection of the Quran: Contrast this with the Quran. Under the meticulous supervision of Caliph Uthman and the Prophet’s chief scribes, the master text was compiled directly from verified primary materials backed by mass oral preservation (Hifz). Today, peer-reviewed radiocarbon dating from independent scientific bodies—including the University of Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, ETH Zürich, and the University of Tübingen—has scientifically verified that 7th-century Quranic manuscripts (such as the Birmingham Quran manuscript) match the exact text we recite today down to the letter.

7. The Pre-Ordained Plan (Qadar) and the Final Criterion (Muhaymin). You demand to know why Allah allowed previous scriptures to be altered, citing Surah 5:44 and 5:48 out of context.

The Wisdom of Divine Decree (Al-Qadar): The Torah and Gospel were given as specific, regional covenants entrusted to past communities, who failed to safeguard them, allowing human hands, political redactions, and pagan assimilation (such as the Roman imperial merger that birthed modern Trinitarianism) to alter the text. To conclude you have exhausted every deflection, hidden behind an AI-generated copy-paste script, insulted grammar while butchering your own logic, and run away from the hard scientific and historical facts of manuscript corruption.

text:
At 16, Brian Banks was one of the best high school linebackers in America. USC had offered him a full scholarship. Pete Carroll personally called him.

One afternoon at school he made out with a classmate. Consensual. By the end of the day he was in jail, charged with kidnapping and rape.

She said he dragged her into a stairwell. It never happened.

The DNA came back negative. His mother sold her house and her car to pay for a lawyer.

He couldn’t make bail. He spent a year behind bars waiting for trial.

His lawyer told him: plead no contest, or risk 41 years in prison. He was 17. He took the deal.

He did 5 years in prison. Then 5 more on parole. Registered sex offender. GPS monitor on his ankle. Couldn’t go near schools or parks. No one would hire him.

Meanwhile, the girl and her mother sued the school district for not keeping her safe. They won $1.5 million.

In 2011, a Facebook friend request popped up on his screen.

It was her.

She wanted to “let bygones be bygones.”

Brian went to a private investigator. They hid cameras in the office and invited her to talk. She came by bus.

On tape, she admitted it. He never raped her. He never kidnapped her.

Then she said she still wouldn’t tell prosecutors the truth. Because she’d have to give back the money.

In May 2012, a judge cleared his name. The hearing took less than a minute.

10 years of his life. Gone in one lie. Erased in 60 seconds.

A few days later his phone rang. “I’m looking for a linebacker. You know where I can find one?”

It was Pete Carroll. The same coach who recruited him 10 years earlier.

He finally signed with the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons. At 27. The dream he had at 16.

She was ordered to pay $2.6 million back.

What should happen to someone who steals 10 years of your life with one lie? https://t.co/9zpJ2GiLhn

text:
Nvidia has approached Arm's chief Rene Haas to replace Jensen Huang, the FT reports. Some employees want Huang back instead

Nvidia's search for a new CEO has a first named target. The company's board approached Rene Haas, chief executive of British chip designer Arm, as a possible successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported. Haas is one of several candidates, and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or take it, according to the FT.

Nvidia's board says it is still choosing a search firm and has not formally engaged anyone. "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature," it said. Arm declined to comment.

Haas knows the company. He spent seven years at Nvidia, rising to run its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm's CEO in 2022 and took it public in 2023. "Rene is one of few external candidates who wouldn't need to be brought up to speed on Nvidia," said Shay Boloor of Futurum Equities.

Not everyone inside wants a successor. Wired reported that a longtime Nvidia engineer posted internally urging the board to weigh employee sentiment, and the post drew more than 1,600 comments, several pushing to bring Huang back. Elon Musk said on X that he would sign a petition to reinstate Huang. Reuters could not verify those reports.

Huang quit on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, one involving a suspected Chinese spy whose former company is under scrutiny for allegedly diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China. China calls the allegations baseless. Nvidia lost about 573 billion dollars in market value over the week, Reuters calculated. Colette Kress, the finance chief, is interim CEO.

That is the real stake. Huang personally handled Nvidia's export fights with Washington and its China business. Whoever replaces him inherits those fights with a Congress that wants tighter chip controls. Other names floated by analysts include AMD's Lisa Su and Nvidia's own CUDA chief Ian Buck. Trump suggested Tim Cook.

🇺🇦 Zelensky clears top security officials named on drug-cartel wiretaps, and warns the Russian-linked cartel is moving into Poland and Germany

Ukraine's biggest corruption scandal of the fall has a new turn. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that anti-corruption investigators told him several senior officials whose names came up on wiretaps in the "Operation Carthage" probe have no ties to the criminal network.

According to Ukrinform, Zelensky named Ihor Klymenko, Ivan Vyhivskyi and SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad, as well as Health Minister Viktor Liashko and ruling-party faction leader David Arakhamia. "I asked representatives of NABU and SAPO about the surnames heard on the tapes: 'Do you have anything on them?' 'No,'" he said. He added: "The story is very unpleasant, very wrong. But there is an investigation, and I support this investigation. And there will be further personnel changes." Those assurances come from Zelensky. NABU and SAPO have not published such findings themselves.

The probe, disclosed on Nov. 4, alleges officials in the SBU, the National Police and the Prosecutor General's Office protected fraud call centers, drug trafficking, counterfeit currency and illegal tobacco in return for payoffs. NABU says the network was run by a Russian national with FSB ties, code-named "Mexican," who founded the Khimprom synthetic drug cartel. An SBU major general arrested in the case was released on Friday after his 65 million hryvnia bail, about 1.5 million dollars, was posted, his lawyer said largely with money from SBU staff.

Zelensky's warning was aimed at Europe. "They have already entered Poland, and they are trying to enter Germany," he said of the cartel, and claimed it "does not operate without the support of special services, and not only Russian ones." He did not say which other services, and offered no public evidence.

For Ukraine's partners, the timing matters. Kyiv is asking Europe for tens of billions while negotiating with Moscow through Washington, and a scandal reaching into the security services is the kind of story donors notice. https://t.co/6z0PB6QQGK

text:
Anthony Teso Unsubscribe

11:28 AM (2 hours ago)

to Tempest
📷
The National Committee returned to the question a week after the vote. Its editorial declines the celebration on offer that same week in Democratic Left, and it concedes a significant deal. DSA-aligned candidates ran behind the centrists. Many of the newly elected joined recently and may see the label as a route to office. The socialists going to Washington will be a minority that the leadership does not need in order to pass anything. The executive office has contained every progressive who won it on the Democratic line, from Katie Wilson in Seattle to Brandon Johnson in Chicago to Mamdani. I have nothing to add to that account, and anyone in DSA still arguing for the governing-power road should have to answer it.
The strategy follows. There are two fronts: defense against an administration that is wounded and still dangerous, and a campaign to “force the Democrats” to restore Medicaid funding now and to enact Medicare for All and the abolition of ICE later. A workers’ party is to come out of that fight.
The editorial’s own analysis takes the lever away. It reports that the Democrats lack a veto-proof majority and expects Trump to veto nearly everything they send him. It says the balance of class forces still favors the ruling class, that socialist sentiment is unorganized at work sites and in communities, and that no movement of the last two decades has frightened capital into concessions. Forcing requires a force. The editorial describes that force as missing and then assigns it a legislative program.
Then there is the agent. The defeat of Trump is credited to a “mass, cross-class resistance,” and the return to the Democrats is treated as a danger that might derail it. But the vote was the resistance in action. The people who protested for two years went to the polls and elected Democrats, most of whom, by the editorial’s own description, are pro-capitalist centrists. A cross-class movement produced a cross-class result. The National Committee names the composition in three words and never asks what it implies for a movement expected to carry the next stage.
Every demand in the piece has the same addressee.
Mass protest is to keep Hakeem Jeffries out of the Speaker’s chair. Medicaid is to be restored by Democrats under pressure. Howard Zinn is brought in to say that what counts is who is sitting outside the White House. The movement stays in the street, and the party inside the building remains the thing that acts. The editorial condemns the old cycle in which insurgents vote Democratic and wait. Marching and waiting is a shorter version of it.
Who, finally, is “we”? The pronoun covers Tempest, the Left, the unions and the social movements, sometimes inside one paragraph. So the call for “a party of our own” arrives without an author. A militant minority is supposed to cohere in the process. The editorial does not say who coheres it, around what literature, or in relation to the DSA members who will watch six new socialist representatives vote on appropriations, ICE, and the war. Those members are told to abandon their strategy. Nobody proposes to argue with them while they find out what it yields.
Draper’s political center was designed for this situation. In the papers of 1971 and 1973, it is a publication and an editorial board producing a body of literature, with no membership discipline, whose readers take its views into the places where they already work and organize. His model was Iskra, whose readers were Iskraists before there was a party for them to join. Tempest has the publication. What the November editorial shows is a publication addressing the Left in general, and I do not think that addressee exists.
I do not know how many DSA members read Tempest. The case for a center depends on that number, and the National Committee could fairly say the readership is too small to bear the weight. It is still a question the Committee can answer and has not asked.
The first test is close. The House elects its Speaker in January, and by the editorial’s own report, AOC has already pledged her vote to Jeffries.

text:
Putin Wants to Divide Europe Again. Europe Should Tell Him to Go Fuck Himself.

How should Europe respond to the Kremlin's latest imperial demands? Simple. Tell that balding little Kremlin bastard and his entire gang to go fuck themselves — straight in the direction of the Russian warship. According to a report attributed to The New York Times, Moscow has proposed returning to the Cold War system of dividing Europe into spheres of influence. The Kremlin apparently dreams of resurrecting something resembling the Warsaw Pact, forcing NATO back to its 1997 positions, and giving Russia the right to dictate the future of independent European nations. In other words, Putin wants to turn the clock back 80 years and have Washington recognize his imaginary empire.

The demands are breathtaking in their arrogance. Ukraine must surrender territory, abandon NATO, and weaken its armed forces. Finland, the Baltic states, Moldova, and other European countries are supposed to accept Moscow's interference in their sovereign decisions. Sixteen NATO members would effectively be told that their security arrangements are subject to Russian approval. And all this is being presented as some magnificent new architecture of European security. The Kremlin calls it indivisible security. I call it the geopolitical fantasies of an aging dictator who still cannot accept that the Soviet Union is dead, the Warsaw Pact is buried, and Eastern Europe is no longer Moscow's private prison.

But the most outrageous part is the very assumption that Europe can be divided between Washington and Moscow without asking Europeans themselves. Who the hell gave Putin the right to decide Poland's future? Who authorized the Kremlin to dictate Finland's security policy? Why should the Baltic nations, which spent decades escaping Russian imperial domination, suddenly accept another arrangement negotiated over their heads? Europe is not a collection of territories waiting to be distributed between great powers. These are sovereign countries with their own governments, armies, citizens, and democratic institutions. The fact that Moscow still thinks otherwise tells us everything we need to know about the nature of Putin's regime.

Europe's answer must be brutally simple: no territorial concessions imposed on Ukraine, no Russian veto over NATO membership, no withdrawal of Allied forces to satisfy Kremlin fantasies, and absolutely no negotiations about Europe's future without Europe. Strengthen European armies, expand military production, arm Ukraine, and make Russian aggression increasingly expensive. Putin understands strength far better than diplomatic courtesy. Every attempt to appease him has only encouraged further demands. He wants another Yalta, another Warsaw Pact, another generation of European nations living under Moscow's boot. Europe should give him precisely what the defenders of Snake Island offered the Russian warship.

Russian imperialism can go fuck itself. Europe belongs to Europeans. Ukraine belongs to Ukrainians. And Putin can take his spheres of influence straight to hell.

P.S. I am a Ukrainian war veteran who served in the 54th Mechanized Brigade. After leaving Twitter/X, I moved my independent journalism to Substack. My family and I are living in Canada, where we are struggling with the costs of maintaining an old, poorly insulated house and keeping it warm through the winter. So, of course, this is a logistical nightmare. More than 200,000 people go through this airport every day. You can imagine a big portion of those have been affected and we'll have to continue to deal with the situation as the day progresses.

Wolf Blitzer: I want to bring in Stephen Wallace right now. the former director of access. over at the FAA. He's here with me in Washington. What jumped out at you?

Steven Wallace: Well, the first thing that jumped out at me is that we are discussing this matter as a major, major inconvenience, which it was. And we're not discussing it as a critical safety issue. We're not discussing it as a tragedy. So. the system worked. I mean, if the worst result is a major inconvenience and headache and cost, that's still better than anything tragic happening. I mean, the operators are of the system, the air traffic controllers, the airlines. Everybody in this business. is pretty conservative.

Wolf Blitzer: But we did repeatedly hear from Sean Duffy, the Transportation Secretary, safety is paramount. That's priority number one, to make sure the people who fly are safe and are not gonna get killed in the process of taking a trip to go see a grandmother or go to a wedding or go for business or whatever. Safety is paramount. We kept hearing that and that's. originally requested to improve all the technology, get rid of the technology of the '60s, '70s, and '80s and bring it up to date, you know, move it from copper to wire and all of that. But he's going to need $50 billion, and he's asking Congress to approve that money right now. What do you say?

Steven Wallace: I agree with him. And safety is the top priority. And what he said also in this was, we don't want to piecemeal this. Let's not piecemeal this. Build it safely, but build it fast. And this discussion has been going on for decades. I think it's gaining critical momentum. and the FAA administrator, Brian. one point, I took notes, he said and I'm quoting him now, "It will continue these problems with air safety and everything. It will continue to break until we replace it." So he's also making the case that they have to modernize all of this equipment around the country to make sure it's safe. Do you agree? Absolutely. and people in this business have been saying... I mean, you know, we have the biggest system in the world. We operate, airlines operate 28,000 flights a day. The FAA manages 45,000 flights a day 'cause of general aviation and military. So, and you know, most passengers just take their safety for granted. And the system is wonderful. those of us in the business never take it for granted.

Wolf Blitzer: And we did hear from Sean Duffy the Transportation Secretary saying this was not a cyber security threat no foreign actors were involved at least that's the assessment right now.

Steven Wallace: yes I I've heard that from from day one yesterday and and I have

Wolf Blitzer: I'm quoting now, "The worst is behind us." That's what we just heard from federal officials as thousands of travelers across the country are still facing delays and uncertainty after an FAA ground stop of aviation. Chris Sununu is joining us right now. He's the president and CEO of Airlines for America, the former governor of New Hampshire. Governor, thanks so much for joining us. Let me start with your reaction to the news. conference that we just heard.

Chris Sununu: Well, the good news is, again, as you just said, the worst is behind us. I think the backlog of nearly 9000 cancellations yesterday, it's down to a couple 1000 today, because again, they're trying to move equipment and crews into place. And so for the customers out there, right, whether you are stranded, or you have an upcoming piece of travel, have confidence in the system aid that it is safe, of course. and B, that it's back online and people should be comfortable as they kind of book into that holiday season.

Wolf Blitzer: You think, Governor, from the airlines' perspective, that there's still confidence in the leadership of Secretary Duffy and Administrator Brian Bedford?

Chris Sununu: 100%. Oh, unquestionable. Look, as soon as this issue happened, we were on the phone, all the CEOs, myself, the folks from across the. on the phone with Brian Bedford. He was communicating everything that was happening in real time as they understood it. Because we've been with them kind of hand in glove through this whole process of upgrading and modernizing the system, there was a pretty good understanding of what might be happening. Was it the routers, basically a new piece of technology, not working very well with and peace of old technology along those old copper lines as they're being replaced. So because they've been so transparent in the process to date, it allowed the conversation and understanding of what was happening just a lot easier. And within two hours, they had the ground stop lifted and the ground stop was the right thing. When you're not a hundred percent sure what's happening, you make sure everyone's safe, you take a pause on the system. And then within a couple hours, they had everybody up and running again, which was terrific. Obviously a traffic jam, big hassle for a lot of the customers, But no, through this-- do you think uh governor another 50 billion dollars in additional funding is enough to fix all these problems yes look that that's the amazing part you know 50 billion sounds like this massive number but when you're looking at rebuilding the entire air traffic control infrastructure, as well as airports and towers and runways. It's less than 5% of what we put every year into defense. It is a fraction, it is a tiny fraction. And so the return on investment is huge, but they've laid it out so carefully in terms of radar systems, radios, surface awareness systems, the new cooperative fiber, the routers, the terrible old towers, digitizing towers, the new simulators that are gonna come on board to help air traffic controllers get on board. And the big piece next. takes all the different systems that are out there and gets them talking on the same language. So it's a big undertaking. They're moving incredibly fast. I mean, the fact that we have folks from the press asking, are you going too fast? No one's ever asked the government, are you going too fast, right? But they are moving at light speed as they need to, because we're so far behind the eight ball. This should have been done. So, you know, is that enough? Yes, we absolutely believe it is. We believe it more than covers the technology. It absolutely covers the airports and some of the new expansion projects that are out there, all in the name of a safe, much more efficient, and much more customer friendly system.

Wolf Blitzer: Yeah, and safety for the passengers and the flight crews and everyone else is priority number one. what is an incident like this wind up both operationally and financially?

Chris Sununu: Financially, we're looking at about $250 million just last night. I mean, it really hits hard because now we're moving passengers, we're making sure they get hotels, we're finding other ways to get there. We're trying to put folks on planes. Some of the passengers get compensated if they get bumped on planes. So we have a waiver process for all of our passengers in that process. in one night when you Oh, and by the way, we're getting crushed with fuel prices. By the way, we're getting crushed with other regulatory issues. So there's a huge cost here along the line. And what we don't want to do is see that fall down to the customer, right? We're trying to stay that, keep that competition, keep the prices at a very sensible rate. As we go into the holiday season, knowing all of America is dealing with affordability constraints. And so issues like last night are tough, but we can get through it. And again, the customer comes first in terms of providing the opportunity.

Wolf Blitzer: And thousands of flights are still being delayed and thousands are being canceled, even as we speak. Former Governor Krista Nunez, thanks very much for your expertise.
